title: Metals - properties
subject: chem
definition: A metal is a class of element that can be recognised by a set of special physical properties. After learning in earlier work that every material has properties such as hardness, flexibility and transparency, you now meet the idea of classification at the level of elements. The simplest forms of matter are called elements, and one of the most useful ways of sorting elements is to decide whether they behave as metals or as non-metals. In this node we look only at metals. A metal usually has a bright, shiny surface called lustre. Polished gold, freshly cleaned copper and a new aluminium vessel all show this characteristic metallic shine. Most metals allow heat and electricity to move through them easily; this is called conductivity, and it is the reason copper and aluminium are used for electrical wires and why cooking pans made of iron or aluminium heat up quickly. Metals can be beaten into thin sheets without breaking; this property is called malleability. Goldsmiths beat gold into very thin leaf to cover temple idols, and blacksmiths flatten iron nails on anvils. Metals can also be drawn into thin wires; this property is called ductility. Copper wires carry current in homes, and aluminium wires are used in overhead power cables. When a metal piece is struck or dropped, it gives a ringing sound; this is called sonority, and it is the reason bells are often made of metals such as bronze. Most metals have high melting points and high boiling points, though there are differences. Iron melts at about 1538 degrees Celsius, while the metal zinc melts at a much lower 419 degrees Celsius and lead at only 327 degrees Celsius. Density is the mass contained in a given volume; iron is dense, but aluminium is light for the same volume, which is why aluminium is chosen for aircraft parts. Strength is the ability to resist being broken or bent; iron and steel are used for bridges, railway tracks and building frames because they are strong. We can therefore classify an element as a metal if it shows a combination of properties such as lustre, conductivity, malleability, ductility, sonority, high melting and boiling points, high density and great strength. The common metals you must remember are iron, gold, copper, aluminium, zinc, lead and magnesium. Iron is used for tools, machines and construction; gold is used for jewellery and decorative work; copper is used for electrical wires and utensils; aluminium is used for foil, aircraft bodies and kitchenware; zinc is used to coat iron to prevent rusting later and in alloys; lead is used in batteries; and magnesium is used in fireworks and light alloys. In the laboratory you can show these properties by activities such as beating a metal strip with a hammer to show malleability, connecting a metal wire into an electric circuit to show conductivity, and dropping a small metal piece on a hard surface to hear its ringing sound, which shows sonority.
eli5: Metals are a special group of elements. They usually shine, let electricity and heat pass through them, can be hammered into flat sheets or pulled into wires, and make a ringing sound when dropped. Iron, gold, copper and aluminium are some common metals we use every day.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the main physical properties used to decide whether an element is a metal. For each property, give one clear Indian or everyday example of a metal and the object in which it is used.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The main physical properties used to classify an element as a metal are lustre, conductivity of heat and electricity, malleability, ductility, sonority, high melting point, high boiling point, high density and strength. Lustre is the shining surface of a metal; gold ornaments worn during Indian festivals and polished copper vessels in the kitchen both show lustre. Conductivity is the ability to allow heat and electricity to pass through; copper wires in household circuits and aluminium wires on electric poles in Indian streets show electrical conductivity, while iron and aluminium pans show heat conductivity because they warm up quickly. Malleability means the metal can be beaten into a thin sheet without breaking; goldsmiths beat gold into thin leaf to cover idols in temples, and blacksmiths flatten iron nails on anvils. Ductility means the metal can be drawn into thin wires; copper wire is used in almost every electrical fitting in a house. Sonority means the metal makes a ringing sound when struck; bronze and brass bells in schools and temples are made of metals because of this property. Most metals have high melting points and high boiling points, so they can be used in hot places such as engines and furnaces. Density means that a small piece of metal can be heavy; iron is much denser than aluminium, which is why aluminium is chosen for aircraft. Strength means that a metal resists breaking under a load; iron and steel are used for railway tracks, bridges and building frames. A good answer names each property clearly and supports it with the correct example.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A metal spoon left in a cup of hot tea becomes hot because the metal traps heat inside it." Explain why this statement is not correct, and describe a simple school activity with an iron rod and a wooden rod that would prove the correct property of the metal.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is not correct because a metal does not trap heat; it actually allows heat to pass through it easily. This property is called heat conductivity. A metal spoon becomes hot because heat from the tea travels quickly through the metal and reaches your hand. Materials that trap heat, such as wood or plastic, are poor conductors of heat, which is why the handles of many cooking pans are made of wood or plastic even when the pan itself is metal. To prove the correct property in school, take a long iron rod and a wooden rod of the same length and thickness. Stick a few small wax pieces or small pieces of paper along each rod at equal distances. Hold one end of each rod over the same small flame, such as a candle or a spirit lamp, for the same length of time. You will notice that the wax or paper on the iron rod falls off or burns much sooner, showing that heat has travelled quickly along the iron. The wax on the wooden rod does not melt or burn as quickly, because wood is a poor conductor. This activity shows that the metal conducts heat, while the non-metal does not. A good answer also connects this to the name of the property, heat conductivity.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A shopkeeper tells a customer, "Aluminium cooking pans are better than iron ones because aluminium and iron are both metals, so they will conduct heat in exactly the same way. Therefore, the cheaper aluminium pan is always the better choice." Evaluate this statement and decide whether the customer's choice should depend only on price.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The shopkeeper's statement is only partly true and needs careful evaluation. It is true that both aluminium and iron are metals, and both conduct heat. It is also true that aluminium is cheaper and lighter than iron, so an aluminium pan costs less and is easy to lift. However, the statement that the two metals conduct heat in exactly the same way is incorrect. Different metals conduct heat at different rates. Copper and aluminium are very good conductors, but iron is also a good conductor, though not quite as fast. More importantly, other properties matter in choosing a cooking pan. Aluminium is soft and can be scratched or bent more easily than iron, so an aluminium pan may not last as long. Iron is much stronger, so an iron pan can take rougher use. Iron is also denser, which gives a heavy base and helps food cook evenly. Another important difference is that some iron pans can add a small amount of iron to food, which can be useful for health, while aluminium may react with some sour foods. The customer should not decide only on price. The correct decision must consider the use of the pan, how long it is expected to last, how evenly it must heat, and how strong it must be. Therefore the shopkeeper's argument is too simple, and a balanced choice depends on more than just the common fact that both metals conduct heat.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Your teacher gives you a small, unknown, hard, silvery strip and asks you to find out whether it is a metal. Design a simple activity using three separate tests: one for malleability, one for electrical conductivity and one for sonority. List the materials you would need and the exact steps you would follow.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The three tests will be malleability, electrical conductivity and sonority, and each one shows a typical metallic property. For malleability, I need a hammer and a hard, flat surface such as a metal anvil or a thick stone slab. I will place the strip on the surface and strike it gently with the hammer several times. If the strip flattens or spreads without breaking or cracking, it is malleable. For electrical conductivity, I need a small battery, a torch bulb fixed in a bulb holder, connecting wires and the strip itself. I will first connect the battery and bulb with the wires to make a complete circuit without the strip. The bulb should glow. Then I will break the circuit and use the strip to join the two broken ends. If the bulb glows again, the strip conducts electricity. For sonority, I need only a hard floor or a stone slab. I will hold the strip a few centimetres above the surface and drop it. If it produces a clear ringing sound, the strip is sonorous. If the strip passes all three tests, it is almost certainly a metal, because malleability, electrical conductivity and sonority together are strong signs of metallic properties. A safe student would also wear safety glasses and keep fingers away from the hammer and the electric circuit.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are preparing a wall poster for your school science club that shows how five metals, iron, gold, copper, aluminium and zinc, can be grouped by their properties. Design the poster by choosing three physical properties and writing the labels an ICSE examiner would expect to see for each sample.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The poster would have a clear title, "Properties of Metals," and would be divided into three labelled columns. The first column could be titled "Lustrous Shiny Metals." Under this I would place gold, because gold ornaments and temple idols are highly lustrous, and copper, because a polished copper plate or vessel has a bright reddish shine. The second column could be titled "Good Conductors of Electricity and Heat." Under this I would place copper, because copper wires carry electric current, and aluminium, because aluminium is used for overhead electric cables and heats quickly in cooking pans. The third column could be titled "Strong and Useful in Construction." Under this I would place iron, because iron and steel are used in railway tracks, bridges and building frames, and zinc, because zinc is used to coat iron and to make brass, an alloy used in fittings. The examiner labels for each sample would include the property name and the example of use: for iron, "Strong, used in railway tracks and building frames"; for gold, "Lustrous, used in jewellery"; for copper, "Good conductor of electricity, used in wires"; for aluminium, "Light and a good conductor, used in aircraft and electric cables"; for zinc, "Used for galvanising iron to protect it." The poster would also include small pictures or symbols, such as a wire, a railway track, an ornament and an aeroplane, to make the classification easy to remember. This creative task shows that the same metal can appear under more than one property, because metals have many useful features.

masteryCriteria: Can state four physical properties of metals (shiny/lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, solid at room temperature except mercury); can give three examples of metals (iron, copper, aluminium); can state two chemical properties (react with acids to produce H2, form basic oxides).

title: Non-metals - properties
subject: chem
definition:
Elements are the simple substances from which every material around us is made. In earlier classes we grouped materials by what they looked like and what they could do; now we begin to group the elements themselves. The two largest groups are metals and non-metals. A non-metal is an element that does not show the typical metallic properties of being lustrous, malleable, ductile and a good conductor of heat and electricity. Instead, a non-metal is usually dull in appearance, meaning it lacks the bright metallic shine; it is brittle, so that it breaks into pieces rather than flattening into sheets or drawing into wires; and it is non-conductive, so it will not allow an electric current to pass through it. Coal, a form of carbon, is mined in places such as the Raniganj coalfield in West Bengal and the Jharia mines in Jharkhand. If a piece of coal is beaten with a hammer, it shatters like a biscuit, because non-metals are brittle and not malleable. If sulphur is placed in a simple electric circuit, the bulb does not glow, because non-metals are non-conductive.

Between the two families lies a special set of elements called metalloids. These are elements that show properties of both metals and non-metals, just as a bilingual person can speak two languages. For your syllabus the metalloids are silicon, germanium, tungsten and antimony. Silicon and germanium are used in electronic chips and solar-cell industries in places like Bengaluru and Gujarat; tungsten is used to make the very thin wire inside electric bulbs that glows without melting easily; and antimony is used in some alloys and battery plates. It is worth noting that in more advanced chemistry tungsten is usually classed as a metal, but the ICSE/ISC Class 6 syllabus places it in the metalloid list for this stage, so you must remember the four names together.

The same kind of careful thinking applies to corrosion, the slow wearing away of a metal when it reacts with substances in the air or water. Rusting is the special name for the corrosion of iron. An iron nail rusts only when both moisture and oxygen are present. You can show this with test tubes: a nail in dry air does not rust, a nail in boiled water covered with oil does not rust because oxygen is kept out, but a nail in ordinary moist air soon turns reddish-brown and flaky. A green deposit on copper articles is another kind of corrosion; it is copper carbonate formed when copper reacts with carbon dioxide, moisture and oxygen over time, and it is often seen on old copper utensils in humid coastal cities such as Kochi and Mumbai.

Because rusting damages bridges, ships, railings and tools, prevention is important. The five methods you must learn are oiling, painting, chrome plating, galvanization and tinning. Oiling covers the iron with a greasy layer that keeps out air and water; painting does the same and is used for gates, bridges and ships; chrome plating gives a shiny, protective layer on taps and bicycle parts; galvanization is covering iron with a thin coat of zinc, often used for buckets, roofing sheets and nails; and tinning is coating iron with tin, used for food cans. Each of these methods works by keeping the iron away from moisture and oxygen, the two things rusting needs.
eli5: Non-metals are the opposite of metals. Metals are shiny, bendy and let electricity pass through them, but non-metals are dull, break when hit and stop electricity. Some elements, called metalloids, sit in the middle and show a little of both. Iron rusts when both water and air meet its surface, so we paint gates, oil bicycle chains, or cover iron with zinc, tin or chromium to keep it safe.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a non-metal and a metalloid. List four properties that help us distinguish non-metals from metals, and give one example each of a non-metal and a metalloid from your syllabus.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A non-metal is an element that does not show the typical properties of metals. Non-metals are usually dull, meaning they do not have a shiny metallic surface; brittle, meaning they break into pieces when hammered or pressed; and non-conductive, meaning they do not allow heat or electricity to pass through them easily. Common examples are carbon, sulphur and phosphorus. A metalloid is an element that shows properties of both metals and non-metals. For the ICSE/ISC Class 6 syllabus, the metalloids are silicon, germanium, tungsten and antimony. Silicon and germanium are important in electronics, tungsten is used in electric-bulb filaments, and antimony is used in batteries and some alloys. The key distinction is that metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and conductive, while non-metals are the opposite and metalloids sit between the two groups. You can test an unknown sample by checking its shine, its ability to bend without breaking, and whether it carries an electric current.

diagnosticQuestions.question: An iron nail is placed in each of three test tubes: (A) dry air, (B) boiled water covered with oil, and (C) moist air containing both water and air. In which tube will the nail rust, and why will it not rust in the other two?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Rusting is the corrosion of iron, and it needs both moisture and oxygen together. Tube A contains air but no moisture, so the nail cannot rust because the water needed for the reaction is missing. Tube B contains water, but the water has been boiled to remove dissolved oxygen and the oil layer on top keeps fresh air out, so oxygen is missing; the nail will not rust there either. Tube C contains both moisture and oxygen, so the iron reacts with them to form hydrated iron oxide, the reddish-brown rust. This shows that neither water alone nor air alone causes rusting; both must be present at the same time. The practical conclusion is that any method of prevention must keep iron away from at least one of these two things.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says: "Graphite is black, can conduct a small amount of electricity, and is used in pencil leads, so it must be a metal." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is not correct, even though it begins with true observations. It is true that graphite, which is a form of carbon, is black and can conduct a small amount of electricity, and it is indeed used in pencil leads. However, a single property is not enough to decide whether an element is a metal or a non-metal. The classification is based on a whole set of properties. Graphite is not lustrous and does not have a metallic shine; it is brittle and breaks into flakes; and it is not malleable or ductile like metals. A metal shows a combination of lustre, malleability, ductility and good conductivity, while a non-metal shows the opposite. Graphite is therefore an exception in one property, not a member of the metal family. It is best described as an allotropic form of the non-metal carbon. Some non-metals, like graphite, can show one metallic property without changing their overall classification. The student has also ignored the fact that metals are usually solid at room temperature, dense, sonorous and good thermal conductors, and graphite does not match all of these. So the statement is not only incomplete but also misleading, because it confuses one unusual behaviour with a whole group identity.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A coastal school in Mumbai wants to protect an iron window-grill and a set of iron garden benches from rusting during the monsoon. Suggest two different methods of prevention, one for each object, and explain why each method is suitable.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For the window-grill, painting is suitable because it forms a solid, coloured coating that seals the iron from the humid monsoon air and rain. It is also cheap and can be reapplied every few years. For the garden benches, galvanization is a good choice because it coats the iron with a layer of zinc, which not only blocks moisture and oxygen but also protects the iron even if the coating is scratched; the zinc reacts first and sacrifices itself. Both methods work by keeping the iron away from the moisture and oxygen needed for rusting, and they are chosen because the window-grill is decorative and stationary while the benches face soil, dampness and possible knocks. In a coastal city like Mumbai, the salty, moist air is an even stronger rusting agent, so a thick protective layer is particularly important.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple school-laboratory activity to prove that both moisture and oxygen are needed for the rusting of an iron nail. Give the aim, materials, steps, the expected observations in each case and the conclusion.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The aim of the activity is to show that rusting of iron takes place only when both moisture and oxygen are present. The materials required are three clean, rust-free iron nails, three test tubes, a cork or rubber stopper, cotton wool, anhydrous calcium chloride, a Bunsen burner or spirit lamp, a beaker, boiled water and a little oil. First set up three test tubes. In tube A, place a nail with anhydrous calcium chloride and cotton wool to keep the air dry, then stopper it. In tube B, half-fill the test tube with boiled water to remove dissolved oxygen, place the nail in it, and then pour a thin layer of oil over the water to stop air from entering. In tube C, place the nail with a little damp cotton wool and leave it open to the air. Leave all three tubes for several days, preferably a week. The expected observation is that the nail in tube A stays bright because there is no moisture, the nail in tube B stays bright because there is no oxygen, and the nail in tube C turns reddish-brown because both moisture and oxygen are present. The conclusion is that rusting needs both moisture and oxygen together, and preventing either one will stop rusting.

masteryCriteria: Can state four physical properties of non-metals (dull, brittle, poor conductors, exist as solids/liquids/gases); can give three examples of non-metals (oxygen, sulphur, carbon); can state two chemical properties (react with oxygen to form acidic oxides, do not react with dilute acids to produce H2).

title: Air and its composition
subject: chem
definition: Air is a mixture of gases that surrounds the Earth and forms the atmosphere we breathe and live within. It is not a single substance, but a physical combination of several different gases mixed together in the atmosphere. The composition of air is approximately 78% nitrogen by volume, 21% oxygen, and the remaining 1% consists of carbon dioxide, water vapour, noble gases such as argon, neon and helium, along with tiny amounts of other substances like dust and pollutants. Because the concentration of these components is not exactly the same everywhere, air is classified as a mixture rather than a compound. In a compound, two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion by mass, and their properties change completely; in air, the gases are simply blended together, each retaining its own properties, and their percentage can vary from place to place and from time to time. For example, the air over a humid coastal city such as Kochi or Mumbai contains a higher percentage of water vapour than the dry desert air over Jaisalmer or Ladakh. Similarly, the carbon dioxide percentage near a busy traffic intersection or an industrial area may be slightly higher than in a quiet forest in the Western Ghats. Nitrogen is the largest component of air, making up a little more than three-fourths of the atmosphere by volume. It is used in the manufacture of fertilisers, in the preservation of packaged food, and in the production of ammonia. Oxygen, the second largest component, is essential for respiration in animals and human beings, and it supports many life processes. Carbon dioxide, though present in very small percentage, is absorbed by plants during photosynthesis and is important for the growth of vegetation. Water vapour in the air determines humidity, influences weather patterns, and is responsible for rainfall. Noble gases such as argon are chemically very unreactive and are used in electric bulbs and special lighting. A pie chart is a very useful way to present the composition of air because it shows each component as a sector of a circle, making the percentage of every gas easy to compare at a glance. The largest sector represents nitrogen at 78%, the next sector represents oxygen at 21%, and the remaining tiny sectors show carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases. The variation in the percentage of these minor components from one location to another is the strongest evidence that air is a mixture of gases and not a compound.
eli5: Air is like a fruit salad. It is made of many different gases mixed together, not one single thing. The biggest part is nitrogen, then comes oxygen, with tiny bits of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases. Because the amount of each gas can change from place to place, air is called a mixture. A pie chart is just like slicing a pizza to show which gas takes up the most space.

misconceptions.belief: "Air is mostly oxygen because living things need it for breathing." The board examiner observations for percentage-composition questions show that students often fail to identify and emphasise the main component clearly. Just as some candidates listed extra metals without naming aluminium as the primary metal in Duralumin, many Class 6 students remember that oxygen is important and forget that nitrogen is the largest component at about 78%. The correction is to state clearly that nitrogen makes up 78% of air, oxygen only 21%, and the rest is a tiny mixture of other gases.

"The composition of air is fixed everywhere, so it must be a compound." The examiner observations also note that students often confuse mixtures with compounds by not paying attention to exact composition. A compound has a fixed ratio of elements joined chemically, but a mixture has a variable composition. The concentration of water vapour is much higher over humid coastal places like Chennai or Kochi than over dry regions like Rajasthan, and the carbon dioxide percentage can be higher near cities and factories. This variation proves that air is a mixture.

"The remaining 1% of air is only carbon dioxide." Similar to the way candidates in alloy questions added extra or incorrect components, some students think that all the remaining air after nitrogen and oxygen is carbon dioxide. The correction is that the remaining 1% is shared by several components: noble gases such as argon, neon and helium, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other trace substances. Carbon dioxide is only a small part of that remaining 1%.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the approximate percentage composition of air by volume. Name the two major components and two minor components.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Air contains approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% of other gases by volume. The two major components are nitrogen and oxygen. The two minor components you should remember are carbon dioxide and water vapour, though the remaining 1% also includes noble gases such as argon, neon and helium. Nitrogen is the largest component and makes up a little more than three-fourths of the atmosphere. It is used in the manufacture of fertilisers, in food packaging to prevent spoilage, and in the production of ammonia. Oxygen is the second largest component and is essential for breathing and many life processes in animals and human beings. Carbon dioxide, although present in a very small percentage, is used by plants during photosynthesis. Water vapour varies from place to place and is responsible for humidity, cloud formation and rainfall. Noble gases such as argon are chemically inert and are used in electric bulbs. When answering this question in the exam, always write the percentages in the correct order and use the word approximately, because the exact values can change slightly depending on location and conditions.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is air considered a mixture and not a compound? Support your answer using the percentages of the gases in air.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Air is considered a mixture and not a compound because it is made up of different gases that are physically mixed together rather than chemically combined. In a compound, elements combine in a fixed proportion by mass and lose their individual properties. For example, water is a compound because hydrogen and oxygen always combine in a fixed ratio of 1:8 by mass. Air, however, does not have a fixed composition everywhere. While dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, the remaining 1% is made up of variable amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases. The percentage of water vapour changes greatly from place to place; humid air over coastal cities like Mumbai or Kochi contains much more water vapour than dry air over Jaisalmer or Ladakh. The carbon dioxide percentage can also vary depending on vegetation, traffic and industrial activity. Because the concentration of these components is not fixed at all places, air fits the definition of a mixture, which is a physical combination of substances in any proportion. Each gas in air still keeps its own properties, and they can be separated by physical methods such as fractional distillation of liquid air.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Air is a compound because dry air always contains 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, so the proportions are fixed." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is not correct, although it contains a small grain of truth that needs careful examination. It is true that the major components of dry air are roughly 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen at most places on Earth, which makes the atmosphere stable enough to support life. However, the percentages 78% and 21% are average values, not exact fixed values. The proportion of oxygen can change slightly with altitude, and the proportion of water vapour, carbon dioxide and other gases can vary greatly from one place to another. For instance, the air over the Amazon rainforest or the Western Ghats contains more carbon dioxide at night and more oxygen during the day because of plant processes. Similarly, the water vapour percentage over a desert such as the Thar Desert is much lower than over the coastal plains of Kerala. In a true compound, the elements are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio by mass and the composition is exactly the same everywhere. Air does not meet this condition because its components are not chemically bonded and their proportions can vary. Therefore, even though the two main gases appear in a fairly stable ratio, the overall composition of air is not fixed, and air should correctly be described as a mixture of gases, not a compound. The student has focused only on the two major components and ignored the variation in the minor components and the physical mixing of the gases.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Draw a pie chart to show the composition of air. If the pie chart is drawn inside a circle of radius 5 cm, calculate the approximate angle of the sector representing oxygen.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To draw the pie chart, start by drawing a circle of any convenient radius. The radius of 5 cm given in the question is simply the size of the chart and does not affect the angles of the sectors. The whole circle represents 100% of the air and has 360 degrees. Oxygen makes up 21% of the air, so the angle of the oxygen sector is 21% of 360 degrees, which equals 0.21 multiplied by 360, giving approximately 75.6 degrees. You can round this to 76 degrees if you are using a protractor. The nitrogen sector, being 78%, will have an angle of 0.78 multiplied by 360, which is approximately 280.8 degrees. The remaining 1% shared by carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases will have an angle of 0.01 multiplied by 360, which is about 3.6 degrees. In your diagram, draw the largest sector for nitrogen and label it 78%, the next largest for oxygen and label it 21%, and the tiny remaining sector for the other gases with the label 1%. Make sure all sectors are clearly named and the percentages are written inside or beside each slice. A neat and correctly labelled pie chart shows that you understand both the composition and the method of presentation expected in the board exam.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are a Class 6 science teacher. Design a short classroom activity that helps your classmates remember the composition of air and why it is a mixture.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would design an activity called "The Air Pizza." First, I would bring a large round cardboard disc to represent a pie chart, and several small coloured paper cut-outs. The red pieces would represent nitrogen, the blue pieces oxygen, the green pieces carbon dioxide, the yellow pieces water vapour and the grey pieces noble gases. I would ask five volunteers to come to the front. The first volunteer would place 78 red pieces on the disc to show that nitrogen is the largest component. The second would place 21 blue pieces for oxygen. The third, fourth and fifth would place tiny green, yellow and grey pieces for the remaining 1%. Then I would ask the class to observe that the red and blue pieces take up almost the whole pizza. Next, I would change the number of yellow water-vapour pieces: more pieces for a humid place like Kochi and fewer for a dry place like Jaisalmer. I would ask the students, "Did the total pizza change?" and "Can the amounts of one gas change without changing the whole disc?" This would help them see that the percentages of gases in air are not fixed everywhere. Finally, I would ask each volunteer to pick up their coloured pieces and move to a different place in the classroom, showing that the gases can be physically separated, which is another property of a mixture. The activity would end with the class drawing the same composition as a real pie chart in their notebooks.

masteryCriteria: Can state the composition of air (nitrogen ~78%, oxygen ~21%, argon ~1%, carbon dioxide ~0.04%, water vapour, noble gases); can describe one test for oxygen (glowing splint relights) and one for CO2 (limewater turns milky); can state the importance of oxygen (breathing, burning) and nitrogen (plant growth).

title: Oxygen and its role
subject: chem
definition:
Oxygen is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas that makes up about twenty-one percent of ordinary air. In the clean air over the Indian plains, the Himalayan foothills and the coastal belt from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu, this proportion stays roughly the same because air is a mixture and oxygen is one of its most important ingredients. The presence of oxygen explains why a matchstick flares in a classroom in Delhi, why a Diwali diya keeps glowing and why a cyclist breathing heavily after a climb recovers by taking in more air.

The physical properties of oxygen are easy to remember once you test the gas yourself: it has no colour, no smell and no taste. It is only slightly soluble in water, which is exactly why it can be collected over water in the school laboratory. A simple but striking test is the glowing splint test; if you place a glowing wooden splint into a jar of oxygen, it bursts into flame, showing that the gas supports combustion.

Combustion is a rapid chemical reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen and gives out heat and light. Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame to form a white solid called magnesium oxide; in words we write Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide. Sulphur burns with a blue flame to give sulphur dioxide, carbon burns to give carbon dioxide, and phosphorus burns with a bright yellow flame to give phosphorus pentoxide. Among metals, sodium and potassium react vigorously to form their oxides, calcium forms calcium oxide and magnesium forms magnesium oxide. These word equations show a real union: the starting substance has joined with oxygen to make a new substance with new properties.

Burning also brings a change in mass. If you heat a piece of magnesium ribbon in a crucible, the product is heavier than the original metal because the magnesium has combined with oxygen from the air. A burning candle, on the other hand, seems to lose mass because the wax combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, and these gases drift away into the room. The lesson is that mass is conserved in a closed system, but in the open laboratory we observe only the part that remains with us.

Rusting and respiration are two quieter ways in which oxygen takes part in change. Rusting is the slow combination of iron with oxygen and water to form a brown flaky substance; it happens to school gates, bicycle chains and railway tracks during the monsoon. Respiration is the slow and controlled release of energy inside living cells when food combines with oxygen; we breathe out carbon dioxide and water vapour. Combustion and respiration both need oxygen and both release energy, but respiration has no flame and happens at body temperature. Rusting is like a very slow, cold burn that produces no light.

Oxygen can be prepared in the school laboratory in two familiar ways. Heating potassium chlorate with a little manganese dioxide gives potassium chloride and oxygen; the word equation is Potassium chlorate -> Potassium chloride + Oxygen. Adding manganese dioxide to hydrogen peroxide at room temperature gives water and oxygen; Hydrogen peroxide -> Water + Oxygen. In both cases manganese dioxide is the catalyst. A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. After the experiment the manganese dioxide can be filtered, washed, dried and reused, and its mass remains almost the same. This idea helps chemists carry out reactions safely and economically without wasting materials.
eli5: Oxygen is an invisible gas in the air. It helps fires burn bright and helps your body turn food into energy. You can make it in the lab by mixing a special liquid called hydrogen peroxide with a helper powder called manganese dioxide. The helper makes the gas come out fast, but it does not get used up. When things burn, they join with oxygen; some get heavier, and some make gases that float away.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State any two physical properties of oxygen and write the word equation for the reaction of magnesium with oxygen.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Oxygen is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas. It has no colour that you can see, no smell that you can detect and no taste. It is only slightly soluble in water, which is why it can be conveniently collected over water in the laboratory. When a glowing wooden splint is introduced into a jar of oxygen, it bursts into flame, showing that the gas supports combustion. The word equation for the burning of magnesium is Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide. During this reaction the bright magnesium ribbon catches fire and produces a dazzling white light. The white solid that remains is magnesium oxide, and because oxygen from the air has joined with the magnesium, the product has more mass than the original ribbon.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why the mass of a piece of magnesium increases when it burns in air, while the mass of a burning candle appears to decrease.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When magnesium burns in air, the hot magnesium metal combines with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Since the product is a solid that contains both the original magnesium and the oxygen taken from the air, the mass of the solid in the crucible becomes greater than the mass of the starting ribbon. This is why the balance shows an increase. On the other hand, when a candle burns, the wax is a compound of carbon and hydrogen. It reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour. These products are gases, so they rise and spread into the surrounding air and are no longer part of the candle. Because the gaseous products leave, the candle appears to lose mass. However, if the candle were burned inside a sealed container and all the gases were kept, the total mass before and after would be the same. This teaches us that mass is not really lost; it is only that the products of burning a candle are gases which escape, while the product of burning magnesium is a solid which stays in the dish.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A catalyst is a special kind of reactant that is used up during the reaction, so we have to keep adding more of it." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is largely incorrect, although it does show that the student has noticed that a catalyst is present during the reaction. A catalyst is a substance that increases the speed of a chemical reaction without itself being permanently changed or used up. It is true that the catalyst takes part in the reaction while it is happening, but at the end it can be recovered in almost the same amount as at the start. Manganese dioxide is a good example; when it is added to hydrogen peroxide, the hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen much faster, but the manganese dioxide remains behind. The same manganese dioxide can be filtered, washed, dried and used again, and again. Therefore it is wrong to call a catalyst a reactant in the ordinary sense, because a reactant is a starting material that disappears and becomes part of the product. A catalyst is not shown on the reactant side as something that gets consumed. The student is right that the catalyst is present and important, but wrong that it is used up. In some industrial processes a catalyst may become less effective over a long time because of impurities, but this is not the same as being consumed in the reaction. So the correct view is that a catalyst makes the reaction faster, is not used up and can usually be reused.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe how you would prepare oxygen in the school laboratory using hydrogen peroxide and manganese dioxide, and state the test you would use to identify the gas.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To prepare oxygen in the school laboratory, place a small amount of hydrogen peroxide in a conical flask. Add a little manganese dioxide to it. The manganese dioxide acts as a catalyst, so the reaction starts quickly at room temperature without needing strong heat. Bubbles of oxygen gas are produced, and the word equation is Hydrogen peroxide -> Water + Oxygen. The gas can be collected over water in an inverted gas jar, because oxygen is only slightly soluble in water. To show that the gas is oxygen, take a glowing wooden splint and insert it into the mouth of the jar. If the splint bursts into flame, the gas is oxygen. This test is called the glowing splint test and works because oxygen supports combustion. Care should be taken not to add too much hydrogen peroxide at once, because the reaction can become vigorous. Also, the manganese dioxide should be kept away from the eyes and skin. After the experiment the manganese dioxide can be filtered from the mixture and reused, proving that it is not used up.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple experiment to show that oxygen is needed for a candle to keep burning, using two similar candles, two glass jars and water in a shallow dish.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Take two similar candles and fix them on a shallow dish containing a little water. Light both candles and place identical glass jars over them one at a time, or place one jar over the first candle while the second candle is left open to the air as a control. Observe what happens. The candle inside the closed jar will burn for a short time and then go out, while the candle open to the air will keep burning. The reason is that the burning candle uses up the oxygen inside the closed jar. When most of the oxygen has been used, the flame cannot continue. In the jar, the water level rises slightly because the oxygen is consumed and the pressure inside the jar becomes lower than the atmospheric pressure outside. The control candle, however, has a continuous supply of fresh air containing oxygen, so it keeps burning. This simple experiment shows that oxygen is necessary for burning, just as it is necessary for our breathing. You can make it more convincing by using a larger jar for one candle and a smaller jar for the other; the candle in the smaller jar, which has less oxygen, goes out first.

masteryCriteria: Can describe the laboratory preparation of oxygen (decomposition of H2O2 with MnO2 catalyst, or heating KClO3); can state two tests for oxygen (glowing splint relights, burning splint burns brighter); can state two uses of oxygen (breathing, burning, medical use, welding).

title: Carbon dioxide and nitrogen in air
subject: chem
definition: Air is not just one substance; it is a mixture of gases that surrounds our planet. Two of these gases, carbon dioxide and nitrogen, make up very different fractions of air and play very different chemical roles. Nitrogen is by far the larger partner, making up about 78% of the air we breathe. It is a colourless, odourless, unreactive gas that is essential for plant growth when it is converted into compounds such as the nitrates used in fertilisers. Carbon dioxide is much less abundant, only about 0.04%, yet it is vital for plant photosynthesis and is also involved in the chemistry of air pollution. When fuels burn in factories, power stations and vehicle engines, carbon dioxide is released, along with other waste gases such as sulphur dioxide and various nitrogen oxides. These gases are acidic oxides, which means they can dissolve in the water droplets that make up rain to form acids such as carbonic acid, sulphurous acid and nitric acid. This process produces acid rain, a kind of rainfall that is more acidic than normal rainwater and can cause serious damage. Because the rain falls on buildings, bridges, cars, machines, forests, farms and water bodies, its effects spread through every part of the environment. For example, the white marble of heritage buildings such as the Taj Mahal at Agra contains calcium carbonate, which reacts with the acids in rain, causing the surface to corrode and lose its beauty. In the same way, bridges and cars made of metal suffer corrosion more quickly, while machines and statues wear away. When acid rain flows into lakes, rivers and the sea, it harms aquatic organisms such as fish and the tiny animals and plants that build coral reefs. On farms, acid rain can damage crops and reduce the fertility of soil, which in turn affects agriculture. The overall condition of the air, called air quality, tells us how much pollution it contains. Emissions from factories and vehicles are the main human sources of these waste gases, and they are steadily changing the composition of the air. Yet these same gases also have useful sides. Carbon dioxide is used in fire extinguishers, fizzy drinks and to help plants grow in greenhouses. Nitrogen is used to make fertilisers, explosives, and to provide an unreactive atmosphere for storing food or preserving medicines. Oxygen is used in hospitals, welding and in the breathing apparatus used by mountaineers and divers. Learning to balance the harm and the help of these gases is the central theme of this chapter.
eli5: Air is a mixture. Nitrogen is the biggest part of air and helps plants grow when it is made into plant food. Carbon dioxide is a tiny part, but it is food for plants and can also dissolve in rain. Factory and car smoke put extra acidic gases into the air, and these dissolve in rain to make acid rain. Acid rain can eat the marble of old buildings like the Taj Mahal and hurt fish, farms and bridges.

misconceptions.belief: "All oxides that dissolve in water make the water acidic, so carbon dioxide must be a harmful, reactive gas." This is not true. The 2025 CISCE Common board exam error pattern reported that many candidates confused acidic, basic, amphoteric and neutral oxides, calling some "basic" when they were amphoteric or "neutral" when they were acidic. Carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are specifically acidic oxides because they dissolve in water to form acids. Nitrogen itself, however, is not an acidic oxide; it is an unreactive gas and only forms oxides when heated or combined with oxygen at high temperatures. A correct statement is: carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are the acidic oxides involved in acid rain, while nitrogen is mainly a dilute, unreactive gas.

"The white colour of the Taj Mahal turns yellow because the rain itself is coloured, not because of any chemical reaction." The real problem is the reaction between the acids in rain and the calcium carbonate of the marble. The 2025 examiner observations remind us that students often miss the chemical identity of oxides and the products formed. The acids formed from sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react with calcium carbonate, causing corrosion and discolouration. A good answer would name the acidic oxide, the acid, the building material and the effect: "Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rainwater to form acids; these acids react with calcium carbonate in the marble of the Taj Mahal, causing it to corrode and turn yellow."

"Nitrogen is useless in the air because plants cannot use it directly." Nitrogen is the largest part of air, and although most plants cannot take it directly from the air, it is essential for making proteins. When converted into nitrates, it becomes a fertiliser that helps agriculture. A weak answer might say nitrogen is "just there" or "does nothing." A correct answer says it is unreactive but very important, mainly used to make fertilisers and provide an inert atmosphere for storing food and medicines.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Name the main gases that make up air and give one use each of oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Air is a mixture of several gases. The two most abundant gases are nitrogen and oxygen, with nitrogen making up about 78% of air and oxygen making up about 21%. Carbon dioxide is present in a much smaller amount, only about 0.04%. Water vapour is also present in varying amounts. Because these gases have different properties, each has its own uses. Oxygen is used in hospitals to help patients breathe, in welding to produce a very hot flame, and in breathing apparatus for mountaineers and divers. Nitrogen is used to make fertilisers that help crops grow, to preserve food by keeping out reactive oxygen, and to provide an unreactive atmosphere for storing medicines. Carbon dioxide is used in fire extinguishers because it does not support burning, in fizzy drinks to give them bubbles, and by plants in greenhouses to increase the rate of photosynthesis. A strong answer would also mention that air quality depends on keeping the percentages of these gases in balance and that waste gases from factories and vehicles can change this composition.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain how acidic oxides in the air cause acid rain, and describe what happens to the Taj Mahal when acid rain falls on it.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Acidic oxides are oxides that dissolve in water to form acids. The main acidic oxides responsible for acid rain are carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. When these gases are released into the air from burning fossil fuels in factories, power stations and vehicle engines, they mix with the water vapour in clouds. The water droplets dissolve the gases and form acids such as carbonic acid, sulphurous acid and nitric acid. When these droplets fall as rain, the rain is more acidic than normal and is called acid rain. The Taj Mahal in Agra is built of white marble that is mostly calcium carbonate. When acid rain falls on this marble, the acids react with the calcium carbonate and slowly dissolve the surface. This causes the marble to lose its shine, turn yellowish and become rough. The chemical change is called corrosion. If this continues, the fine carvings on the monument can be worn away and the structure can be weakened. This is why the monument is regularly cleaned and why efforts are made to reduce pollution around it.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Factories and vehicles are essential for the country's progress, so acid rain is just a small price we should accept without trying to reduce it." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly true and needs careful evaluation. It is true that factories and vehicles are important for a country's economy. They provide jobs, transport, electricity and goods that people need. Without them, life would be very difficult, especially in a large country like India where millions of people depend on industries and public transport. However, this does not mean that we should ignore acid rain. Acid rain causes serious damage that also harms the economy and people's lives. It corrodes heritage buildings such as the Taj Mahal, bridges, cars and machines, costing money for repairs and replacement. It makes lakes and rivers too acidic, killing fish and other aquatic organisms. It also harms coral reefs and can damage farms, reducing crop yields and affecting agriculture. Therefore, accepting acid rain as a "small price" is not wise. A balanced approach is to continue using factories and vehicles but to reduce their harmful emissions by using cleaner fuels, fitting filters in factory chimneys, using catalytic converters in vehicles, planting more trees, and following laws that control air quality. In this way, the country can develop and also protect its buildings, environment and people's health. So the statement is too simple and should be rejected in its strong form, although the need for industry and transport is accepted.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A thermal power station near a town releases sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides into the air. During the monsoon, the residents notice that the metal railings of the local bridge are rusting faster and that the leaves of some plants look damaged. Explain why this happens and suggest two practical steps the town can take to reduce the problem.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The waste gases from the power station are acidic oxides. When they dissolve in the rain that falls during the monsoon, they form acids such as sulphurous acid and nitric acid. This acid rain falls on the bridge and speeds up the corrosion, or rusting, of the metal railings. It also falls on the leaves and soil of the plants and can damage the leaf surface, making it harder for the plants to make food and grow well. The problem is made worse if the town has many vehicles or other factories releasing more of these gases, because the air quality becomes poor. To reduce the problem, the town can take two practical steps. First, the power station can be asked to fit devices such as scrubbers in its chimneys to remove sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides before the waste gases are released. Second, the town can encourage public transport, car pooling and the use of cleaner fuels such as compressed natural gas, so that vehicle emissions are reduced. Planting more trees also helps because leaves can trap some pollutants. These steps would improve the air quality and reduce the harm to the bridge, the plants and the people living in the town.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are the head of an eco-club in your school. Design a simple project that helps your school community understand how the composition of air is changing and what it means for acid rain. Your answer should include the name of the project, one activity, and one message you want everyone to remember.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The project would be called "Clean Air, Bright Marble." The aim is to show how small changes in the composition of air can lead to acid rain and damage important buildings and living things. The main activity would be a two-week observation. Students would set up a small rain-collection station using a clean funnel and a plastic jar placed in an open area of the school. They would collect rainwater and note its appearance and the date of collection. Another group would collect samples of soil from the school garden and leaves from common plants. The students would then compare their samples with images and simple pH charts to understand how rain can become acidic. They would also make posters showing how sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from factories, power stations and vehicles dissolve in rain to form acids. The posters would explain how this acid rain harms the Taj Mahal, bridges, cars, aquatic organisms and agriculture. The message would be: "Every gas we add to the air changes its composition and its quality. By walking or cycling short distances, by saving electricity, and by asking industries to reduce emissions, we can keep the air cleaner and protect both our heritage and our health." This project would help students move from "air is a mixture of gases" to "the gases in air have real chemical effects on our world."

masteryCriteria: Can describe the test for CO2 (turns limewater milky: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O); can state two roles of nitrogen in air (dilutes oxygen, essential for plant growth); can state two roles of CO2 (photosynthesis, greenhouse effect); can explain why nitrogen is inert at room temperature.

title: Water - physical properties
subject: chem
definition:
Water is one of the most familiar and important substances on Earth and it exists naturally in all three states of matter: the solid state as ice, the liquid state as water, and the gaseous state as water vapour or steam. In this node we study the physical properties of water, which are the properties we can observe or measure without changing water into a new substance. The most important of these are the boiling point and the freezing point. Pure water boils at 100 deg C under normal atmospheric pressure and freezes at 0 deg C. These two temperatures are special because they are fixed points on the Celsius scale and they mark where water changes from one state to another. The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid begins to change rapidly into a gas, and for water this rapid change happens at 100 deg C. The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid begins to change into a solid, and for water this happens at 0 deg C.

When water changes from one state to another, we call the process a state interconversion. Melting is the change from solid ice to liquid water and it takes place at 0 deg C. Freezing is the opposite: liquid water changes into solid ice, also at 0 deg C. Evaporation is the slow change of liquid water into water vapour and it can happen at any temperature below the boiling point. Boiling is rapid evaporation throughout the liquid and for pure water it occurs at 100 deg C. Condensation is the change of water vapour back into liquid water and it happens when water vapour loses heat and cools. All of these processes are physical changes because the substance remains water in every state. No new substance is formed; only the arrangement and the movement of the water particles change. In ice, the particles are held tightly in fixed positions and can only vibrate, which gives ice a definite shape and volume. In liquid water, the particles are close together but can slide over one another, so water takes the shape of its container but keeps the same volume. In steam, the particles are far apart and move freely in all directions, so steam fills whatever space is available.

The state interconversions of water are also reversible. Ice can melt to form water, and the same water can be frozen again to form ice. Water can evaporate to form steam, and the same steam can condense back to water. We can show these changes by simple experiments. For example, an ice cube placed in a dish at room temperature slowly becomes a puddle of water; this is melting. If the water is heated in a beaker, it begins to boil at 100 deg C and steam is seen rising; this is boiling. When the steam touches a cold glass plate held above the beaker, it forms tiny droplets; this is condensation. If the beaker of water is placed in a freezer, it turns to ice; this is freezing. We can also see these changes in everyday life: ice melting on a cold drink, water boiling in a kettle, drops forming on the outside of a cold bottle, and ice cubes forming in a freezer. In the Himalayan region water exists as snow and ice, while on the hot plains it flows as liquid in rivers and may evaporate quickly. Understanding the physical properties and state interconversions of water helps us explain rain, snow, dew, clouds, and the working of many household and industrial machines.
eli5: Water can be solid ice, liquid water, or gas called steam. Ice melts into water at 0 degrees. Water boils into steam at 100 degrees. Steam can cool back into water, and water can freeze back into ice. Nothing new is made, so these are called physical changes. The temperatures where these changes happen are special properties of water.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define boiling point and freezing point of water. Name the four state interconversions of water and state the temperature at which each one occurs for pure water under normal atmospheric pressure.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which it begins to change rapidly into a gas, with bubbles forming throughout the liquid and rising to the surface. For pure water under normal atmospheric pressure, this temperature is 100 deg C. The freezing point of a liquid is the temperature at which it begins to change into a solid. For pure water under normal atmospheric pressure, this temperature is 0 deg C. The four state interconversions of water are melting, freezing, evaporation, and condensation. Melting is the change from solid ice to liquid water and it takes place at 0 deg C. Freezing is the change from liquid water to solid ice and it also takes place at 0 deg C. Evaporation is the slow change from liquid water to water vapour and it can occur at any temperature below the boiling point. Boiling is rapid evaporation throughout the liquid and it takes place at 100 deg C. Condensation is the change from water vapour back into liquid water and it happens when the gas cools down, with no fixed temperature but whenever the vapour loses enough heat. In all these changes, the substance remains water and no new substance is formed, so they are physical and reversible changes.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Match the following and explain each match: Column A: (a) melting, (b) freezing, (c) evaporation, (d) boiling, (e) condensation. Column B: (i) water vapour to liquid, (ii) liquid to water vapour at 100 deg C, (iii) solid to liquid at 0 deg C, (iv) liquid to water vapour at any temperature, (v) liquid to solid at 0 deg C.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The correct matches are (a)-(iii), (b)-(v), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii), and (e)-(i). Melting is the process in which a solid turns into a liquid and for water this occurs at 0 deg C, so ice melts into liquid water at 0 deg C. Freezing is the reverse process in which a liquid turns into a solid and for water this also occurs at 0 deg C, so liquid water freezes into ice at 0 deg C. Evaporation is the slow change of a liquid into a gas that happens at the surface and can occur at any temperature below the boiling point, such as a puddle drying on a warm day. Boiling is a special, rapid kind of evaporation that happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature and for water this temperature is 100 deg C. Condensation is the change from the gaseous state back into the liquid state and it happens when water vapour loses heat, for example when steam touches a cold surface and forms tiny droplets. In every case, the substance is still water; only the state of matter and the arrangement and movement of the particles change. These are physical changes, not chemical changes, because no new substance is formed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "When water is boiled, it changes into steam and disappears, so a new substance has been formed. Therefore, boiling water is a chemical change." Evaluate this statement. Is the student correct? Give a balanced argument with reasons for and against the statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is not correct. Boiling water is a physical change, not a chemical change. The part of the statement that is correct is the observation that the liquid water seems to disappear and becomes steam. This is a real change of state from the liquid to the gaseous state, and it can be seen and felt. However, the conclusion that a new substance has been formed is wrong. In a physical change, the substance remains the same; only its state, shape, or size changes. When water boils, the H2O particles absorb heat, move faster, and move farther apart until they become water vapour, which is steam. The chemical composition of the particles does not change. If the steam is cooled, it condenses back into liquid water, and the same water can be collected. This shows that the change is reversible. A chemical change would produce a new substance with different properties; for example, if water were broken down into hydrogen and oxygen by passing electricity through it, that would be a chemical change because hydrogen and oxygen are different substances. In boiling, no new substance is produced. The steam has the same composition as liquid water and shows the same properties when it is cooled. On the other hand, one could support the student by saying that the student has at least noticed a real and visible change and has correctly used the word "change." The mistake is only in the type of change. Therefore, the balanced view is that the student has made a good observation but has drawn the wrong conclusion because they did not check whether the water could be recovered unchanged. Boiling water is a physical and reversible change of state.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe a simple experiment you can do in the laboratory or at home to show melting, boiling, and condensation of water. State what you would observe at each stage and how it proves that the changes are physical changes.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Take a few ice cubes and place them in a clean beaker or a small metal pan on a tripod stand or a stove with a wire gauze. Put a thermometer in the ice. As the ice absorbs heat from the surroundings, it begins to melt and a puddle of liquid water forms at the bottom of the beaker. If you watch the thermometer, the ice melts at about 0 deg C. This is melting. As you continue heating, the temperature of the water rises until it reaches 100 deg C, when the water begins to boil. You will see bubbles rising rapidly throughout the liquid and steam leaving the surface. This is boiling. Hold a cold glass plate or a metal lid a few centimetres above the beaker. After a short time, you will notice tiny droplets of water forming on the underside of the plate. This is condensation because the hot steam cools when it touches the cold surface and changes back into liquid water. To prove that the changes are physical, collect the condensed water in a clean container and let it cool. It will look and behave like ordinary water. You can also place the beaker in a freezer and the water will freeze into ice again. Because the original water can be recovered and no new substance has been made, melting, boiling, and condensation are physical and reversible changes of state.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple model, diagram, or demonstration that you could use to teach a younger student that ice, water, and steam are the same substance. Explain how your model shows the arrangement of particles in the three states and the conditions needed for each change.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: My model uses small glass marbles inside a transparent plastic box to represent water particles. For the solid state of ice, the marbles are glued or fixed in a neat, ordered pattern and are only allowed to vibrate slightly in their places. This shows that in ice the particles are tightly packed in fixed positions, so ice has a definite shape and a definite volume. For the liquid state of water, the marbles are placed close together but are not fixed; they can slide over one another when the box is tilted. This shows that the particles in liquid water are close but can move past one another, so water takes the shape of its container but has a fixed volume. For the gaseous state of steam, a few marbles are placed in a much larger box and allowed to roll freely in every direction. This shows that the particles in steam are far apart and move rapidly, filling all the space they are given. To show melting, I gently shake the ice box and remove some of the fixing points, so the marbles begin to slide at 0 deg C. To show evaporation, I move some of the marbles from the liquid box into the larger gas box at any warm temperature. To show boiling, I shake the liquid box strongly and let many marbles jump into the gas box at 100 deg C. To show condensation, I slow the marbles down and guide them back from the gas box into the liquid box. Because the same marbles are used throughout, the student sees that ice, water, and steam are the same water, only with different arrangements and speeds of particles.

masteryCriteria: Can state five physical properties of water (colourless, odourless, tasteless, transparent, liquid at room temperature, boils at 100 deg C, freezes at 0 deg C, density 1 g/cm3); can state that pure water is a poor conductor of electricity; can test transparency and boiling point experimentally.

title: Water - chemical properties
subject: chem
definition:
Water is one of the most familiar substances on Earth, yet it is also an active participant in many chemical changes. In this node, the student explores the chemical properties of water -- the ways in which water reacts with other substances to produce new substances with new properties. A chemical property is not something you can see when the sample is sitting still; it shows itself only when the sample interacts with something else. When water shows its chemical properties, it ceases to be merely a solvent and becomes a reactant.
For instance, water takes part in a reaction with highly reactive metals such as sodium and potassium, producing a metal hydroxide and releasing hydrogen gas with a vigorous fizzing sound. Even with a less reactive metal like calcium, water can cause a slow release of gas and leave an alkaline, slippery solution. Water also reacts with oxides. Quick lime, the common name for calcium oxide, is made in lime kilns across India, for example in parts of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. When a small piece of quick lime is added to water, the mixture becomes very hot, a hissing sound is heard, and a white solid called slaked lime is produced. The quick lime has changed into a different substance, so this is a clear case of a chemical change marked by heat evolution.
Ammonium chloride behaves differently. When it is stirred into water it disappears and the beaker feels cool, but no new substance appears; if the water is gently evaporated, the white solid returns. This is a physical change, a dissolution, and the cool feeling is due to the energy needed to separate the particles, not a chemical reaction. The same careful thinking applies to everyday examples. Dissolving sugar in water is a physical change because the sugar remains sugar, though invisible, and can be recovered by evaporation. Burning a match stick is a chemical change because heat, light, gas evolution and a new smell and ash appear. Respiration inside our cells is a chemical change because glucose and oxygen form new substances and release energy. Boiling an egg is a chemical change because the heat permanently changes the proteins and the egg can never become raw again. A taste change can also signal a chemical change; for example, cooked egg white tastes different from raw egg white. By understanding these signs, the student learns that water is not inert; its chemical properties include reaction with metals and oxides, and its involvement in processes that produce new substances.
eli5: Water is like a helpful friend who sometimes only mixes with things and sometimes really changes them. When sugar or salt disappears in water, you can get it back by drying the water -- that is a physical change. But when quick lime meets water, the mixture becomes hot and turns into a new chalky stuff called slaked lime, and a match stick burns to make ash and smoke -- those are chemical changes. The big idea is to watch for new stuff, heat, bubbles, light or a changed taste.

misconceptions.belief:
"Water is only a solvent; it never takes part in a chemical reaction."
The board examiner observations for 2024 and 2023 classification tasks noted that candidates could not correctly place water and other substances in the right columns, and the remedy given was to "Review topic fundamentals." This shows that many students see water only as something that dissolves other things. The correction is that water does have chemical properties; it can react with active metals and with oxides such as quick lime to form new substances, so it is not merely a mixing agent.

"If the beaker feels cool when ammonium chloride is added to water, a new substance must have formed."
The exam guidance on related topics show that students often confuse temperature changes with the formation of a new compound, and the remedy is again to review the fundamentals. The correction is that dissolving ammonium chloride is a physical change. The cool feeling comes from the energy needed to pull the particles apart, not from a chemical reaction. A new substance would have to show other indicators such as gas evolution, heat evolution or a permanent change in colour and taste.

"If a solid disappears in water, it has dissolved chemically."
The board examiner observations repeatedly point out that students fail to distinguish between simple disappearance and a real chemical change, which is why they must review topic fundamentals. The correction is that disappearance alone is not enough. Sugar disappearing in water is a physical dissolution because the sugar can be recovered unchanged. Quick lime disappearing in water is a chemical change because it becomes slaked lime, a new substance, with heat evolution and different properties.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What are the four main indicators that help us recognise a chemical change, and how do these indicators show that dissolving quick lime in water is a chemical change while dissolving sugar is a physical change?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The four main indicators that help us recognise a chemical change are the evolution of heat, the evolution of light, the evolution of a gas and a change in taste or smell. Sometimes a change in colour or the formation of a new residue can also help. When quick lime is added to water, several of these signs appear together: the mixture becomes very hot, which is heat evolution; a hissing sound is heard, which is caused by gas evolution; and the white solid that remains is a new substance called slaked lime, with different properties from quick lime. These signs make it clear that a chemical change has taken place and that water has taken part in a reaction with an oxide. On the other hand, when sugar is dissolved in water, none of these strong indicators is present. The sugar simply disappears into the water, but the water tastes sweet only because sugar is still present. If the water is allowed to evaporate, the sugar comes back in exactly the same form. There is no heat evolution, no gas evolution, no light and no change in the taste of the sugar itself. Therefore dissolving sugar in water is a physical change, a dissolution, while dissolving quick lime in water is a chemical change because a new substance is formed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student adds ammonium chloride to water and feels the beaker become cool. She says, "A new substance has formed because the temperature has changed." Is she correct? Compare what happens here with what happens when quick lime is added to water.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student is not correct, because a change in temperature by itself does not prove that a new substance has formed. When ammonium chloride is dissolved in water, the beaker feels cool because energy is taken in from the surroundings to separate the ammonium chloride particles and spread them through the water. This is a physical change, not a chemical reaction. If the water is slowly evaporated, the white ammonium chloride crystals reappear in their original form. No gas is evolved, no light is produced, and the substance does not change its identity; only its state of mixing changes. In contrast, when quick lime is added to water, a true chemical reaction takes place. The mixture becomes very hot because heat is evolved, a hissing sound shows that a gas is being released, and the quick lime is converted into a new substance, slaked lime, which has different properties from the starting material. The coolness of the ammonium chloride solution is an energy effect of dissolving, whereas the heat from quick lime and water is a sign that new chemical bonds are being made and a new substance is being produced.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Consider the statement: "Since water is needed for life and feels so ordinary, it does not take part in chemical reactions; it only dissolves things." Evaluate this statement, giving examples to support your judgment.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly true and is misleading as a whole. It is true that water is needed for life and that it often acts as a solvent. Many everyday changes, such as dissolving sugar or ammonium chloride in water, are physical dissolutions in which water simply spreads the other substance around without changing its chemical identity. In this sense, water behaves as a wonderful mixing agent. However, the claim that water never takes part in chemical reactions is false. Water has definite chemical properties and can react with certain metals and oxides. For example, when a small piece of calcium is dropped into water, hydrogen gas is released and a slippery, alkaline substance forms. When quick lime reacts with water, a new substance called slaked lime is formed and the mixture becomes very hot. Water is also involved in burning and respiration, where it appears as a product of the chemical change. Therefore, the correct view is that water is a versatile substance: sometimes it only dissolves things physically, and sometimes it joins a chemical reaction to form a new substance. The examples of quick lime, reactive metals, burning and respiration all show that water is far from being chemically inert, so the statement should be rejected as a general rule.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Four events are described: A) A piece of sodium is dropped into water, bubbles appear and the water becomes soapy; B) Sugar is stirred into a glass of water; C) A matchstick is struck and burns, producing light, heat and a black residue; D) An egg is boiled in water until it becomes solid and its taste changes.
