Borewell water in many parts of Punjab and Haryana passes through soil and rocks rich in calcium and magnesium salts, so it dissolves these mineral ions and becomes hard. The Munnar rainwater sample is soft water because rainwater has very few dissolved salts and lathers quickly. To soften the Ludhiana sample, the student could first boil a small amount and see whether a white scale forms. If the hardness is temporary, boiling will convert the soluble bicarbonates into insoluble carbonates and the water will lather more easily. If the water is still hard after boiling, the hardness is likely permanent, and adding a small amount of washing soda would be more suitable. The washing soda provides carbonate ions that react with the calcium and magnesium ions to form insoluble carbonates, which settle out and can be removed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple activity for your class to show the difference in lather formation between hard and soft water using only soap, water samples and washing soda.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, collect two labelled samples, one of hard water and one of soft water. The hard water can be taken from a tap known for hardness or made by dissolving a tiny amount of calcium chloride, CaCl2, in soft water, while the soft water can be distilled or rainwater. Take two identical test tubes or small glass bottles. Add equal amounts of each sample and a few drops of a soap solution. Stopper and shake each one for the same number of seconds. The soft water will produce a thick, stable lather quickly, while the hard water will first form a sticky white scum at the top and lather poorly. Next, add a small pinch of washing soda to the hard-water tube and shake again. The students will see that the lather improves because the washing soda has removed the calcium and magnesium ions by forming insoluble carbonates. This activity clearly shows both the lather test for hard and soft water and the softening action of washing soda.

masteryCriteria: Can define hard water (does not lather with soap easily due to dissolved Ca and Mg salts) and soft water (lathers easily); can distinguish temporary hardness (removed by boiling: caused by bicarbonates) from permanent hardness (not removed by boiling: caused by chlorides/sulphates); can state one method to remove each type.

title: Carbon - occurrence and allotropes
subject: chem
definition:
Allotropy is the property by which one and the same element can exist in two or more different physical forms, each of which is called an allotrope. Carbon is the best example of an element that shows this remarkable behaviour. Diamond, graphite, coke, coal, and soot are all forms of the same element, carbon, yet they look and behave very differently because the carbon atoms are joined together in different ways. The forms in which the atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern are called crystalline allotropes, while those in which the atoms lack such a regular arrangement are called amorphous allotropes. Diamond and graphite are the most important crystalline allotropes of carbon. In diamond, each carbon atom is strongly bonded to four other carbon atoms in a rigid three-dimensional network, which makes diamond extremely hard, transparent, and a non-conductor of electricity. In graphite, each carbon atom is bonded to three others in flat, hexagonal layers, and the layers are held loosely by weak forces so that they can slide over one another. This layered arrangement makes graphite soft, black, slippery, and a good conductor of electricity because some electrons can move freely between the layers.

The amorphous forms of carbon include coal, coke, and soot. Coal is a natural, black, amorphous solid found in layers under the earth, especially in the coal fields of Jharia, Bokaro, and Raniganj in India. It is used mainly as a fuel. Coke is obtained by heating coal strongly in the absence of air, and it is used as a fuel and as a reducing agent in the extraction of metals in blast furnaces. Soot is the fine, black powder left behind when carbon-rich substances like wood, coal, or diesel burn in a limited supply of air; it is used in making printer's ink, shoe polish, and carbon black. A fullerene, such as buckminsterfullerene, is also a form of carbon, though it is not a focus at this stage. The most important idea to remember is that all these substances contain only carbon atoms, so they have the same chemical properties. For example, each of them burns in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide. However, their physical properties, such as hardness, colour, electrical conductivity, and thermal conductivity, are very different, and these differences arise entirely from the different arrangement of carbon atoms in their structures.
eli5: Carbon is like one kind of Lego brick that can be built into many different things. If you build it into a strong cage, you get diamond, which is very hard and shiny. If you build it into flat sheets that can slide, you get graphite, which is dark and can be used in pencils. If you just pile the pieces messily, you get things like coal and soot. They are all made of the same carbon brick, but the shape they are built into makes them look and behave differently.

misconceptions.belief: Some students think that diamond and graphite are different elements because they look and behave so differently. This is like the confusion examiners reported when candidates wrote the name of a product or chose the wrong reagent because they did not read the question carefully. The correction is that diamond and graphite are both pure carbon; they are allotropes of the same element, and their different physical properties are due to their different structures, not because they are different elements.

Some students believe that amorphous forms such as coal, coke, and soot are not forms of carbon because they are black, soft, and do not have a crystal shape. This is a mistake similar to the examiner observation that candidates sometimes give the formula or name of a compound instead of the answer the question really wants. The correction is that these amorphous substances are also mostly carbon, just without the regular arrangement of atoms found in diamond and graphite.

Some students say that diamond and graphite have different chemical properties because their structures are different. The correction is that their physical properties are different, but their chemical properties are the same. For instance, both diamond and graphite burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide, because both contain only carbon atoms.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define allotropy and give the names of two crystalline and two amorphous allotropes of carbon.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Allotropy is the property by which an element exists in two or more different forms, each of which is called an allotrope. These different forms contain the same kind of atoms but differ in the way the atoms are arranged. For example, carbon shows allotropy in several forms. The two important crystalline allotropes of carbon are diamond and graphite. Diamond has a rigid three-dimensional arrangement of carbon atoms, while graphite has carbon atoms arranged in flat, hexagonal layers. The two important amorphous allotropes are coal and coke. Coal is a natural, black, amorphous solid found under the earth and used mainly as a fuel. Coke is produced by heating coal in the absence of air and is used as a fuel and as a reducing agent in the extraction of metals. Soot is another amorphous form of carbon, produced by the incomplete burning of carbon-rich substances. Thus, crystalline forms show a regular arrangement, while amorphous forms do not, but all of them are made of carbon atoms.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms, yet diamond does not conduct electricity while graphite does. Explain why this is so.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms, but they have very different structures, and this makes their electrical conductivities different. In diamond, every carbon atom is bonded to four other carbon atoms in a strong three-dimensional network. All the outer electrons of the carbon atoms are used up in forming these strong covalent bonds, so there are no free electrons that can move and carry electric current. That is why diamond is an electrical insulator. In graphite, every carbon atom is bonded to three other carbon atoms in flat layers. Because each carbon atom forms only three bonds, one electron in each atom is left free. These free electrons are shared within each layer and can move easily from one carbon atom to another. When an electric field is applied, these free electrons move along the layers, allowing graphite to conduct electricity. However, the movement is easier within the layers than between them, so the conductivity of graphite is higher along the layers than across them. This difference in the bonding and arrangement of atoms explains why graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Diamond and graphite are different substances because they have different arrangements of carbon atoms, so they must also have different chemical properties." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly true, and the conclusion is wrong. It is true that diamond and graphite have different arrangements of carbon atoms, and that is why they are called allotropes. In diamond the atoms are arranged in a strong three-dimensional network, while in graphite they are arranged in flat, sliding layers. This difference in structure gives diamond and graphite very different physical properties: diamond is hard, transparent, and a non-conductor of electricity, whereas graphite is soft, black, slippery, and a good conductor of electricity. However, the arrangement of atoms does not change the kind of element. Both diamond and graphite contain only carbon atoms, so they have the same chemical properties. For example, both of them burn in air or oxygen to give the same product, carbon dioxide. Both of them react in the same way when heated strongly with oxygen, and both would be oxidised to the same oxide because the element is the same. Therefore, the student is correct in saying that the arrangements are different, but incorrect in saying that the chemical properties are different. The correct view is that diamond and graphite have the same chemical properties but different physical properties, and these physical differences are due only to the different arrangement of atoms.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Choose the most suitable carbon allotrope for each of the following uses and explain your choice: (a) making the point of a pencil that leaves a dark mark, (b) cutting a glass sheet, (c) lining the inside of a chimney to collect a black pigment, (d) reducing iron oxide in a blast furnace. Refer to Indian examples where possible.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For the point of a pencil, graphite is the most suitable choice. Graphite is made of layers of carbon atoms that slide over one another easily, so it leaves a soft, dark, slippery mark on paper. That is why pencil leads, especially those made from graphite mined in places like Sivaganga in Tamil Nadu, write smoothly. For cutting a glass sheet, diamond is the most suitable choice. Diamond is the hardest natural substance known because its carbon atoms are held in a very strong three-dimensional network. Diamonds from the Panna mines in Madhya Pradesh are used in cutting tools and drills. For collecting a black pigment from a chimney, soot is the obvious choice. Soot is the black, powdery residue formed when carbon fuels burn incompletely, and it is used to make black inks, paints, and carbon black. For reducing iron oxide in a blast furnace, coke is the best choice. Coke is made by heating coal strongly in the absence of air, and it is a strong reducing agent and a good fuel. Indian steel plants such as those at Bhilai and Rourkela use coke in their blast furnaces to reduce iron ores to iron.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple working model or demonstration that can help your classmates see why diamond is hard and why graphite is slippery.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A good model can be built using only two things: strong glue and a stack of light cardboard or thin plastic sheets. To show the structure of diamond, take many small beads or balls and glue them together so that each ball is joined to four others at the corners of a small pyramid or cage. This makes a rigid, three-dimensional structure that cannot be pressed or pulled out of shape easily. When your classmates try to squeeze or bend it, they will feel how strong it is, just like diamond. To show the structure of graphite, take several rectangular sheets of cardboard or plastic and stack them on top of one another without gluing between them. Tape one end of the stack to the table so that it does not fall, and let your classmates slide the sheets sideways with their fingers. The sheets will move easily over one another, showing how the layers in graphite can slide and make the substance feel slippery. You can also draw hexagons on each sheet to show the ring arrangement of carbon atoms within each layer. Label both models clearly, and write a short note saying that both are made of carbon but the different arrangement of atoms makes one hard and the other soft and slippery.

masteryCriteria: Can state that carbon occurs in nature as diamond and graphite (allotropes); can define allotropes as different forms of the same element; can compare diamond (hardest, transparent, non-conductor) and graphite (soft, black, conductor); can state two uses of each (diamond: jewellery, cutting; graphite: pencils, electrodes).

title: Reactivity series of metals
subject: chem
definition:
The reactivity series of metals is a ranked list of common metals arranged in order of their chemical reactivity, from the most reactive to the least reactive. The standard order you must remember for the ICSE Class 8 syllabus is: potassium > sodium > calcium > magnesium > aluminium > zinc > iron > copper > silver > gold. This order is built on how vigorously a metal reacts with cold water, hot water, steam and dilute acids, and on whether one metal can displace another metal from its compound. At the top, potassium and sodium are so reactive that they fizz, dart about and may even catch fire when dropped into cold water, so they are stored under oil. Calcium reacts with cold water more gently, producing hydrogen gas and a milky suspension of calcium hydroxide. Magnesium reacts only slowly with cold water but burns brightly in steam to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen. Aluminium, zinc and iron react with steam when heated, giving their oxides and hydrogen, but they do not react usefully with cold water. Copper, silver and gold are far less reactive and do not react with water or dilute acids under ordinary conditions; that is why gold and silver can occur in nature as free metals, for example in the Kolar Gold Fields of Karnataka or in the silver-rich ores of Rajasthan.

Reactivity is best understood as a metal's eagerness to lose electrons and become a positive ion, called a cation. The higher a metal sits in the series, the more readily it loses electrons. This idea explains the most important use of the reactivity series: predicting displacement reactions. A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from an aqueous solution of its salt, because the more reactive metal has a stronger tendency to form ions in solution. For instance, when a strip of zinc is dipped into blue copper(II) sulphate solution, the zinc slowly disappears and a reddish-brown coating of copper appears; the blue colour fades because zinc has displaced copper from the solution, forming colourless zinc sulphate. Similarly, when an iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulphate solution, the iron becomes coated with copper and the solution loses its blue colour. The reverse does not happen: a copper strip placed in zinc sulphate or iron(II) sulphate solution will show no reaction, because copper is less reactive than both zinc and iron.

The reactivity series also helps us explain why some metals are extracted from their ores by simple heating, while others need smelting or electrolysis. Reactive metals such as aluminium need expensive extraction because they hold their oxygen very tightly, whereas less reactive metals such as iron can be extracted from haematite in the blast furnaces of Rourkela or Durgapur using coke as a reducing agent. Copper from the Khetri mines of Rajasthan and iron from the Singhbhum belt of Jharkhand make sense in an Indian context once you see that India's mineral wealth and the reactivity of the metal together decide how the metal is obtained. The key terms to carry forward are reactivity series, reactive metal, less reactive metal, displacement, and the names of the metals themselves: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver and gold.
eli5: Imagine a ladder of metals, with the strongest jumpers at the top. Potassium and sodium leap straight into cold water; calcium climbs slowly; magnesium and zinc need a hot stove; copper and gold just sit still. A metal higher on the ladder can push a lower metal out of its compound, but a lower metal cannot push a higher one. That ladder is the reactivity series.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Write the reactivity series of the following metals in the correct order: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold. Also state the general rule that this series helps you predict.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The correct reactivity series, from the most reactive to the least reactive, is potassium > sodium > calcium > magnesium > aluminium > zinc > iron > copper > silver > gold. This order can be remembered by the behaviour of these metals with water and steam. Potassium and sodium react explosively with cold water; calcium reacts steadily; magnesium, aluminium, zinc and iron need steam or dilute acids; copper does not react with water or dilute acids; silver and gold are very unreactive. The general rule the series helps us predict is that a more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a compound. Therefore, if a metal higher in the series is added to the salt solution of a metal lower in the series, a displacement reaction will occur and the lower metal will be set free. If the reverse is tried, no displacement takes place. This rule is useful in the laboratory for preparing one metal from another and in industry for choosing methods of extracting metals from their ores.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution, using the example of iron and copper(II) sulphate solution.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal because it has a greater tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions in solution. In the reactivity series, iron is above copper, which means an iron atom loses its outer electrons more easily than a copper atom. When an iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulphate solution, each iron atom gives up two electrons to become an iron(II) ion and enters the solution. The copper(II) ions in the solution accept these electrons and are reduced to copper atoms, which settle as a reddish-brown solid on the nail. The blue colour of the copper(II) sulphate solution fades because the copper ions are being removed and replaced by colourless iron(II) ions. The overall reaction is Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. This is a single displacement reaction driven by the difference in reactivity. Copper cannot do the same to iron because copper atoms hold their electrons more tightly and are less willing to become ions.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student claims that, if copper powder is heated strongly in zinc sulphate solution for a long time, copper will finally displace zinc from the solution because heat gives the copper atoms enough energy. Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's claim is not correct for ordinary laboratory conditions, and the reasoning confuses the effect of heat on reaction speed with the possibility of the reaction itself. The reactivity series is based on the inherent tendency of metals to lose electrons. Zinc is above copper, so zinc atoms have a stronger tendency to form ions than copper atoms do. This means zinc can displace copper from copper(II) sulphate, but copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulphate. Heating the mixture may make the particles move faster and could speed up a reaction that is already possible, but it cannot reverse the order of reactivity. No amount of ordinary heating will make copper atoms give away electrons to zinc ions because copper is the less reactive metal. On the other hand, the balanced part of the argument is that energy from an external electric current, as in electrolysis, can force a non-spontaneous change. In electrolysis, electrical energy drives oxidation and reduction in a way that heat alone cannot. However, in the context of a simple displacement reaction, the correct evaluation is that copper will not displace zinc from zinc sulphate, even on strong heating, because copper is below zinc in the reactivity series.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Predict whether the following displacement reactions will occur. Where a reaction occurs, write the balanced word or chemical equation; where it does not, write "no reaction" and give a reason. (i) Zinc granules are added to copper(II) sulphate solution. (ii) A copper wire is dipped into iron(II) sulphate solution. (iii) A magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (i) The reaction will occur because zinc is above copper in the reactivity series. Zinc is more reactive and displaces copper from copper(II) sulphate. The blue solution slowly becomes colourless as zinc sulphate forms, and reddish-brown copper metal is deposited. The equation is Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu. (ii) No reaction will occur. Copper is below iron in the reactivity series, so copper cannot displace iron from iron(II) sulphate solution. The copper wire remains unchanged and the green colour of iron(II) sulphate stays the same. (iii) The reaction will occur because magnesium is well above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas, which is seen as brisk effervescence. The equation is Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. These three examples show how the reactivity series can be used to predict not only metal-to-metal displacement but also reaction with acids.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple laboratory experiment, using zinc granules, an iron nail and a piece of copper wire, to show the relative reactivity of these three metals. Include the materials, procedure, observation table and the expected conclusion.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The experiment can be performed with three small test tubes, copper(II) sulphate solution, iron(II) sulphate solution, zinc sulphate solution, zinc granules, a clean iron nail and a small piece of copper wire. Label three test tubes A, B and C. In tube A place zinc granules in copper(II) sulphate solution. In tube B place the iron nail in copper(II) sulphate solution. In tube C place the copper wire in zinc sulphate solution. For an extra comparison, you may also place zinc in iron(II) sulphate. Leave the tubes for about fifteen minutes and observe. In tube A, the zinc granules become coated with a reddish-brown solid and the blue colour fades, showing zinc displaces copper. In tube B, the iron nail also becomes coated with copper and the blue colour fades, but more slowly, showing iron is less reactive than zinc. In tube C, no change is seen, confirming copper cannot displace zinc. The conclusion is that the reactivity order among these three metals is zinc > iron > copper. For safety, wear gloves and goggles; do not touch the metals with bare hands after the reaction; and wash the apparatus thoroughly after use.

masteryCriteria: Can state the reactivity series (K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu > Ag > Au); can use the series to predict if a displacement reaction will occur; can explain why potassium reacts violently with water while gold does not react at all.

title: Hydrogen - preparation and properties
subject: chem
definition:
Hydrogen is the lightest known gas and the first element in the periodic table. In its free state it exists as a diatomic molecule, written H2, which means every molecule of hydrogen contains two atoms of the same element joined together. Because it is so simple and so common, hydrogen appears in many substances the child already knows: water (H2O), acids such as hydrochloric acid (HCl) and sulphuric acid (H2SO4), ammonia (NH3), methane (CH4), and in all living things. In ICSE Class 8 the focus is on the laboratory preparation of hydrogen and a careful study of its physical and chemical properties.

In the laboratory, hydrogen is prepared by the action of a dilute acid on a reactive metal. The metal must be above hydrogen in the reactivity series, because only such a metal is active enough to displace hydrogen from the acid. Zinc is the most convenient choice for school laboratories. It reacts at a safe, steady rate and is cheap and easy to handle. The usual apparatus is a Woulfe's bottle fitted with a thistle funnel and a delivery tube. Clean zinc granules are placed inside the bottle and dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid is poured through the thistle funnel. The acid rises to cover the zinc and bubbles of hydrogen gas begin to form. The chemical reactions may be written as: zinc plus dilute hydrochloric acid gives zinc chloride and hydrogen, and zinc plus dilute sulphuric acid gives zinc sulphate and hydrogen. The equations are Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 and Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2. The gas is collected by downward displacement of water, because hydrogen is only slightly soluble in water and is far lighter than air. An inverted jar or trough filled with water is placed over the delivery tube; the gas bubbles in, pushes the water out, and the jar becomes full of hydrogen.

Hydrogen has clear physical properties that help to identify and collect it. It is colourless, odourless, and tasteless. It is the lightest gas known, with a vapour density of one, and this low density explains why it rises rapidly in air. It is almost insoluble in water, neutral to litmus, and difficult to liquefy. Its chemical properties are just as important. Hydrogen burns in air or oxygen with a pale blue flame, producing water. This reaction is described as the combustion of hydrogen. When a burning splinter is brought near a jar of hydrogen, the gas burns with a characteristic 'pop' sound; this is the famous pop test used to recognise hydrogen. Hydrogen is also a good reducing agent. When passed over heated black copper oxide, it removes oxygen and converts the oxide to reddish-brown copper metal while itself forming water. This behaviour is called reduction, and it shows that hydrogen has a strong attraction for oxygen. Hydrogen can also take part in hydrogenation, in which it adds to unsaturated organic compounds such as vegetable oils to make them more saturated, a reaction used in making vanaspati ghee in Indian kitchens. Overall, the study of hydrogen in Class 8 connects the reactivity series, the language of chemical equations, and the practical skills of gas preparation and testing.
eli5: Hydrogen is a very light, invisible gas. In the lab we make it by dropping clean bits of zinc into a weak acid. Bubbles of hydrogen form, and we trap them in an upside-down jar full of water. Hydrogen rises like a balloon and burns with a small "pop" sound. It can also pull oxygen away from some hot powders, turning them back into shiny metals.

misconceptions.belief: "The gas is H, not H2." CISCE Common board exam error pattern data from 2020 notes that some candidates "got confused with Hydrogen" when identifying compounds. The correction is that free hydrogen gas is a diatomic molecule and must always be written as H2. The letter H alone is the symbol for one atom of hydrogen or the hydrogen ion in an acid.

"Any metal with any acid will give hydrogen." Many students ignore the reactivity series and choose copper, silver, or even concentrated sulphuric acid. The correction is that only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series, such as zinc, magnesium, or iron, react with a dilute acid to produce hydrogen. Copper will not react, and concentrated sulphuric acid is not the right choice because it acts as an oxidising agent.

"Because hydrogen is the lightest gas, we collect it with the mouth of the jar upward." This is wrong. The correct method is downward displacement of water, that is, an inverted jar filled with water. Hydrogen is only slightly soluble in water and lighter than air, so it pushes the water out and stays trapped inside the inverted jar.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe the laboratory preparation of hydrogen using zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid. Your answer should include the apparatus, the balanced equation, and the method of collection.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In the laboratory, hydrogen is prepared by reacting clean zinc granules with dilute hydrochloric acid in a Woulfe's bottle. The bottle is fitted with a rubber stopper carrying a thistle funnel and a delivery tube. The lower end of the thistle funnel is dipped below the acid so that the gas formed cannot escape through the funnel. When dilute hydrochloric acid comes into contact with the zinc, a brisk but controlled reaction takes place and bubbles of hydrogen gas are liberated. The balanced equation is Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. One atom of zinc reacts with two molecules of hydrochloric acid to produce one molecule of zinc chloride and one molecule of hydrogen gas. The hydrogen gas is collected by downward displacement of water because it is only slightly soluble in water and is much lighter than air. An inverted gas jar is placed over water with the mouth below the water level, the delivery tube is inserted, and the hydrogen bubbles rise into the jar, pushing the water out. Once filled, the jar can be removed and tested. It is important to use dilute acid and clean zinc granules; dirty zinc with a surface oxide layer reacts slowly at first, and concentrated acid would give different products such as sulphur dioxide.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is hydrogen collected by downward displacement of water, and why is zinc rather than copper the preferred metal for this preparation?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Hydrogen is collected by downward displacement of water for two reasons: it is almost insoluble in water, and it is the lightest gas known. Because it is much lighter than air, an open jar held mouth upward would allow the gas to escape quickly. When the jar is inverted and placed over water, the hydrogen rises through the delivery tube into the jar and pushes the water downward and out, so the jar fills with pure gas. If the gas were highly soluble, it would dissolve in the water before the jar could be filled, so this method would not work. Zinc is preferred over copper because zinc is well above hydrogen in the reactivity series. A metal above hydrogen is reactive enough to displace hydrogen from an acid. Copper lies below hydrogen, so it cannot displace hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid and no hydrogen is produced. Zinc is also preferred over very reactive metals such as sodium or potassium because it reacts at a safe, steady rate and does not cause a violent explosion. The large surface area of granules gives good contact with the acid while keeping the reaction under control. Thus the choice of zinc and the method of collection are both dictated by the physical and chemical properties of hydrogen and the position of the metal in the reactivity series.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Hydrogen can be prepared safely in the school laboratory by adding a large piece of sodium to dilute sulphuric acid and collecting the gas in a jar held mouth upward over water, because hydrogen is the lightest gas." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly correct but mostly incorrect, and it would be unsafe if followed. It is true that hydrogen is the lightest known gas, and it is true that it is produced when an active metal reacts with an acid. However, using a large piece of sodium is a serious mistake. Sodium is a very reactive alkali metal that lies well above hydrogen in the reactivity series. It reacts explosively with dilute acids and even with water, producing a large amount of heat and hydrogen so rapidly that the gas can ignite. Therefore sodium is completely unsuitable for the safe, controlled preparation of hydrogen in a school laboratory. The correct metal is zinc, which reacts at a moderate and manageable rate. The second error is the collection method. Although the statement correctly notes that hydrogen is the lightest gas, it draws the wrong conclusion. Hydrogen is not collected with the mouth of the jar upward; it is collected by downward displacement of water, which means the gas jar is inverted and placed over water. This works because hydrogen is almost insoluble in water and is lighter than air, so it rises into the jar and displaces the water. If the jar were held mouth upward, the hydrogen would escape into the air and the water would fall out, so almost no gas would be collected. In summary, the statement contains a grain of truth about the lightest gas, but its choice of metal and its collection method are wrong and dangerous. A safe, correct description uses zinc granules with dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid in a Woulfe's bottle, and collects the gas by downward displacement of water.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student is given four samples: magnesium ribbon, copper turnings, dilute hydrochloric acid, and dilute sulphuric acid. He also has a Woulfe's bottle, a thistle funnel, a delivery tube, a water trough, and an inverted gas jar. Which metal and which acid should he choose to prepare hydrogen safely? Draw or describe the correct set-up and the test he should use to confirm that the gas is hydrogen.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student should choose magnesium ribbon and either dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid. Magnesium is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it will displace hydrogen from the acid. Copper is below hydrogen, so it will not react and should not be chosen. Magnesium reacts more vigorously than zinc, so the student should use small pieces and control the acid flow through the thistle funnel to keep the reaction manageable. If he chooses dilute hydrochloric acid, the reaction is Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. The apparatus is set up as follows: place the magnesium in the Woulfe's bottle, fit the rubber stopper carrying the thistle funnel and the delivery tube, and add the acid until the lower end of the funnel is under the acid surface. The delivery tube is led into a water trough under an inverted gas jar so that the hydrogen is collected by downward displacement of water. To confirm the gas, he should bring a lighted splinter to the mouth of the gas jar. Hydrogen burns with a pale blue flame and a characteristic 'pop' sound. If the gas were air or carbon dioxide, it would either not burn or would extinguish the splinter. A steady collection of colourless, odourless gas that produces a pop on testing confirms that the gas is hydrogen.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a safe and clear classroom demonstration to show that hydrogen is a reducing agent. List the materials, the steps, and the expected observations, and explain the chemistry in simple terms.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To demonstrate that hydrogen is a reducing agent, the teacher should use a hard glass test tube, a small amount of black copper(II) oxide, a source of dry hydrogen, a Bunsen burner, a delivery tube with a small jet, and a clamp stand. First, heat the copper(II) oxide strongly in the hard glass test tube. Then pass a slow stream of dry hydrogen through the tube so that it flows over the hot oxide. The black powder will slowly turn reddish-brown, and tiny droplets of water will appear on the cooler parts of the tube. The chemistry is that hydrogen takes oxygen away from the copper oxide, leaving copper metal behind. This removal of oxygen is called reduction, and the substance that causes it, hydrogen, is called the reducing agent. The equation is CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O. To make the demonstration safe, the teacher should make sure the hydrogen is dry and that the tube is heated gently at first, because a mixture of hydrogen and air can explode. The experiment should be done in a fume-free, well-ventilated area, and the mouth of the tube should be directed away from students. After the reaction, the copper should be allowed to cool in a stream of hydrogen to prevent it from re-oxidising in hot air. This demonstration gives a clear, visible proof that hydrogen can remove oxygen from a metal oxide and is therefore a good reducing agent.

masteryCriteria: Can write equations for hydrogen preparation (Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2); can describe the apparatus and collection method (downward displacement of water); can state three properties of hydrogen (lightest gas, colourless, burns with pop sound) and two uses (fuel, reducing agent).

title: Water - properties and composition
subject: chem
definition:
Water is the most familiar and essential compound on Earth, represented by the chemical formula H2O. This formula tells us that a single molecule of water is made up of two atoms of hydrogen and one atom of oxygen joined together chemically in a fixed proportion. When water is decomposed by electrolysis, hydrogen and oxygen gases are produced in the ratio of two volumes of hydrogen to one volume of oxygen, which is why we say that the composition of water is H2O with hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 ratio by volume. Since the two elements have combined in a fixed ratio and have lost their original properties, water is a compound and not a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.

Water is called the universal solvent because it can dissolve a large number of substances, especially salts such as sodium chloride, sugar, copper sulphate, and many acids, bases, and gases. When a substance dissolves in water, the substance that gets dissolved is called the solute and the liquid that does the dissolving is called the solvent. The liquid formed after dissolution is called a solution. A solution is a homogeneous mixture, which means that the solute particles are evenly spread throughout the solvent and you cannot see them separately. For example, when sodium chloride is stirred into water, the salt crystals disappear and the water tastes salty throughout, showing that the mixture is homogeneous.

The physical properties of pure water are easy to observe in daily life. It is a colourless, odourless, and tasteless liquid under ordinary conditions. It boils at 100 degrees Celsius at normal atmospheric pressure and freezes at 0 degrees Celsius to form ice. It is also a poor conductor of electricity in its pure state, though it can conduct electricity when salts, acids, or bases are dissolved in it. Water exists in all three states of matter: as ice in the solid state, as water in the liquid state, and as steam or water vapour in the gaseous state.

Water is used for many purposes in everyday life. In households it is used for drinking, cooking, cleaning, washing, and bathing. In agriculture it is used for watering plants and irrigating fields. Industries need water for cooling, cleaning, and as a solvent in many chemical processes. We obtain water from natural resources such as wells, rivers, hand pumps, lakes, and ponds. In India, the Ganga, the Yamuna, the Godavari, the Krishna, and the Kaveri are major rivers, while lakes such as Dal Lake in Kashmir, Chilka Lake in Odisha, and Hussain Sagar in Telangana also hold large quantities of water. Hand pumps and tube-wells are common sources in rural areas, especially in states such as Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh. Because all life on Earth depends on water for survival, it is one of the most important substances we study in chemistry.
eli5: Water is a special liquid that every living thing needs. It is made of tiny building blocks called H2O, with two parts of hydrogen and one part of oxygen. Water can mix with many things like salt and sugar, so it is called a universal solvent. It has no colour, no smell, and no taste, and it turns to ice when very cold and to steam when very hot.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define solute, solvent, and solution. Give one example of each from the case of sodium chloride dissolving in water.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A solute is the substance that gets dissolved in a liquid to form a solution, a solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving, and a solution is the homogeneous mixture that is produced. In the case of sodium chloride dissolving in water, sodium chloride is the solute because it is the solid that breaks up and spreads through the liquid, water is the solvent because it is the liquid that dissolves the salt, and the clear salty liquid that results is called a solution. This solution is a homogeneous mixture because the salt particles are evenly distributed and the liquid looks the same throughout. If you take a spoonful from any part of the glass, it will taste equally salty, which shows that the salt has not settled down or disappeared but has mixed uniformly. The process by which the solute mixes with the solvent is called dissolution, and it is important to remember that the solute keeps its chemical identity even though we cannot see it as a separate substance.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is water called a universal solvent? Explain with the help of its composition.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Water is called a universal solvent because it has the ability to dissolve a large number of substances, especially salts such as sodium chloride, sugar, copper sulphate, and many common acids and bases. The reason for this behaviour is found in its composition. A water molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom arranged in a bent shape with the formula H2O. This arrangement makes the water molecule behave like a tiny magnet, with a slightly positive side near the hydrogen atoms and a slightly negative side near the oxygen atom. When an ionic compound such as sodium chloride comes into contact with water, the water molecules pull the positive sodium ions and the negative chloride ions away from each other and spread them throughout the liquid. Because water can do this for many ionic and polar substances, it is called a universal solvent. It is important to note that water does not dissolve every substance; oils, fats, and many non-polar substances do not dissolve in it, so the word "universal" means "a very wide range" and not "all" substances.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Because water is a universal solvent, it can dissolve every substance. Therefore, it does not matter which source of water we use for drinking or for industry." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true but mostly incorrect, so it must be evaluated carefully. It is true that water is often called a universal solvent because it dissolves a very large number of substances, especially salts, sugars, acids, and bases. This property makes it extremely useful in homes, farms, and industries. However, the first part of the statement is wrong because water cannot dissolve every substance. Substances such as oil, grease, sand, and chalk are not soluble in water, and even among salts, the amount that can dissolve is limited. Therefore, "universal solvent" means that water dissolves many substances, not all. The second part of the statement is also wrong because the source of water matters a great deal. Water from a river, lake, well, or hand pump may contain dissolved salts, mud, bacteria, and pollutants. Some dissolved salts make water hard, which is not good for washing or industrial boilers, while some pollutants can make water unsafe for drinking. Sea water contains many dissolved salts and is not safe to drink without treatment. Therefore, we must choose water sources carefully and, when necessary, purify water before using it for drinking or for sensitive industrial work. In conclusion, the student's statement is an oversimplification and is not correct as it stands.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A colourless, odourless, and tasteless liquid is given to you in a beaker. A student claims it must be pure water. Describe how you would check whether it is really pure water, and if 50 cm3 of this liquid is electrolysed completely, what would you expect to observe at the electrodes?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Although the liquid is colourless, odourless, and tasteless, these are only some of the physical properties of water. To confirm that it is pure water, I would also check its boiling point and freezing point. Pure water boils at exactly 100 degrees Celsius at normal atmospheric pressure and freezes at 0 degrees Celsius. If the liquid boils a few degrees above 100 degrees Celsius or freezes a few degrees below 0 degrees Celsius, it probably contains dissolved substances and is not pure water. I would also check whether it conducts electricity; pure water is a very poor conductor, while water containing dissolved salts will conduct electricity. If 50 cm3 of the pure liquid is electrolysed, it would break into hydrogen and oxygen gases. The volume of hydrogen gas collected at the cathode would be twice the volume of oxygen gas collected at the anode, that is, about 33.3 cm3 of hydrogen and about 16.7 cm3 of oxygen. This 2:1 volume ratio is the test that confirms the composition of water as H2O.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine that your school wants to start a project to protect a local water resource such as a pond, lake, well, or hand pump. Design a simple action plan that uses what you have learnt about water and its properties.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For the school project, I would choose a village pond near the school and name it "Clean Water for Life." First, I would form a team of students and teachers to study the pond. We would observe the colour, smell, and clarity of the water and check whether any waste or garbage is being thrown into it. Since water is a universal solvent, it can easily dissolve harmful chemicals and animal waste, so keeping the pond clean is very important. Next, we would install dustbins around the pond and put up posters telling people not to throw waste into the water. We would also plant a few trees on the banks to prevent soil from washing into the pond. Once a week, students would test the water by observing whether it is clear and odourless, and we would report any change in colour or smell to the village head. Finally, we would hold a small meeting with parents and villagers to explain that water is needed for life, that it can dissolve many substances, and that a dirty pond can spread disease. Through this project, the whole village would learn to value and protect its water resource.

masteryCriteria: Can state the composition of water (H2O: two hydrogen atoms, one oxygen atom); can describe the electrolysis of water (H2 at cathode, O2 at anode, ratio 2:1 by volume); can state five physical properties (colourless, tasteless, odourless, boils at 100 deg C, freezes at 0 deg C, density 1 g/cm3).

title: Water - treatment and pollution
subject: chem
definition:
Water is a chemical compound of hydrogen and oxygen, but the water we meet in daily life is never H2O alone; it carries dissolved salts, gases, and sometimes living organisms. When these extra substances are harmless, we may call it fresh or potable; when they become harmful to life or use, we call the condition water pollution. Water pollution is the introduction of unwanted and dangerous matter into rivers, lakes, ponds, seas, groundwater, or even stored tanks in amounts that make the water unsafe for drinking, agriculture, industry, or for the organisms that live in it. The common causes of water pollution are the discharge of sewage, which is the waste water containing human and animal excreta, washing and kitchen refuse from homes and institutions; industrial waste, the liquid effluents from factories, tanneries, textile mills, and chemical plants that often carry heavy metals, acids, alkalis, and poisonous compounds; agricultural runoff, which is the rain or irrigation water that flows from fields and carries fertilisers, pesticides, and insecticides into nearby water bodies; and oil spills, which occur when crude oil or petroleum products leak from tankers, pipelines, refineries, or storage depots and coat the surface of rivers or seas with a thick layer, killing fish, birds, and plants. Other sources include washing clothes and cattle in ponds, dumping garbage and plastics, and thermal pollution from cooling water released by power plants. The effect is the destruction of aquatic life, spread of water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid, and shortage of usable water.

Water treatment is the set of processes by which polluted or raw water is made safe and acceptable for use. The most important municipal methods include filtration, in which suspended particles are removed by passing water through sand, gravel, or special membranes; sedimentation, in which water is left undisturbed in large tanks so that heavier particles settle to the bottom; chlorination, in which a controlled amount of chlorine is added to kill disease-causing bacteria and other microbes; and boiling, a simple home method in which water is heated to a rolling boil for a few minutes to destroy harmful germs. It is important to remember that boiling kills microbes but does not remove dissolved chemicals, oil, or heavy metals.

Conservation of water is the careful use and management of available water. Scarcity of water is already felt in many parts of India, especially during summer and in regions that receive low or uneven rainfall. Practical methods of conservation include rainwater harvesting, in which rain is collected from rooftops, courtyards, or catchments and stored in tanks, wells, or allowed to recharge underground sources; reducing domestic consumption by repairing leaking taps, using water-efficient taps and mugs, turning off taps while brushing, reusing water from washing vegetables to water plants, and taking shorter baths; and carrying out a water audit at home, in which the family records how much water is used each day and looks for places where it is being wasted. Projects such as the Ganga Action Plan, lake restoration in Bengaluru, and mandatory rooftop rainwater harvesting in Chennai show how treatment, prevention, and conservation work together to protect water resources.
eli5: Water is H2O with extra things dissolved in it, such as salts, air, and sometimes germs. When harmful extras from homes, factories, farms, or oil spills enter rivers and lakes, the water becomes polluted. We can clean it by letting mud settle, filtering it, adding a safe amount of chlorine, or boiling it. We can also save water by collecting rain, fixing leaking taps, washing cars with a bucket, and reusing water for plants.

misconceptions.belief: Many students say, 'If water looks clear, it is pure and safe to drink.' This is wrong because pollution can be invisible. Heavy metals, pesticides, and disease-causing microbes may be dissolved in clear water; that is why treatment is needed.
misconceptions.correction: Clearness only tells us there is no floating mud; it does not prove the water is free from germs or dissolved chemicals. Always use sedimentation, filtration, and chlorination for municipal water, and boil water if you are unsure of its source.

misconceptions.belief: board examiners have noticed that students often give incomplete answers. In the provided examiner observations, candidates wrote only 'concentrated' instead of 'concentrated sulphuric acid' and lost marks. The same error appears in water treatment: a learner may write just 'chlorine' or 'filter' without naming the full process.
misconceptions.correction: In an exam, give the complete term and explain it: chlorination is the addition of chlorine to kill microbes; filtration is passing water through sand or a filter to remove suspended particles; sedimentation is allowing suspended particles to settle. Full sentences with complete terms fetch full marks.

misconceptions.belief: A common confusion, reflected in exam guidance on similar questions, is mixing up the conditions for two different reactions. In water studies, the parallel error is to treat chlorination and softening as the same thing, or to think that boiling removes every kind of impurity.
misconceptions.correction: Water softening removes calcium and magnesium salts from hard water; chlorination kills bacteria; boiling kills germs and removes temporary hardness but does not remove industrial chemicals, pesticides, or dissolved heavy metals. Filtration and sedimentation remove suspended matter, not dissolved chemicals. Keep the four methods and their purposes separate.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the four main causes of water pollution and explain the main stages through which raw water is treated in a municipal plant. Also give two ways to conserve water in a household.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
Water pollution has four main causes, and each comes from a different human activity. Sewage is waste water from homes, schools, hospitals, and animal sheds, containing excreta, soaps, food waste, and disease-causing germs. Industrial waste includes liquid effluents from factories, tanneries, and chemical works, which may contain acids, alkalis, heavy metals like lead and mercury, and poisonous organic compounds. Agricultural runoff is water that flows from fields after irrigation or rain, carrying fertilisers, pesticides, and insecticides into rivers, lakes, and ponds. Oil spills occur when petroleum products leak from tankers, pipelines, refineries, or road accidents, forming a layer on the water that stops oxygen from reaching aquatic life.

The treatment of raw water in a municipal supply usually follows a sequence. First, large floating matter is removed by screens. Then sedimentation is carried out, in which the water is held in large tanks so that heavier, suspended particles sink to the bottom. The partially settled water is then passed through beds of sand and gravel in filtration to remove finer suspended particles. Finally, chlorination is done by adding a measured amount of chlorine to kill harmful bacteria and viruses. At home, water can be made safer by boiling, which destroys disease-causing germs but does not remove dissolved chemicals.

Conservation can be practiced at home by reducing domestic consumption and by rainwater harvesting. Reducing consumption means turning off taps when they are not needed, using a mug or bucket instead of running water, repairing leaks, and reusing waste water for cleaning or gardening. Rainwater harvesting means collecting rain from rooftops, storing it in tanks, or directing it into wells and boreholes so that groundwater is recharged.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student argues that since boiling can make water safe, a city does not need sedimentation, filtration, and chlorination. Explain why the student is wrong, using the difference between suspended matter and dissolved or microscopic impurities.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Boiling is an excellent domestic method for killing many disease-causing germs, but it cannot solve every kind of water problem, so it cannot replace the full treatment given by a city. First, boiling does not remove suspended matter such as mud, sand, dead leaves, and solid waste. If a whole city tried to boil muddy river water, the water would still look dirty and taste unpleasant, and the suspended particles could carry chemicals on their surfaces. That is why the city first lets the water stand for sedimentation, so that the heavy particles sink, and then passes it through filtration to remove the lighter, finer particles. Second, boiling does not remove dissolved impurities such as dissolved salts, acids, alkalis, pesticides, or heavy metals. In cities such as Kanpur, the Ganga carries effluents from tanneries that may contain dissolved chromium and other chemicals; boiling would not remove these. Third, boiling cannot be used to treat the huge volumes of water supplied to thousands of homes; it is slow and needs fuel. Chlorination, on the other hand, can disinfect very large quantities of water with a measured dose of chlorine, making it suitable for an entire population. Therefore, boiling is useful for the final step at home, but sedimentation, filtration, and chlorination are necessary for a clean and safe public water supply.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Consider this statement: 'If every house in India simply boils its drinking water, then water pollution in rivers and lakes will be solved and there will be no need for laws against industrial waste or sewage discharge.' Evaluate the statement, giving a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
This statement is only partly true and is mostly wrong, because it confuses two different things: making a small amount of water safe for one family, and keeping the whole water environment clean. Boiling is a good household practice. When water from a reliable source is heated to a rolling boil, most of the disease-causing germs are killed, so the family can drink it with less risk of cholera, typhoid, or dysentery. In this narrow sense, boiling does protect people.

However, the statement is wrong when it claims that boiling would solve water pollution in rivers and lakes. Boiling only kills germs; it does not remove the cause of pollution. Sewage, industrial waste, agricultural runoff, and oil spills would still continue to pour into rivers. Boiling does not remove heavy metals like lead and mercury, pesticides, fertilisers, or oil. It also does nothing for the fish, plants, and animals that live in the polluted water. The argument is also wrong because it ignores conservation. If people boil all their water on a large scale, it will use a great deal of fuel and cause air pollution. Finally, laws and rules are needed because industries and towns will not stop polluting on their own. For example, the Ganga Action Plan and the rules of pollution control boards exist precisely because public awareness alone is not enough.

Therefore, we should encourage boiling at home for safety, but we must also have laws, treatment plants, rainwater harvesting, and public education to protect rivers and lakes. Boiling is one step for one family; protecting all water is a task for the whole society.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A family of four in a town near the Ganga uses 150 litres per person per day. Design a one-day water audit and suggest how the family could save at least 20% of its daily water without spending much money.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
First, the family should calculate the total daily use: 150 litres multiplied by four members gives 600 litres a day. A water audit is a careful record of how much water is used for each purpose. The family can watch the water meter, if there is one, or estimate use from the number of buckets, flushes, showers, and washes during a normal day. They may find, for example, that the toilet flush uses about 10 litres each time, a long shower uses 50 litres, washing vegetables under a running tap wastes water, and a leaking tap may lose many litres overnight.

To save at least 20%, or 120 litres, they can take several low-cost actions. They can place a filled bottle in the toilet cistern to reduce the flush by about one litre. They can take bucket baths instead of showers. They can turn off the tap while brushing, shaving, or washing dishes. They can collect the water used for washing vegetables and rice and use it for watering plants. If there is a leaking tap, they can change the washer, which is cheap and quick. They can also start a simple rainwater harvesting system, such as placing a drum under a downpipe from the roof during the monsoon. These steps together can easily save more than 120 litres, reduce the family's water bill, and also lower the pressure on the town's water source.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine your school is in a city with water scarcity every summer. Design a project for your school that combines prevention of water pollution with conservation of water. Describe at least three actions and explain how each helps.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The project would be called 'Every Drop Counts and Every River Matters.' The first action would be to install rooftop rainwater harvesting structures on all school buildings. During the monsoon, rain falling on the roof would be directed through pipes into a storage tank or a recharge pit. This would provide water for cleaning, watering the garden, and even for drinking after simple treatment, and it would also reduce the amount of water the school takes from the ground or the municipality, helping to fight scarcity. The second action would be to prevent pollution by keeping the school drains and the nearby roadside drains free of plastic, paper, and food waste. Students would form a 'water watch' group to check that no one throws waste into open drains, because such waste blocks the drains and eventually carries harmful matter into rivers and lakes. The third action would be to change the way water is used for cleaning and gardening. Instead of washing corridors and vehicles with running water from a hose, the school would use buckets and mops, and the garden would be watered in the early morning or evening to reduce evaporation. Plants that need less water, such as native Indian species, would be chosen. These three actions together would make the school a model of water conservation and pollution prevention, and the students could then explain the same ideas to their families.

masteryCriteria: Can name three causes of water pollution (sewage, industrial waste, agricultural runoff); can describe three water treatment steps (sedimentation, filtration, chlorination); can state two effects of polluted water (diseases, harm to aquatic life) and two prevention methods (treat sewage, avoid chemical dumping).

title: Carbon dioxide - preparation and properties
subject: chem
definition:
Carbon dioxide, usually written as CO2, is a colourless and odourless gas that forms a small but important part of the atmosphere, about 0.04% by volume. It is a greenhouse gas that helps keep Earth warm, but human activities are increasing its amount in the atmosphere. In the ICSE Class 8 syllabus, this node focuses on the systematic laboratory preparation of CO2 and its key physical and chemical properties.

In the laboratory, carbon dioxide is prepared by the action of dilute hydrochloric acid on marble chips, which are pieces of calcium carbonate (CaCO3). The reaction is carried out in a conical flask or Woulfe's bottle fitted with a thistle funnel and a delivery tube. A brisk effervescence is seen. The balanced equation is CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2^. Calcium chloride, water, and carbon dioxide gas are produced. Because carbon dioxide is heavier than air, it is collected by upward displacement of air, with the delivery tube reaching the bottom of the gas jar so the heavier gas sinks and pushes the lighter air out.

The physical properties of CO2 are that it is colourless, odourless, heavier than air, and does not support combustion. When a burning splint is lowered into a jar of the gas, the flame is extinguished. The chemical properties include its reaction with lime water, which is an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2). When CO2 is bubbled through lime water, the clear solution turns milky due to the formation of insoluble calcium carbonate. The reaction is Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. If excess CO2 is passed for a long time, the milkiness disappears because calcium bicarbonate is formed, but the standard test uses a short bubbling time.

The causes of increasing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere are linked to day-to-day human activities. Burning of fuels such as wood, coal, petrol, diesel, and natural gas in homes, vehicles, factories, and thermal power stations releases CO2. Deforestation reduces the number of trees that absorb CO2, adding to the rise. In India, cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, and Chennai have high vehicular and industrial emissions, while states with large forests help remove the gas. The syllabus wants students to discuss these causes clearly and link them to the rise of this greenhouse gas in the atmosphere.

Key terms to master are carbon dioxide, CO2, laboratory preparation, marble chips, calcium carbonate, dilute hydrochloric acid, lime water, milky, heavier than air, combustion, upward displacement of air, greenhouse gas, atmosphere, and burning fuel. These terms must be used accurately in both descriptive and reasoned answers, with balanced chemical equations and correct observations.
eli5: Carbon dioxide is a gas in the air that we cannot see or smell. In school, we make it by dropping marble chips into dilute acid, then collect it in an upside-down jar because it sinks like honey. It puts out flames and turns lime water white and cloudy. Cars, factories, and burning fuel add extra CO2 to the air, which can warm our planet.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe the laboratory preparation of carbon dioxide using marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid. Include the method of collection and a balanced chemical equation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Carbon dioxide is prepared in the laboratory by the action of dilute hydrochloric acid on marble chips. Marble chips are pieces of calcium carbonate, with the formula CaCO3. The apparatus consists of a conical flask fitted with a thistle funnel and a delivery tube. A few marble chips are placed in the flask, and dilute hydrochloric acid is added through the thistle funnel. A brisk effervescence is seen as carbon dioxide gas is liberated. The balanced chemical equation is CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2^. In this reaction, calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid to give calcium chloride, water, and carbon dioxide. The gas is collected by upward displacement of air because carbon dioxide is heavier than air. It sinks to the bottom of the gas jar and gradually pushes the lighter air upwards and out. The delivery tube should extend to the bottom of the gas jar for efficient collection. This method is preferred in schools because the reactants are cheap, safe to handle, and the gas is produced at a convenient rate.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is carbon dioxide collected by upward displacement of air and not by downward displacement of air? Explain with reference to the molecular mass of the gas and the composition of air.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Carbon dioxide is collected by upward displacement of air because its molecular mass is greater than the average molecular mass of air. The molecular mass of CO2 is 12 + 16 x 2 = 44, while the average molecular mass of air is approximately 29. Nitrogen, which makes up about four-fifths of air, has a molecular mass of 28, and oxygen, which makes up about one-fifth, has a molecular mass of 32. Since 44 is much greater than 29, a given volume of carbon dioxide is heavier than the same volume of air at the same temperature and pressure. When the gas enters the jar, it sinks to the bottom. More gas continues to enter, pushing the lighter air upward until the jar is almost entirely filled with carbon dioxide. If we collected it by downward displacement of air, the lighter air would remain at the bottom and mix with the gas, giving an impure sample. This is why the delivery tube must be long enough to reach near the bottom of the jar. The same principle explains why carbon dioxide fire extinguishers work: the gas settles over a fire and cuts off the oxygen supply.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Carbon dioxide is essential for life because plants use it for photosynthesis, so increasing its amount in the atmosphere can only be good for plants and for us." Evaluate this statement with a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partially correct but overall misleading. It is true that carbon dioxide is essential for life. Plants use carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll to make glucose and oxygen during photosynthesis. Without CO2, green plants could not produce food, and the oxygen content of the atmosphere would not be replenished. In controlled conditions, such as greenhouses, farmers sometimes add extra CO2 to boost plant growth. However, the second part of the statement is not correct. An increase in atmospheric CO2 beyond natural levels does not only help plants; it also has serious consequences. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, meaning it traps heat from the Earth's surface and prevents it from escaping into space. A moderate greenhouse effect keeps the planet warm enough for life, but an enhanced greenhouse effect, caused by burning fossil fuels and deforestation, leads to global warming. This warming can change rainfall patterns, cause more frequent heat waves, melt glaciers, raise sea levels, and disturb agriculture and ecosystems. In India, coastal cities and Himalayan regions are especially vulnerable to these changes. Some plants may grow faster with more CO2, but this advantage is often limited by water, nutrients, and temperature stress. Therefore, the statement ignores the imbalance in the natural carbon cycle. A balanced conclusion is that CO2 is necessary in the right amount, but an excess caused by human activities is harmful to the environment and to human society.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student set up the apparatus to prepare carbon dioxide by reacting marble chips with dilute hydrochloric acid. The gas was passed through lime water for a few seconds and the lime water turned milky. After a few minutes, the milky appearance disappeared. Suggest why this happened, and write the equations for the two reactions involved.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The first change, the milkiness, is the standard test for carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide in lime water to form insoluble calcium carbonate. The tiny particles of calcium carbonate remain suspended in the liquid, giving a milky white appearance. The equation for this reaction is Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. If the student continues to pass carbon dioxide through the lime water for several minutes, the milky precipitate of calcium carbonate reacts with more carbon dioxide and water to form soluble calcium bicarbonate. Because calcium bicarbonate is soluble, the white suspension disappears and the solution becomes clear again. The equation for this second reaction is CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 -> Ca(HCO3)2. In the laboratory, the first reaction is the one used to identify the gas, so a few seconds of bubbling is enough. Prolonged bubbling gives the second reaction, which is why the milkiness disappears. A careful student would stop the experiment as soon as the milkiness appears and report it as a positive test.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple, safe classroom demonstration that proves carbon dioxide is heavier than air and does not support combustion. Describe the materials, the procedure, and the expected observations.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For this demonstration, the materials needed are a small candle fixed at the bottom of a small beaker or a glass jar, another empty beaker, some marble chips, dilute hydrochloric acid, a spoon, a matchbox, and a pair of tongs. First, light the candle and place it on the laboratory bench. Then, in a separate beaker, add a few marble chips and pour a small amount of dilute hydrochloric acid down the side so that the acid reacts with the chips and carbon dioxide is produced. After about thirty seconds, the beaker will be filled with carbon dioxide. The gas is invisible; students should be warned not to inhale it in large amounts. Using tongs, carefully tilt the beaker of carbon dioxide and pour the gas, like an invisible liquid, over the burning candle. The expected observation is that the candle flame is extinguished almost immediately, even though the gas was not poured directly onto the wick. This shows two properties at once: carbon dioxide is heavier than air because it can be poured from one container to another, and it does not support combustion because it extinguishes the flame. The teacher can enhance the demonstration by placing a second candle at a higher level and showing that only the lower candle is extinguished, proving that CO2 settles downward. Safety precautions include wearing gloves and goggles, keeping the acid away from skin and eyes, and performing the demonstration in a well-ventilated room.

masteryCriteria: Can write the equation for CO2 preparation (CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2); can describe the apparatus (Woulf's bottle, delivery tube, gas jar); can state three properties of CO2 (colourless, odourless, denser than air, does not support combustion); can test for CO2 (turns limewater milky).

title: Electronic configuration and valency
subject: chem
definition: The heart of this section is the idea that an atom is not a chaotic swarm of particles but a tiny solar system of shells, with each shell holding a definite maximum number of electrons. Electronic configuration is the precise way in which the electrons of an atom are arranged in these shells, written as a set of numbers such as 2, 8, 1 for sodium or 2, 6 for oxygen. In the first twenty elements, the shells fill in the order K, L, M, N, where the K-shell holds at most two electrons, the L-shell holds at most eight, the M-shell also holds at most eight for the elements we study, and the N-shell begins to receive electrons from potassium and calcium onward. Valency is the combining capacity of an element, the number of electrons an atom can lose, gain, or share when it joins with other atoms to form a molecule or a compound. Because the outermost shell, also called the valence shell, is the one that takes part in bonding, the number of electrons in that shell decides the valency. When the outermost shell has one, two, three, or four electrons, the atom usually gives away or shares those electrons, so the valency is equal to that count, as in sodium with 2, 8, 1 giving valency 1 or carbon with 2, 4 giving valency 4. When the outermost shell has five, six, or seven electrons, the atom finds it easier to gain or share electrons to reach the stable octet of eight, so the valency is eight minus that count, as in oxygen with 2, 6 giving valency 2 or nitrogen with 2, 5 giving valency 3. The first twenty elements are the practice ground for this: hydrogen is 1 and has valency 1, helium 2 and valency 0, lithium 2,1 and valency 1, beryllium 2,2 and valency 2, boron 2,3 and valency 3, carbon 2,4 and valency 4, nitrogen 2,5 and valency 3, oxygen 2,6 and valency 2, fluorine 2,7 and valency 1, neon 2,8 and valency 0, and so on through sodium, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, phosphorus, sulphur, chlorine, argon, potassium, and calcium. Molecules of elements such as O2, N2 and H2 form when two like atoms share electrons so that each attains a stable or stable-like configuration, while molecules of compounds such as H2O, CO2, NO2, CaO and ZnCl2 form when atoms of different elements combine in fixed ratios determined by their valencies. The octet rule, the tendency of atoms to have eight electrons in the outermost shell, is the guiding force, and a stable octet explains why noble gases like neon and argon show valency 0.
eli5: Atoms are tiny balls with layers, and each layer can hold only a certain number of electrons. The last layer, the outermost shell, tells us how many friends the atom can hold hands with; that number is called valency. If the outer shell is full like neon, the atom does not want any more friends.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Write the electronic configuration of the following elements: sodium, carbon, neon, and chlorine. Also state the valency of each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Sodium has atomic number 11, so its electronic configuration is 2,8,1. The outermost shell has one electron, which it can lose, so its valency is 1. Carbon has atomic number 6, so its electronic configuration is 2,4. The outermost shell has four electrons, and carbon can share all four, so its valency is 4. Neon has atomic number 10, so its electronic configuration is 2,8. The outermost shell is already full, giving it a stable octet, so its valency is 0. Chlorine has atomic number 17, so its electronic configuration is 2,8,7. The outermost shell has seven electrons, so it needs one more to complete the octet; therefore its valency is 1. Remembering this pattern is the foundation for everything else in this node.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why does oxygen have a valency of 2, while nitrogen has a valency of 3?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Oxygen has atomic number 8 and its electronic configuration is 2,6. Its outermost shell, the L-shell, contains six electrons. To reach the stable octet of eight electrons, oxygen can gain or share two more electrons; therefore its valency is 2. Nitrogen has atomic number 7 and its electronic configuration is 2,5. Its outermost shell contains five electrons, so it can gain or share three more electrons to complete the octet; therefore its valency is 3. The difference is not a rule to be memorised blindly but a consequence of counting how many electrons are missing from eight. An atom tends to choose the path that requires the least effort, and for oxygen that is two electrons, for nitrogen three.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student claims: "The valency of an element is always equal to the number of electrons in its outermost shell." Evaluate this statement with suitable examples.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly true. It is true when the outermost shell has one, two, three, or four electrons because the atom can readily lose or share that many electrons. For example, sodium with 2,8,1 has one electron in its outermost shell and valency 1; magnesium with 2,8,2 has two electrons and valency 2; boron with 2,3 has three and valency 3; carbon with 2,4 has four and valency 4. However, the statement is false when the outermost shell has more than four electrons. In those cases the atom prefers to gain or share the missing electrons to complete the stable octet of eight, so the valency is eight minus the number of outermost electrons. For example, nitrogen with 2,5 has five outer electrons but valency 3, because 8 minus 5 equals 3; oxygen with 2,6 has valency 2, because 8 minus 6 equals 2; fluorine with 2,7 has valency 1, because 8 minus 7 equals 1. The statement also fails for noble gases such as neon with 2,8: it has eight outer electrons but valency 0, because it already has a stable octet and does not need to combine.
