A processing device is hardware that executes instructions and works on data; the CPU is the main example because it fetches, decodes, and carries out the instructions of a program. The GPU is also a processing device, especially useful for images and calculations that can be done in parallel. Being able to list these four categories with correct examples is the foundation of this topic.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is a mouse called an input device but a monitor is called an output device?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The difference between an input device and an output device depends on the direction in which data travels. A mouse is an input device because it sends information from the user into the computer. When you move the mouse, a sensor detects the movement and sends a signal telling the computer where the pointer should appear on the screen. A monitor, on the other hand, is an output device because it receives a video signal from the computer and displays it for the user. It does not send any information back into the computer; it only shows what the computer has already produced. This is why the mouse is on the “in” side and the monitor is on the “out” side. The same rule works for other devices: a keyboard, scanner, and microphone bring data in, while a printer and speaker carry results out.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, “A pen drive is both a storage device and an input device because we put data into the computer when we plug it in.” Is this statement correct? Evaluate with a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is partly true in one narrow sense but incorrect overall. It is true that, when you copy a file from a pen drive into the computer, data is moving from the pen drive into the computer. However, the pen drive itself is not an input device. The function of an input device is to collect new data from the outside world or from a user, such as a keyboard collecting key presses or a microphone collecting sound. A pen drive’s real job is to hold data safely when the computer is switched off; that is why it belongs to the storage-device family. The confusion comes from the act of transferring data, but the transfer is only possible because the data was already stored. In an input device, the data is being created or captured for the first time. In a storage device, the data already exists and is being saved or moved. Therefore, the pen drive should be classified as a storage device, not an input device, even though data may travel from it to the computer. This balanced view respects the true function of each category.

diagnosticQuestions.question: In a school computer lab in India, the following devices are on a desk: a keyboard, a mouse, a monitor, a printer, a pen drive, and the CPU inside the cabinet. Classify each device into the correct hardware category and explain what would happen if the CPU were removed.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The keyboard and mouse are input devices because they send the user’s instructions and data into the computer. The monitor and printer are output devices because they show or print the results for the user. The pen drive is a storage device because it keeps files safe and can move them between computers. The CPU inside the cabinet is the processing device because it executes instructions and processes data. If the CPU were removed, the computer would not be able to do anything useful. The monitor might still light up, but nothing would be calculated, and no instructions would run. The keyboard and mouse would send signals, but no part of the machine would understand what to do with them. The printer would not print because there would be no processed results to send, and the pen drive would still hold files but no one could open or run them. The CPU is therefore the most important processing unit in the whole system.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a small computer setup for an Indian village information centre. Choose at least one input device, one output device, one storage device, and one processing device. Explain why each device is needed.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For an Indian village information centre, I would choose a keyboard and mouse as input devices, a monitor and a small speaker as output devices, a hard disk and pen drives as storage devices, and a CPU as the processing device. The keyboard and mouse let the village operator type in names, forms, and questions, and move around the screen easily. The monitor is essential because many users may not read English well, so the operator can show forms, crop information, or video tutorials in regional languages. The speaker can play audio instructions or educational videos. A hard disk inside the computer will store all the records and programs safely, while extra pen drives will let farmers carry copies of land records or application forms to government offices. The CPU is the most important part because it will process every request, search the database, and display the right information. Since village centres often have limited electricity, the CPU should be in a desktop or a low-power mini-computer. This setup keeps the four categories clear and makes sure each device does the right job.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to classify any given piece of hardware into one of the four functional families—input, output, storage, or processing—and justify the choice by stating the direction of data flow or the job the device performs. They must name at least two correct examples for each of the four categories, using real devices such as the keyboard, mouse, monitor, printer, hard disk, pen drive, CD, CPU, and GPU, and must be able to explain the CPU’s special role as the processing unit that fetches, decodes, and executes instructions (with the ALU, Control Unit, and registers). They must also be able to correct a misclassification, such as calling a monitor an input device or the CPU a storage device, by referring back to the defining function of each family.

title: File management - organisation of data, file types and extensions
subject: cs
definition:
File management is the careful and systematic way of storing, naming, sorting and finding data on a computer. Every time you save a project, a picture, a song or a document, your computer stores it as a file. The way these files are arranged is called the organisation of data. A well-organised computer keeps related items together so that they can be opened, edited and shared without confusion.

One of the most useful ideas in file management is the file extension. A file extension is the short group of letters that comes after the last dot in a file name, such as .doc, .xls, .jpg, .mp3, .mp4, .html and .pdf. The extension acts like a surname for the file: it tells the computer and the user what kind of information the file contains. For example, a file ending with .doc is usually a document, .xls is a spreadsheet, .jpg is an image, .mp3 is an audio file, .mp4 is a video file, .html is a web page and .pdf is a portable document that keeps its layout fixed. Each of these file types has a special structure inside it, even though the icons on the screen may look different.

File extensions matter because they help the operating system decide which application should open the file. If you double-click a .xls file, the computer understands that it should open it with a spreadsheet program, not a music player or an image viewer. If the extension is wrong or missing, the computer may become confused and show an error message or open the file with the wrong software. This is why students must be careful when renaming files: changing only the name does not change what the file actually is inside.

Another important part of file management is organising files into folders and subfolders. Just as a school library in Delhi might sort books by subject and then by class, a computer can sort files by file type, by project or by date. For instance, a Class 6 student in Mumbai could keep all .jpg pictures in one folder, all .mp3 songs in another and all .doc and .pdf school reports in a third. Good organisation makes it easy to find files quickly, keeps the Desktop tidy and protects important work from being lost or deleted by mistake.
eli5: A file extension is like a file's last name. It comes after the dot and tells the computer what the file is, such as .doc for a letter, .jpg for a picture, or .mp3 for a song. If you hide the last name, the computer gets confused. Keeping files in folders by type is like sorting toys into separate boxes so you can find them quickly.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List any five file extensions from your Class 6 syllabus, name one application that can open each, and explain why the file extension is important when you double-click a file.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The five file extensions are .doc, .xls, .jpg, .mp3 and .pdf. A .doc file is a document and is usually opened by a word processor such as Microsoft Word or LibreOffice Writer. An .xls file is a spreadsheet and is opened by a spreadsheet program such as Microsoft Excel or LibreOffice Calc. A .jpg file is an image and is opened by an image viewer or editor. An .mp3 file is an audio file and is opened by a music player. A .pdf file is a portable document and is opened by a PDF reader such as Adobe Reader. The file extension is important because it is a short code that tells the operating system what kind of data the file contains. When you double-click a file, the computer uses the extension to choose the correct application. If the extension is wrong or missing, the computer may open the file with the wrong program or show an error message. This is why you must not delete, repeat or mistype the extension.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student has a file named "photo.jpg". He renames it to "photo.mp3". Will the computer now play it as a song? Explain why or why not, and describe what really changes inside the file.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: No, the computer will not play it as a song. Renaming "photo.jpg" to "photo.mp3" only changes the file's name; it does not change the data stored inside the file. The file still contains the same picture data, arranged in the .jpg image format. When the student double-clicks the renamed file, the computer will look at the new .mp3 extension and try to open it with a music player. The music player expects audio data, so it will not understand the picture data and will usually show an error or refuse to play anything. This shows that the extension is like a surname: changing the surname does not change the person. A file must have an extension that matches its true format. If the student wants a song, he must find an actual .mp3 file, not just rename a picture.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "It is always best to store every file on the Desktop so that you can find it quickly. You do not need folders or subfolders to keep things organised." Evaluate this statement, giving arguments for and against it, and state your final view.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement has some truth but is not fully correct. On one side, keeping a few frequently used files on the Desktop can make them easy to find because they are visible as soon as the computer starts. For example, a student might keep a timetable or a homework shortcut on the Desktop for quick access. However, the statement that you do not need folders or subfolders is wrong for most users. If every file is saved on the Desktop, the Desktop becomes crowded and it becomes harder, not easier, to find what you need. Imagine a student in a school in Bengaluru saving all her .doc, .xls, .jpg, .mp3, .mp4, .html and .pdf files directly on the Desktop. After a few weeks, she would have dozens of icons mixed together, and searching for one file would take much longer. Folders and subfolders act like shelves in a library: they group similar files together by project, by subject or by file type. This makes backups safer, mistakes less likely and teamwork easier because everyone knows where to look. My final view is that the Desktop can be used for a small number of shortcuts or urgent files, but most files should be organised into folders and subfolders. Good file management means keeping the Desktop tidy and using a clear folder structure so that you can find and open the right file quickly.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You have been asked to organise the files for a school project about "Famous Monuments of India" on one of your class computers. The folder currently contains report.doc, data.xls, map.jpg, interview.mp3, tour.mp4, facts.html and handout.pdf. Describe a neat folder and subfolder structure, and explain where each file would go and why.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, I would create one main folder named "Famous_Monuments_of_India". Inside it, I would make subfolders for each file type so that every item is easy to find. The subfolders would be "Documents", "Spreadsheets", "Images", "Audio", "Videos", "Web_Pages" and "PDFs". The file "report.doc" would go into "Documents" because it is a Word-style document containing written information about the monuments. "data.xls" would go into "Spreadsheets" because it is a table of facts or numbers. "map.jpg" would go into "Images" because it is a picture. "interview.mp3" would go into "Audio" because it is a sound recording. "tour.mp4" would go into "Videos" because it is a movie. "facts.html" would go into "Web_Pages" because it is a web page that can be opened in a browser. "handout.pdf" would go into "PDFs" because it is a portable document that looks like a printed page. This structure is useful because a teacher or friend can open the main folder and immediately see where each kind of file belongs. It also matches the idea that a file extension tells you the file type, so you can sort files by their extensions.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple poster or handout for a Class 4 computer club that uses the "surname" analogy to explain file extensions. Include one example for each of the file types .doc, .xls, .jpg, .mp3, .pdf, and add one rule about organising files.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The poster should have a friendly title such as "File Extensions Are Like Surnames!" At the top, I would draw a family of files, each with a first name and a last name. The caption would read: "The first name is for people; the last name is for the computer. A surname tells you which family a person belongs to. A file extension tells you which type a file belongs to." Below that, I would give one example for each file type: "report.doc is a document, just like a digital letter you can type; marks.xls is a spreadsheet, just like a digital table of numbers; photo.jpg is an image, just like a digital picture; song.mp3 is audio, just like a digital music file; notes.pdf is a portable document, just like a digital printed page that stays the same on any screen." At the bottom, I would write one rule for organising: "Sort your files into folders by type, just like a librarian sorts books by subject. Put all your .doc files in a Documents folder, .jpg files in an Images folder and .mp3 files in an Audio folder, so you can find them quickly and never lose your work." The poster would use clear pictures, short sentences and a bright layout so that even a Class 4 student can understand.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to list at least five common file extensions from the Class 6 syllabus (.doc, .xls, .jpg, .mp3, .mp4, .html, .pdf) and correctly match each extension to the kind of data it holds and to a suitable application that can open it. The student must be able to explain in their own words why the file extension, not the icon or the file name, is what tells the operating system which program to use, and must be able to predict what will go wrong if an extension is changed, deleted or mistyped (for example, renaming "photo.jpg" to "photo.mp3"). The student must also be able to design a tidy folder-and-subfolder structure that groups a mixed set of files by file type, placing each given file into the correct subfolder and justifying the choice using the extension.

title: File properties - size, type, location, date modified, attributes
subject: cs
definition: File properties are the metadata that describe a file without opening it. Just as a school ID card tells you a student’s name, class, and roll number, the Properties dialog of a file tells you its size, type, location, date modified, and attributes. In Windows, you open this dialog by right-clicking a file and choosing Properties. The most familiar tab is the General tab, where the operating system lists the file’s name, its size in bytes, kilobytes, or megabytes, the type of file as identified by its extension, the full folder path where it is stored, and the date on which it was last changed. Size is usually shown as a plain number of bytes and also as the rounded human-readable value such as 5.12 KB or 2.34 MB. Type is shown as a friendly description, for example "Text Document (.txt)" or "JPEG Image (.jpg)", because Windows reads the extension after the dot. Location gives the complete address, such as C:\Users\Amit\Documents\Projects or D:\School\Computer\Report.docx. Date modified records the last moment when the file’s content was saved or changed. Below these details, the Attributes section contains checkboxes for Read-only and Hidden. Read-only means the file can be opened and viewed but its contents cannot be edited or overwritten until the attribute is removed. Hidden means the file is normally not visible in File Explorer unless the folder view is set to show hidden items. Applying or removing these attributes is also done through the Properties dialog by checking or unchecking the boxes and pressing OK. Understanding file properties is therefore an essential Windows skill: it lets a student locate, identify, protect, and manage files confidently.
eli5: A file has an ID card called Properties. It tells you how big the file is, what kind it is, where it lives, and when it was last changed. You can also make it read-only so no one changes it, or hidden so it does not show normally. You do this by right-clicking the file and choosing Properties.

misconceptions.belief: Students often confuse the number they see in the Size field with the number of pages, words, or characters in the file. The Size field is the amount of storage space the file takes on the disk, measured in bytes, KB, or MB. It is not the length of the document. CISCE examiner comments repeatedly note that candidates who do not read the question or the screen attentively miss such details; for example, one examiner wrote that some candidates "did not read the question attentively and missed checking the equality of the left and right diagonal totals." In the same way, a student looking at the Properties dialog must read each field carefully and not assume that a large number always means a long document.

Some students think that setting the Hidden attribute deletes the file or makes it go to the Recycle Bin. This is not true. A hidden file is still on the hard disk in the same location; it is just not shown in the normal File Explorer view. If the folder view is changed to show hidden items, the file appears again. This is similar to the examiner observation that candidates sometimes "did insertion sort instead of selection sort" — they use the wrong action for the task. Applying Hidden is not the same as deleting, just as choosing a different sorting method is not the same as the one the question asked for.

Students sometimes believe that Read-only means the file is locked with a password and cannot be opened or copied. Read-only does not stop anyone from opening or copying the file; it only stops the current content from being changed and then saved with the same name. You can still open it, read it, and even make a copy. You simply cannot overwrite the original unless the attribute is removed. This connects to the examiner comment about using the wrong data type or the wrong logic: a wrong attribute is chosen to solve a problem that actually needs a password or a different permission.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the five file properties or attributes you can see in the Properties dialog of a file, and briefly explain what each one means.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The first property is File name, which is the title you gave to the file when you saved it. The second is Type of file, which is the friendly name Windows gives based on the extension, such as Text Document (.txt) or JPEG Image (.jpg). The third is Size, which tells how much disk space the file occupies and is usually shown in bytes, KB, or MB. The fourth is Location, which is the full folder path showing exactly where the file is stored, for example C:\Users\Priya\Documents. The fifth is Date modified, which shows the last date and time when the file content was changed and saved. Besides these, two important attributes are Read-only, which stops the file from being edited, and Hidden, which hides the file from the normal File Explorer view. Together these properties help you identify, find, and protect your files without opening them.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student named Arjun saved a project report as "Arjun_Report.docx" and then checked the Hidden attribute in its Properties dialog. When he opened the folder again, he could not see the file. Explain why this happened and how he can make it visible again.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When Arjun checked the Hidden attribute, Windows removed the file from the normal File Explorer display. This is the purpose of the Hidden attribute: it conceals a file from ordinary view without removing it from the computer. The file is still stored in its original location with all its properties unchanged; it is simply not shown by default. To make it visible again, Arjun can either open the Properties dialog by right-clicking the file name if he knows it, or he can change the folder view settings. In Windows File Explorer, he can click the View tab and then check the box for Hidden items, which will show all hidden files in a faded look. Then he can right-click "Arjun_Report.docx", choose Properties, and uncheck the Hidden box. After clicking OK, the file will return to its normal visible state. This shows that Hidden is about visibility, not deletion or movement.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A Class 6 student says, "Making a file read-only means nobody can open it or copy it." Is this statement correct? Evaluate it with reasons.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is not correct. When a file is set to Read-only, the only thing that is blocked is the editing and saving of the original file. The file can still be opened, viewed, printed, and copied to another location. For example, if the school timetable is saved as a read-only file named "Timetable.pdf" or "Timetable.docx", every student can open it and see the timetable, and a teacher can copy it to a pen drive. The only restriction is that a user cannot change the existing content and then save it under the same file name without first removing the read-only attribute. On the other hand, the statement does correctly suggest that Read-only gives some protection, because it prevents accidental or unauthorised changes. Therefore, the true effect of Read-only is limited to editability, not accessibility. It is like a sealed glass case: you can look at the object inside, you can take a photograph, but you cannot move the object until the case is opened. So the student should be told that Read-only means "do not edit," not "do not open."

diagnosticQuestions.question: Your teacher asks you to find the exact location, size, type, and last modified date of a file named "School_Logo.jpg" stored in your computer. Describe the steps you would follow and the values you would expect to record.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To complete the task, I would first open File Explorer and navigate to the folder where I think the image is stored, for example D:\School\Art\. Then I would right-click on the file named "School_Logo.jpg" and choose Properties from the menu. In the General tab of the Properties dialog, I would read each field carefully. The Type of file should be "JPEG Image (.jpg)" because the extension is .jpg. The Size might be something like 85.3 KB or 523,456 bytes, depending on the image. The Location should show the full folder path, such as D:\School\Art. The Date modified should show the date and time when the image was last saved or edited, for example 09-08-2026 10:15 AM. I would also check the Attributes section; if the file is not protected, both Read-only and Hidden should be unchecked. After recording all these values, I can close the dialog. If the file were hidden, I would first enable the Hidden items option in the View tab of File Explorer.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple file management rule for a Class 6 computer lab that uses file properties and attributes to keep important notices safe and easy to find.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In our computer lab, every class will keep a shared folder named "Class_6_Notices" inside D:\School\Class6\. Important notices will be saved with clear names such as "Notice_09Aug_Exam_Rules.docx" so that the file name, type, and location all make sense. After the teacher finalises a notice, the file will be set to Read-only so that students can open and read it but cannot accidentally change the exam rules. The teacher will also set the Hidden attribute for draft files that are not yet ready, so that students do not open them by mistake; these drafts will become visible only when the teacher removes the Hidden attribute. Every Friday, the class monitor will right-click each notice, open Properties, and record the size and date modified in a log to make sure the latest version is being used. This rule uses location, type, size, date modified, read-only, and hidden attributes together to keep the lab files organised, protected, and up to date.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to open the Properties dialog of any file by right-clicking and choosing Properties, and correctly read and state each of the five core properties — size (with the correct unit such as bytes, KB, or MB), type (with the extension such as .txt, .docx, or .jpg), location (as a full folder path like C:\Users\Riya\Documents), date modified (as the last saved date and time), and attributes (Read-only and Hidden). The student must also be able to explain in their own words the exact effect of setting Read-only (blocks editing and overwriting of the original, but allows opening, viewing, and copying) and the exact effect of setting Hidden (conceals the file from normal File Explorer view without deleting or moving it), and must be able to apply or remove these attributes through the Properties dialog. Finally, the student must distinguish clearly between size and document length, between opening and editing, and between hiding and deleting, so that they can answer precise ICSE-style questions without using vague language.

title: Compressing files and folders - zip files, reducing size
subject: cs
definition:
File compression is the process of reducing the size of one or more files or folders so that they occupy less storage space and can be transferred more quickly from one place to another. When we compress a file or folder, we squeeze out the repeated or unnecessary data and pack it tightly, much like pressing clothes flat before putting them into a suitcase. In Windows, the most common way for a Class 6 student to compress files is to create a zip archive, which is a special file that has the .zip extension and acts as a container holding all the original files inside it. The word "zip" itself suggests the idea of closing things up tightly.

To create a zip archive, a student can select one or more files or an entire folder, right-click, and choose the option that creates a compressed (zipped) folder. The computer then reads the files, finds patterns that can be stored more efficiently, and produces a single .zip file. The file size of this .zip archive is usually much smaller than the combined file size of the original uncompressed files. This happens because compression removes gaps and repeated information without losing the actual content of the files. For example, a school project folder containing ten small pictures and a few Word documents that together take 15 MB may shrink to less than 10 MB when zipped.

The difference between a zip archive and a regular uncompressed folder is important. A regular uncompressed folder simply shows all the files as they are, taking their full storage space. A zip archive is one single file with the .zip extension that contains all those files inside in a compressed state. The files inside are still complete, but they have been packed tightly so that they need less room. To use the files again, the student must extract the zip archive, which means telling the computer to open the package and restore the original files exactly as they were before compression. After extracting, the files expand back to their normal size and can be opened and edited as usual.

Compression helps in two main ways: it reduces storage space on the computer's hard disk or pen drive, and it speeds up file transfer when sending the files through email, WhatsApp, or uploading them to a school portal. A smaller file takes less time to send over the internet because there are fewer bytes to move from one computer to another. It is also useful when a student wants to keep many related files together safely, such as keeping all worksheets of a chapter in one .zip file. However, it is important to remember that a .zip file is not the actual working file; it is like a packed suitcase. Until the files are extracted, they cannot be properly edited.

In practical terms, a student should be able to compress a folder into a .zip file, compare the file size before and after compression, extract the zip, and verify that all original files are restored intact. This means checking that every picture, document, and subfolder appears again after extraction with the same names and contents. Through this process, the student learns that compression is a useful file management skill, not a change to the files themselves.
eli5: Imagine you have a big fluffy pillow and a suitcase. The pillow takes too much space. If you squeeze the air out and pack it tightly, it becomes smaller. A zip file does the same thing to your folders. It squishes many files into one small package. You can open the package later and the files come back the same as before.

misconceptions.belief: Students often believe that a .zip file is only a renamed folder. This is like the confusion CISCE examiners observed when candidates mixed up closely related ideas, such as complement and dual, because they looked almost the same on the surface. A .zip file is not just a folder with a different name. It is a single compressed package that contains files packed tightly inside. The correction is to remember that a .zip file is one file with the .zip extension, not a normal folder, and the files inside must be extracted before they can be used.

Some students think that compression deletes parts of the original files. This mirrors the CISCE examiner observation that candidates sometimes failed to allocate memory correctly or handle objects properly because they did not understand what the operation was actually doing. Compression does not delete or damage the files; it only rearranges and shortens the way the data is stored. The correction is to extract the zip and compare each file with the original to verify that every file has been restored intact and nothing is missing.

A third common error is assuming that any file becomes much smaller after zipping. This is similar to the CISCE examiner comment that some candidates chose an answer simply because it looked reasonable without checking the details. In reality, some files such as .txt documents and bitmap images can be compressed a lot, while other files such as .jpg images and .mp3 songs are already compressed and do not become much smaller. The correction is to always compare the file size before and after compression for the specific files you are using, rather than assuming the result.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is the purpose of file compression, and what is the extension of a compressed archive created in Windows?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The purpose of file compression is to reduce the storage space needed by files and folders and to make file transfer faster. When a folder is compressed into an archive, the data is packed more tightly using special coding techniques that remove unnecessary or repeated information. The most common compressed archive created in Windows is a zip archive, and it has the .zip extension. For example, if a student compresses a folder called "Holiday Homework," the result will be a single file called "Holiday Homework.zip." This .zip file can be stored on the computer using less space and can be sent through email or shared over the internet more quickly because fewer bytes need to be moved. The .zip extension is like a label that tells the user the file is compressed and contains other files packed inside it.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A folder of school project files is 24 MB. After zipping, the .zip file is 15 MB. Explain why the .zip file is smaller and what happens to the files inside the zip.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The .zip file is smaller because compression reduces the amount of storage space the data needs. The computer looks at the contents of the original files, finds patterns, repeated information, and empty spaces, and then stores the same information in a shorter form. This is similar to how rolling clothes tightly makes them take less space in a suitcase. However, the files inside the zip are not deleted or changed in meaning. They are simply packed tightly inside the archive. To use them again, the student must extract the .zip file, which restores the original files to their normal, uncompressed state. After extraction, the pictures, documents, and other files should look exactly the same and have the same names as before, because the compression process is reversible. The reduction from 24 MB to 15 MB shows that the archive needs 9 MB less storage space and will also take less time to transfer over the internet.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "It is always better to keep all my files as zip archives because they take less space and I can still open and edit them." Is this statement correct? Give a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly correct but also partly wrong, so it needs careful evaluation. The student is correct that zip archives take less space and make file transfer faster. Compressing a folder reduces storage space on the hard disk or pen drive and makes it easier to send many files together as one package. This is especially useful when sharing a school project through email or saving backups on limited storage. However, the student is wrong to say that the files can be opened and edited while they are still inside a .zip archive. A .zip file is a packed container, not a normal folder. The files inside are in a compressed state and cannot be properly edited until they are extracted. If the student tries to open a document directly from inside the zip without extracting, the computer may open a temporary copy, but any changes may not be saved correctly. The balanced view is that zip archives are excellent for storage and transfer, but the files should be extracted when the student actually wants to work on them. Therefore, the best practice is to keep the .zip archive as a backup or a sending copy, and to extract the files into a normal folder when editing is needed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe the steps to compress a folder named "Class 6 Notes" and then extract it to verify that all files are restored.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, open File Explorer and locate the folder named "Class 6 Notes." Right-click on the folder, move the mouse to "Send to," and then click on "Compressed (zipped) folder." The computer will create a new file called "Class 6 Notes.zip" in the same location. To observe the reduction in file size, right-click the original folder and choose "Properties" to note its size, then right-click the new .zip file, choose "Properties," and note its smaller size. To verify that all files are restored, right-click on "Class 6 Notes.zip" and choose "Extract All." Select a destination, such as the Desktop or the Documents folder, and click "Extract." After extraction, open the new folder and compare its contents with the original. Check that every text file, image, and subfolder is present, that the names are the same, and that the files open properly. This proves that compression is reversible and that no files were lost or damaged.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you have collected photographs and information about three famous Indian monuments and you need to send them to a friend. Design a plan showing how you would use file compression to make the transfer easier.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, I would create a folder on the computer and name it "Indian Monuments Project." Inside the folder, I would place the photographs of the Taj Mahal in Agra, the Red Fort in Delhi, and the Qutub Minar, along with a Word document or Notepad file containing the information about each monument. I would check the total size of the folder by right-clicking it and opening "Properties." If the size is too large to send by email or WhatsApp, I would compress the folder by right-clicking it, choosing "Send to," and then selecting "Compressed (zipped) folder." This would create a single file called "Indian Monuments Project.zip." I would then compare the .zip file size with the original folder size to see how much storage space I saved. Finally, I would attach the .zip file to an email or send it through a messaging app. The single .zip file keeps everything organised in one place, takes less time to send, and does not need the friend to download each picture separately. When my friend receives it, they can extract the zip to get the original photographs and text back.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to compress a selected folder or group of files into a .zip archive using the right-click "Send to > Compressed (zipped) folder" option in Windows File Explorer, and produce a single .zip file with the correct extension in the same location as the originals. The student must also be able to compare the file size of the original folder and the .zip archive by opening the Properties of each, state which one is smaller, and give a reason in terms of storage space and transfer speed. Finally, the student must be able to extract a .zip archive using "Extract All," verify that every original file and subfolder is restored with the same names and contents, and explain in their own words that compression is reversible and does not delete or damage the files inside.

title: Word tables - creating, inserting rows and columns, formatting tables
subject: cs
definition:
A table in a word processor is a structured grid made up of horizontal lines called rows and vertical lines called columns. The small rectangular boxes where a row and a column meet are called cells, and each cell can hold its own text, numbers, or other content. The very first row of many tables is called the header row, and it usually contains labels that tell the reader what kind of information appears in each column. In ICSE Class 6 Computer Science, this node teaches how to create such a grid, enter data into cells, change the size and shape of the table by inserting or deleting rows and columns, and then make the table easy to read by applying borders, shading, and careful formatting.

To create a table, a student begins by opening the word processor and choosing the Insert option, then the Table command. Most word processors, such as Microsoft Word or LibreOffice Writer, ask the user to select or type the number of rows and columns. Once the table appears on the page, the cursor can be moved from one cell to the next by pressing the Tab key, and data can be typed into each cell. The table acts like a container in which every item has its own place, just as every book on a shelf has its own slot.

After a table is created, the structure can be changed. Inserting a row gives a new horizontal space for extra data, while inserting a column adds a new vertical section. Deleting a row or column removes the unwanted part. These changes are usually made by right-clicking inside a cell and choosing the insert or delete option, or by using the Table Tools tabs. Formatting a table means changing its appearance. This includes applying borders so that the grid lines are clear, adding shading to cells so that important parts stand out, and styling the header row so that the reader can quickly understand the contents of each column. Students also learn to adjust the column width and row height so that the text fits neatly inside the cells. The practical skill is to build a simple three-column table for Name, Age, and Class, add and delete rows and columns, and format the header row with borders and shading so that the table looks both useful and attractive.
eli5: A table is like a neat box made of smaller boxes. Rows go sideways, columns go up and down, and the tiny spaces where they meet are called cells. You can add more boxes by inserting rows or columns, and you can take boxes away by deleting them. You make the table pretty and clear by drawing borders, colouring the top row, and making the boxes the right size.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What are the steps to create a table with three columns and four rows in a word processor?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To create a table with three columns and four rows, first open the word processor and go to the Insert menu or tab. Choose the Table option, which will either show a small visual grid or open a dialog box. If the visual grid is shown, drag the mouse to select three columns and four rows, then click. If a dialog box appears, type the number of columns as 3 and the number of rows as 4, then press OK. The table will appear on the page with twelve cells. Move the cursor to the first cell using the mouse or Tab key and start typing. Press Tab to move to the next cell. The topmost row is usually used for the header row, where you can type labels such as Name, Age, and Class. After the basic table is ready, you can begin entering data into the remaining cells.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is it better to use the Insert Table command instead of drawing a table with spaces, dashes, and plus signs?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Using the Insert Table command is better because the word processor treats the table as a single structured object. This means the cells are automatically aligned, the column widths can be adjusted together, and rows or columns can be inserted or deleted without changing other parts of the document. If a table is made with spaces, dashes, and plus signs, it is only a drawing of lines on the page and not a real table. The moment the font size changes or the page is printed, the drawing can become crooked. You cannot sort the data, apply borders and shading easily, or insert a new row in the middle without manually retyping every line. The Insert Table command also keeps each piece of data inside its own cell, which is the main purpose of a table. Therefore, for accuracy, speed, and neatness, a real table command is the correct choice.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Formatting a table with borders and shading is only for decoration, so it is not important in a practical assignment." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly true and mostly misleading. It is true that borders and shading make a table look attractive, and a good appearance is one reason for formatting. However, the statement is misleading because it ignores the main purpose of table formatting, which is to make the data clear and easy to read. Borders create a visible grid that helps the reader see where one cell ends and another begins. Without borders, the table looks like a collection of words floating on the page, and the reader may find it hard to match data with its correct column. Shading the header row is especially important because it tells the reader immediately which row contains the labels and which rows contain the data. Adjusting column width and row height also prevents text from being squeezed or spread too far. In a practical assignment, the marks are often given for both correctness and presentation. A well-formatted table shows that the student understands not only how to make a table but also how to make it useful for the reader. So, while decoration is a small benefit, the real value of formatting is communication.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are asked to create a three-column table for a class register with the headings Name, Age, and Class. Add data for four Indian students, then insert a new row after the second data row, delete the column labelled Class, and apply a shaded border to the header row.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, open the word processor and insert a table with three columns and five rows, using one extra row for the header. In the first row, type Name in the first cell, Age in the second cell, and Class in the third cell. Enter data for four students, for example Aarav with age 11 and class 6-A, Meera with age 11 and class 6-B, Vihaan with age 10 and class 6-A, and Ananya with age 11 and class 6-C. To insert a new row after the second data row, click inside the second data row, right-click, and choose Insert row below. Type in the new row, for example Rohan, 10, 6-A. To delete the Class column, click any cell in that column, right-click, and choose Delete column. Finally, select the entire first row, go to the table formatting options, apply a border around all cells in that row, and choose a light shading colour. The result is a neat two-column table with a clearly shaded header and the extra row included.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a Monday timetable for Class 6-A using a Word table. Explain the number of rows and columns, the contents of the header row, and the formatting choices you would apply.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The timetable should have a header row and enough rows for each period of the school day. A good design uses one row for the header and eight or nine rows for the periods, such as Assembly, Periods 1 to 6, and a Lunch break. The table needs at least four columns: Time, Subject, Teacher, and Activity or Room. So the table might have four columns and ten rows. The header row would contain the labels Time, Subject, Teacher, and Room. I would format the header row with a dark but gentle shading such as light blue and a bold border so that it stands out from the data rows. Each period row would show a time like 8:30 to 9:15, a subject such as English, Hindi, Mathematics, Science, Social Studies, or Computer Science, the teacher's initials, and the classroom number. Borders would be applied to every cell so the grid is clear. The column for Time would be narrower, while the Subject and Teacher columns would be wider. This makes the timetable easy to read and similar to the timetables used in Indian schools.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to create a Word table of a given size (for example three columns and four rows) using the Insert Table command, enter data into cells using the Tab key to move between them, and correctly identify rows, columns, cells, and the header row by name. The student must also be able to insert a new row above or below an existing row, insert a column to the left or right of an existing column, and delete a row or column without losing data they did not intend to remove. Finally, the student must be able to apply borders to the whole table, add shading to the header row, and adjust column width and row height so that the table is neat and readable, and must be able to explain why each formatting choice helps the reader.

title: Word mail merge - creating form letters and mailing labels
subject: cs
definition: Mail merge is a powerful feature of a word processor—most commonly Microsoft Word, but also available in similar programs such as OpenOffice Writer and LibreOffice Writer—that lets a user create many personalised documents from a single template. The process is built around two linked parts: a main document and a data source. The main document is also called a form letter when the output is a letter, or a label layout when the output is a sheet of mailing labels. It is a template that contains the text, formatting, and pictures that are the same for every copy, plus special markers called merge fields or placeholders where the recipient's own details will appear. The data source is the second part; it is an organised list of recipients, structured like a table or a spreadsheet. In the data source, each row stands for one person, and each column is a field such as Name, Address, City, Pin_Code, or School_Class. Because the data source is a table, every entry of the same type is kept in the same column, making it easy for the computer to match a placeholder in the main document with the correct value for each row. When the user runs the merge, the word processor reads each row of the data source one by one and creates a separate copy of the main document with the placeholders replaced by the actual values. The result is a set of personalised documents: one for every recipient. For example, a principal of a school in New Delhi who wants to invite parents to an annual day function can write the letter once with placeholders like «Name» and «Address», prepare a data source listing all the parents, and then merge them to produce one printed letter for every family. The same idea is used for mailing labels: the main document shows the size and position of one label, and the data source supplies the names and addresses. When merged, the printer produces one correctly addressed label for each row. The final step is to print the merged letters or labels. Mail merge therefore saves time, reduces errors, and gives every recipient a document that looks as if it was individually prepared.
eli5: Mail merge is like filling a letter with names from a list. You write one letter and leave empty spaces. The computer puts a different name and address in each copy. So every person gets a letter that looks made just for them. It saves you from writing the same letter many times and helps print letters or address labels quickly.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a 'form letter', a 'data source', and a 'merge field' in the context of mail merge. Explain how they work together.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A form letter is the main document that contains the common text and placeholders. A data source is the organised list of recipients, with each row one person and each column a field. A merge field is the placeholder marker in the form letter that tells the computer where to insert a value. They work together because the word processor reads one row of the data source at a time and replaces each merge field in the form letter with the matching column value. For example, if the form letter has «Name» and the data source column is Name, then for the first row the letter could read "Dear Ananya" for a student in Mumbai, while the second row could produce "Dear Vikram" for a student in Delhi. This combination creates many personalised letters without retyping. The same data source can also be used for mailing labels, which shows how the three parts fit into a single mail merge project.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is it better to use merge fields instead of typing each recipient's name directly into the form letter?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Using merge fields keeps the main document flexible and reusable. The same template can generate hundreds of different letters. If you type a real name, the letter is fixed for that person only, and you must start again for the next person. Merge fields also reduce mistakes: a single correction in the data source will update all merged copies. When an invitation is going to parents in New Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai, and Kolkata, a well-designed template with fields like «Name» and «City» will change automatically for each row. Typing names directly is slow, error-prone, and does not allow sorting or filtering later. A strong answer should mention that the main document is a template and the merge fields are placeholders, which is the core idea of mail merge. The data source remains separate and can be edited or reused for other documents.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Mail merge is only useful for printing many form letters; it cannot be used for mailing labels." Do you agree? Justify your answer.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I do not fully agree with the statement. The first part is correct: mail merge is excellent for printing many form letters, because it combines one main document with a data source of names and addresses to create personalised letters. However, the second part is incorrect. Mail merge is also used for mailing labels. In this case, the main document is not a letter; it is a label template that shows the size and arrangement of one label. The data source still contains the names and addresses of the recipients, one row per person. When merged, the word processor places each name and address onto a separate label, arranging several labels on each sheet of paper. Therefore, mail merge is a flexible tool that handles both documents and labels. The statement is only half true. A balanced view recognises that the same two-part structure—main document plus data source—supports different outputs. So, mail merge is useful for both form letters and mailing labels, and neither task needs the user to type every address by hand.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Your school in Bengaluru is organising an inter-school quiz and wants to send individual letters to participants from different cities. The data source has the following fields: Name, Class, Address, City. The first three rows are: Arjun, 6A, 12 Gandhi Road, Bengaluru; Priya, 6B, 34 Park Street, Mysuru; Rahul, 6C, 77 Beach Road, Mangaluru. Show what the main document and one merged result would look like.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The main document, or form letter, is a single template with the common text and placeholders for the fields. It might look like this: "Dear «Name», We are happy to inform you that you have been selected to represent Class «Class» in the inter-school quiz to be held in Bengaluru. Your participation is important to us. Please report to the school auditorium on the given date. Yours sincerely, The Principal." When the merge is run, the placeholder «Name» is replaced by the value in the Name column, and «Class» by the value in the Class column. For Arjun's row, the merged letter would read, "Dear Arjun, We are happy to inform you that you have been selected to represent Class 6A in the inter-school quiz to be held in Bengaluru..." For Priya from Mysuru, the merged letter would say "Dear Priya... represent Class 6B...". The Address and City columns would be used on the mailing labels: one label would read "Priya, 34 Park Street, Mysuru, Karnataka" and another would read "Rahul, 77 Beach Road, Mangaluru, Karnataka". Thus, one template and one data source produce three different, personalised letters and three matching labels.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a mail merge project for a school in Chennai to invite parents to the annual day function. Describe the main document, the data source, the merge fields, and how you would print the letters and labels.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Suppose I am the head of St. Mary's Higher Secondary School in Chennai and need to invite one hundred and fifty parents to the annual day function. First, I would create the main document as a formal invitation letter. It would begin with the date, the school's address in Mylapore, Chennai, and a greeting. The greeting would contain a merge field, «Parent_Name», and the body would include a merge field for the child's class, «Student_Class». Next, I would build the data source as a table with the columns: Parent_Name, Student_Name, Student_Class, House_Number, Street, Area, City, and Pin_Code. Each row would hold the details of one parent, with areas such as T. Nagar, Adyar, Anna Nagar, and Velachery. I would link the main document to the data source and check the preview for a few parents to make sure the address is correct. Then I would complete the merge to create one hundred and fifty personalised letters. To send them, I would also merge the same data source with a mailing-label template that fits on A4 sheets of self-adhesive labels, so each envelope has one printed label. Finally, I would print the letters on A4 paper and the labels on label sheets, then post them. This project shows how one template and one data source can save hours of work and produce neat, professional invitations.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to identify and name the three core parts of a mail merge—the main document (form letter or label layout), the data source (a table of recipients organised as rows and columns), and the merge fields (placeholders)—and explain in their own words how the word processor matches each placeholder to a column value for every row. The student must be able to list the steps of a mail merge in the correct order: create the main document with placeholders, prepare the data source with clear column headings, link the two, preview, merge, and print, and apply this sequence to a real Class 6 scenario such as a school in Bengaluru inviting parents to an annual day function. The student must also be able to distinguish between a form letter output and a mailing-label output, justifying why the same data source can produce both, and must recognise and correct the common error of hard-coding a real name instead of using a merge field.

title: Internal hardware - motherboard, CPU, RAM, ROM, GPU
subject: cs
definition: Internal hardware means the physical parts that are fitted inside the computer case or cabinet and work together to make the machine run. Unlike the keyboard, mouse or monitor, which you can touch from the outside, these parts are hidden inside the system unit. The five internal hardware components you need to know for this chapter are the motherboard, the CPU, RAM, ROM and the GPU. The motherboard is the largest circuit board in the computer and is often called the backbone of the system. It is the main circuit board that connects all the other parts, allows them to communicate with one another and supplies power to them through the buses and circuits printed on it. The CPU, or Central Processing Unit, is the brain of the computer because it fetches, decodes and executes the instructions that make up every program. It is the processing device that performs arithmetic and logical operations on the data. RAM, or Random Access Memory, is the volatile temporary working memory of the computer. It holds the data and programs that are currently in use, but the moment the power is switched off everything stored in RAM disappears. ROM, or Read Only Memory, is the non-volatile permanent storage chip that keeps important instructions such as the boot program or BIOS even when the computer is not receiving power. Finally, the GPU, or Graphics Processing Unit, is the component that processes and renders images, video and anything you see on the screen. It is specially designed to handle a large number of similar calculations very quickly, which makes it ideal for graphics. The key distinction you must remember is that RAM is volatile while ROM is non-volatile, and the motherboard is the central connecting platform on which all these parts sit and through which they talk to one another.
eli5: A computer has hidden parts inside its body. The motherboard is like the backbone because everything connects to it. The CPU is like the brain because it thinks and decides. RAM is like short-term memory because it only remembers while the power is on. ROM is like long-term memory because it keeps important startup instructions even when the power is off. The GPU is like an artist because it makes the pictures and videos appear on the screen.

misconceptions.belief: Writing the name of the part without explaining what it does. CISCE examiners have noted that many candidates write only examples or give vague definitions without the actual meaning, which costs them marks. For example, saying the CPU is the brain is an example or an analogy, not a definition; the correct response must also explain that the CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions and processes data.

Confusing RAM with ROM. Just as some candidates in other topics have mixed up related ideas such as an encoder and a decoder or an OR gate with an AND gate, students often think RAM and ROM are the same kind of memory. RAM is volatile and temporary; it holds currently used data and loses it when the power is switched off. ROM is non-volatile and permanent; it stores boot instructions and keeps them even without power.

Believing that the GPU is only for playing games or that the CPU does all the work including screen pictures. The GPU is responsible for processing and rendering graphics and video. Every image displayed on the monitor, whether from a lesson, a video or a game, is produced with the help of the GPU. The CPU handles general processing and instructions, but the GPU is specially designed for the heavy parallel work that images need.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define each of the five internal hardware components: motherboard, CPU, RAM, ROM and GPU.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The motherboard is the main circuit board inside the computer. It is the central platform that connects all the internal hardware components and allows them to communicate with one another. It also supplies power and data paths through buses and circuits printed on the board. The CPU, or Central Processing Unit, is the brain of the computer. It fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and executes them, performing arithmetic and logical operations on data. RAM, or Random Access Memory, is the temporary working memory of the computer. It stores the data and programs that are currently active while the computer is switched on. It is volatile, which means that all its contents are lost as soon as the power supply is removed. ROM, or Read Only Memory, is the non-volatile permanent memory that stores important instructions such as the boot program. It retains its contents even when the computer is switched off. The GPU, or Graphics Processing Unit, is the component that handles the processing and rendering of images, video and anything that appears on the screen. Together these five parts form the core internal hardware of a computer.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is RAM called volatile memory while ROM is called non-volatile memory? Explain with the help of an example.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: RAM is called volatile memory because it needs a continuous supply of electrical power to hold the data stored in it. When the computer is running, RAM stores the operating system files, the applications that are open and the data you are working on, so that the CPU can access them very quickly. However, as soon as the power is switched off or the system is restarted, all the information in RAM disappears. This is why an unsaved document is lost when the computer suddenly shuts down. ROM is called non-volatile memory because it does not require power to keep its contents. The ROM chip contains permanent instructions, such as the boot instructions or the BIOS, that help the computer start up when it is turned on. These instructions are written at the time of manufacture and remain in the chip even when the computer is unplugged. The difference is therefore about whether the stored information survives without power. RAM is fast but temporary, while ROM is slower to change but permanent.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, A computer used only in a school office for typing and watching educational videos does not need a GPU because GPUs are only meant for gaming. Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true and partly false, so it needs a balanced evaluation. It is true that dedicated high-end GPUs are often chosen for gaming and advanced graphics because they can process millions of pixels very quickly. It is also true that a normal school office computer does not need the most expensive gaming GPU. However, the statement is false in saying that a computer does not need a GPU at all. Every image, icon, letter, diagram and video that appears on the screen must be processed and rendered by a graphics processing unit. Most school computers use an integrated GPU, which is a small graphics chip built into the motherboard or inside the CPU itself. This integrated GPU is enough for typing documents, viewing presentations and watching educational videos. Without any GPU, the monitor would not be able to show anything at all, because the CPU does not handle screen graphics by itself. Therefore, the correct view is that the school computer does not need a powerful dedicated gaming GPU, but it certainly needs some kind of GPU, either integrated or separate, to display everyday graphics and videos.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A computer lab in a school in Bengaluru has twenty desktop computers. After a sudden power cut, all the students lose the documents they were typing but the computers start normally when the power returns. Which component is responsible for the loss of unsaved work, and which component helps the computer start again? Justify your answer.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The loss of unsaved work is caused by the nature of RAM, the volatile temporary memory. While the students were typing, their documents were being held in RAM because the word processor needed fast access to the text while it was being edited. RAM requires power to keep its contents. When the power cut happened, the electrical supply to the RAM stopped, so all the temporary data, including the unsaved documents, disappeared. On the other hand, the computer was able to start normally when the power returned because of ROM, the non-volatile permanent memory. The ROM chip stores the boot instructions that tell the CPU how to begin the startup process, check the hardware and load the operating system. These instructions remain in the ROM even when there is no power, so the computer can begin working again from the same starting point. To avoid losing work in the future, the students should save their documents frequently to a non-volatile storage device such as the hard disk or solid-state drive.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you have to teach a Class 5 student about the five internal hardware components using a single human-body analogy. Design the analogy and explain each comparison clearly.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The human body is a useful analogy for the inside of a computer. The motherboard is like the human skeleton because it holds all the other parts together and gives the system its shape. Just as the spine and ribs connect to the arms, legs and organs, the motherboard connects the CPU, RAM, ROM, GPU and other parts. The CPU is like the brain because it makes decisions and controls the activities of the whole body. The brain reads messages from nerves, just as the CPU fetches and executes instructions from memory. RAM is like short-term memory, which helps you remember the questions on a worksheet while you are solving them, but it is forgotten once the class ends. ROM is like long-term memory or the habits written in your mind, such as remembering how to tie your shoelaces, which stays with you even when you are asleep. The GPU is like the eyes and the visual part of the brain because it processes pictures, colours and movement. Without the eyes, you cannot see the world; without the GPU, the computer cannot show graphics on the screen. This analogy helps a younger student understand how each hidden part has a special role inside the computer.

masteryCriteria: To master this node, the student must be able to give the full form and a correct functional definition of each of the five internal hardware components (motherboard, CPU, RAM, ROM and GPU) without confusing their roles, and must explain why the motherboard is called the backbone or central connecting platform rather than just another board inside the cabinet. The student must also be able to distinguish volatile from non-volatile memory by correctly assigning RAM to the volatile category and ROM to the non-volatile category, and justify the assignment using the behaviour of each when the power supply is removed. Finally, the student must be able to apply this knowledge to a real situation, such as explaining why unsaved work is lost after a power cut while the computer still boots again, naming the specific component responsible for each outcome.

title: Internet advantages and disadvantages
subject: cs
definition: The Internet is a global network of interconnected computers that allows people to share and access information, communicate with one another, enjoy entertainment, and use a wide range of online services. When we study the advantages and disadvantages of the Internet, we are not simply listing what it can do; we are learning to judge its effects on daily life, education, work, and society. On the positive side, the Internet acts like a vast digital library, giving students and adults instant access to information and educational resources. A student in Kolkata can read articles, watch tutorials, and download notes on any subject without visiting a physical library. Communication is another major advantage. Through email, social media, and instant messaging, people can talk to relatives, teachers, or friends across the world almost instantly. A student in Mumbai can email a project to a teacher in Delhi within seconds. Entertainment has also changed because of the Internet. Streaming services and online games provide music, movies, and interactive play at home. Finally, online services such as shopping and banking have made life more convenient. People can buy books, clothes, or groceries from websites and pay for them through net banking or digital wallets. However, the Internet also has serious disadvantages. Internet addiction and excessive screen time can harm health, reduce physical activity, and affect school performance. Privacy loss is another risk because websites and apps collect personal data such as names, addresses, locations, and browsing habits. For example, when a user clicks "accept all cookies" without reading, the site may track which pages are visited and show targeted advertisements. Cybercrime includes hacking, online fraud, phishing, and identity theft. Criminals may send fake emails pretending to be banks to steal passwords or money. Another disadvantage is exposure to inappropriate content, which can be disturbing or misleading for young users. The CISCE syllabus asks Class 7 students to understand these benefits and risks, to list at least three advantages and three disadvantages, and to explain at least one disadvantage with specific examples such as privacy loss through personal data collection.
eli5: The Internet is like a big magic box. It can help you learn new things, talk to faraway friends, watch fun videos, and buy things without going to a shop. But it can also be bad if you use it too much, if strangers take your private details, or if bad people try to cheat you online. So we must enjoy the good parts and be careful of the bad parts.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List three advantages and three disadvantages of the Internet.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The three major advantages of the Internet are access to information, communication, and entertainment. First, the Internet provides access to vast information and educational resources. A student can visit educational websites such as NCERT or online learning platforms to read about topics, watch videos, and download study materials. Second, the Internet enables communication through email, social media, and instant messaging. For example, a student in Delhi can send an email to a relative in Kerala within seconds without paying for a long-distance phone call. Third, the Internet offers entertainment through streaming services and online games. A user can listen to music, watch movies, or play educational quizzes at home. On the other hand, the three major disadvantages are Internet addiction and excessive screen time, privacy loss, and cybercrime. Internet addiction means spending too much time online, which can affect sleep, studies, and physical health. Privacy loss happens when websites and apps collect personal data such as name, age, location, and browsing habits. Cybercrime includes hacking, online fraud, and phishing, where criminals try to steal data or money. A good board answer presents these points clearly and in full sentences.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is it important to understand both the advantages and disadvantages of the Internet before using it regularly?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Understanding both sides is important because the Internet is a powerful tool that can help or harm depending on how it is used. If a student only thinks about the advantages, he or she may spend too much time online, share personal information carelessly, or trust every website and message. This can lead to problems such as Internet addiction, privacy loss, and cybercrime. On the other hand, if a student only thinks about the disadvantages, he or she may miss out on valuable learning, communication, and creative opportunities. By knowing both sides, a student can make balanced decisions. For example, when using a social media app, the student can enjoy connecting with friends while also being careful about what personal details to share. When shopping online, the student can enjoy convenience while also checking that the website is secure. The CISCE syllabus expects this kind of critical thinking, where students do not just memorise points but explain why the balance matters. This also connects to the earlier safety lessons from Class 6, where students learned to evaluate websites and browse safely.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "The Internet is only useful and has no real disadvantages because we can always be careful." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true but too simple. It is true that the Internet is very useful. It gives students access to huge amounts of information, helps people communicate across the world, and provides entertainment and online services such as shopping and banking. Being careful can reduce some risks, such as not clicking on unknown links, using strong passwords, and checking whether a website is trustworthy. However, the statement is not fully correct because the disadvantages are real and not only caused by careless users. First, Internet addiction and excessive screen time can happen even when a person is trying to be careful, because apps and games are designed to keep users engaged for a long time. Second, privacy loss often happens through data collection by websites and apps, sometimes without users fully understanding what they have agreed to. For example, when a user accepts cookies or gives an app permission to access contacts, personal data can be tracked and shared. Third, cybercrime such as hacking and phishing is carried out by criminals, and even careful users can sometimes be tricked by very realistic fake messages. Finally, exposure to inappropriate content can occur by accident through ads, links, or search results. Therefore, a better statement would be: "The Internet is very useful, but we must be aware of its real disadvantages and take steps to stay safe." The best answer gives a balanced view, accepting the benefits while also recognising the risks.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You want to join a new online quiz app that asks for your name, age, email, phone number, and permission to access your contacts and location. What three questions should you ask before signing up, and why do they matter?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Before signing up, you should ask three important questions. First, why does the quiz app need my phone number, contacts, and location? A quiz about general knowledge usually does not need to know where I live or who my friends are. If the app asks for more information than it really needs, it may be collecting data for advertising or sharing with other companies. This relates to the disadvantage of privacy loss. Second, what will the app do with my personal data? You should read the privacy policy or permission message. If it says the data may be shared with third parties, that is a warning sign. A good app collects only the information it needs and keeps it safe. Third, can I trust the app? You can check reviews, ask a teacher or parent, and see whether the website uses a secure connection, usually shown by a lock symbol in the address bar. This connects to what you learned in the Class 6 safety topic about evaluating websites. Asking these questions matters because they protect your privacy, reduce the risk of cybercrime, and help you decide whether the app is safe to use. A weak answer would simply say, "I will not give my details," without explaining why.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are designing a one-page poster for your school on "Safe and Smart Internet Use." Describe the four sections you would include and one example for each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: My poster would have four sections. The first section would be titled "Enjoy the Benefits" and would show how students can use the Internet for learning, communication, and entertainment. For example, I would draw a student using a laptop to research the freedom struggle on a trusted educational website and another student video-calling a grandparent in another city. The second section would be titled "Watch Your Time" and would warn against Internet addiction and excessive screen time. I would show a clock and a healthy routine, with a caption such as, "Take a break every 30 minutes and finish homework before playing games." The third section would be titled "Protect Your Privacy" and would explain privacy loss through personal data collection. I would draw a phone screen asking for app permissions, with a caption such as, "Think before you allow access to contacts or location. Read what you are sharing." The fourth section would be titled "Beware of Cybercrime" and would give tips on avoiding hacking, phishing, and online fraud. I would show an email that says "Click here to win a prize," with a caption such as, "Do not click unknown links. Ask a trusted adult." This poster would help students remember both the advantages and disadvantages of the Internet in a simple visual way.
