Let us design a table called "Class_7_Students" for the students of Class 7. The table will have four fields: Roll Number, Name, Class and Section, and Date of Birth. These fields are the columns of the table. The records, which are the rows, will represent three different students.

| Roll Number | Name | Class and Section | Date of Birth |
| 1 | Aarav Sharma | 7-A | 12 March 2012 |
| 2 | Diya Mehta | 7-A | 5 August 2013 |
| 3 | Ishaan Khan | 7-B | 19 January 2012 |

In this table, the first column, Roll Number, is a field that stores the unique roll number of each student. The second column, Name, is a field that stores the student's full name. The third column, Class and Section, is a field that tells us which class and section the student belongs to. The fourth column, Date of Birth, is a field that stores the student's date of birth. Each row, such as the row for Aarav Sharma or the row for Diya Mehta, is one complete record because it contains all the details about one student. This table is an example of a flat file database, which keeps all the records in a single table. A real school database may have many more fields, such as Address, Parent's Phone Number, and Blood Group, and may also contain other tables for teachers and examinations.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine that you have been asked to create a small database for a local public telephone directory in your town. Describe the table, the fields you would include, and explain how the structure would help a user find a number quickly.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
I would create a single table called "Telephone_Directory" because a small local directory usually fits into a flat file database. The fields, which would be the columns, would include Surname, First Name, House Number, Street or Locality, Town or City, and Phone Number. I might also add an optional field for Mobile Number if many people have more than one number. Each row in the table would be one record, representing one subscriber or one household. For example, one record might be: Surname: Nair, First Name: Priya, House Number: 42, Street: Gandhi Street, Town: Kochi, Phone Number: 0484-1234567.

The structure helps a user find a number quickly because the data is organised. If the records are sorted alphabetically by Surname, a user can go straight to the letter that the name begins with. If the table is on a computer, the user can also search the Surname field and the First Name field to find the record instantly. Because each field contains only one type of data, the directory is much easier to read than a long paragraph of names and numbers mixed together. This is exactly why a telephone directory is a real-world example of a database: it is an organised collection of related data, and its table-record-field structure makes searching fast and accurate.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to define a database in their own words as an organised collection of related data, and clearly distinguish between the three structural building blocks — table, record, and field — using a concrete example such as a school student register or a library catalogue. The student must also be able to identify at least two real-world examples of databases and name the main types (flat file and relational) with one distinguishing feature of each, without confusing the database itself with the software (DBMS) used to manage it.

title: DBMS and MS Access - components, creating a database
subject: cs
definition: A Database Management System, or DBMS, is a special kind of software that acts like an organized digital filing cabinet. It is used to create, manage, and manipulate databases so that large amounts of information can be stored, searched, updated, and shared without confusion. Think of a school that has thousands of students, books in a library, attendance records, and fee payments. If all of this is written on loose sheets of paper, it becomes very difficult to find anything quickly. A DBMS solves this problem by keeping everything in one structured place. Microsoft Access 2016 is an example of a DBMS. When you open Access, you are not just opening a single file; you are opening a complete environment where you can build a database, add tables, forms, queries, and reports. The first step is to start the program, which can be done from the Start menu or desktop shortcut. Once inside, the Access window has three important components that you must remember. The ribbon is the wide toolbar at the top that contains tabs such as File, Home, Create, and External Data. Each tab has groups of commands that help you perform different tasks. The navigation pane is the panel on the left side that lists all the objects in your database, such as tables, queries, forms, and reports. It works like a table of contents, allowing you to move from one object to another. The object window is the large area in the center where the actual work happens, for example, where you view a table or design a form. To create a new database, you choose Blank database, give it a meaningful name, and click Create. Access then saves the database as a file with the .accdb extension. It is important to understand that a database is not the same as a spreadsheet. In a spreadsheet such as MS Excel, data is usually stored in a flat grid of rows and columns, and the main focus is on calculations and charts. In a database, data is stored in related tables, and the focus is on managing and retrieving information accurately and efficiently. A DBMS therefore gives us tools to keep data organized, consistent, and easy to access.
eli5: A DBMS is a computer program that helps people make and take care of big boxes of information called databases. Microsoft Access is one such program. It has a top toolbar called the ribbon, a side list called the navigation pane, and a big work area called the object window. When you make a new database, you name it and save it as a file that ends with .accdb.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a DBMS and name any one example of a DBMS.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A Database Management System, commonly called a DBMS, is a type of software that is specially designed to create, manage, and manipulate databases. It provides tools that allow users to store data in an organized way, search for specific information quickly, update records when changes occur, and share information safely. A DBMS acts as an interface between the user and the actual data, so the user does not need to understand the complex technical details of how data is stored on the computer. One well-known example of a DBMS is Microsoft Access 2016. MS Access allows a user to create a new database, build tables to hold data, design forms for data entry, write queries to ask questions about the data, and produce reports. Because it provides all these database management functions, it is correctly described as a DBMS. Other examples of DBMS software include MySQL, Oracle, and LibreOffice Base, but for the Class 7 syllabus, the focus is on Microsoft Access 2016. The key point to remember in the exam is that a DBMS is software, not the data itself, and it is used for the full lifecycle of a database from creation to manipulation.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why the navigation pane in MS Access is useful when a database has many objects such as tables, queries, forms, and reports.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The navigation pane in Microsoft Access is a panel usually seen on the left side of the Access window. It is useful because it lists all the objects that exist in the database in one clear and organized place. When a database becomes large, it may contain many tables, several forms for entering data, different queries to search information, and reports to display summaries. Without the navigation pane, a user would find it difficult to remember which objects exist and where to find them. The navigation pane works like the table of contents of a book or the list of drawers in a filing cabinet. By clicking on an object in the navigation pane, the user can open that object in the object window and start working with it immediately. For example, if a teacher has a School Database with a Students table, a Marks table, and a Fees table, the navigation pane will show each of these tables clearly. The teacher can click the Students table to view or edit student records, then click the Fees table to check fee payments. Therefore, the navigation pane saves time, reduces confusion, and helps the user move quickly between different parts of the database. It is an essential part of the Access interface that makes database management practical and efficient.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A spreadsheet and a database are the same because both store data in rows and columns." Evaluate this statement with reasons.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true but mostly incorrect, because although spreadsheets and databases both use rows and columns to organize data, their purposes and structures are very different. In a spreadsheet such as MS Excel, data is usually kept in a single flat sheet where each row and column is part of one large grid. Spreadsheets are excellent for quick calculations, making charts, and handling small amounts of data that one person may need to update. However, in a spreadsheet, the same information often has to be repeated in many places, which can lead to mistakes and wasted space. A database, on the other hand, is managed by a DBMS and is designed to store large amounts of related information in separate tables. These tables can be connected to one another through relationships, so information does not need to be repeated. For example, in a school database, a student's name and address can be stored once in a Students table, and every book borrowed by that student can be stored in a Borrowed Books table without copying the student's name each time. This is called reducing redundancy. Another difference is that a spreadsheet focuses on calculations and formulas, while a database focuses on accurate storage, quick searching, and sharing information among many users. Therefore, the student's statement only catches the surface similarity of rows and columns and misses the deeper and more important differences. A fair evaluation is that the statement is too simple and does not correctly describe the real distinction between a spreadsheet and a database.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe the steps you would follow to create a new blank database in MS Access 2016.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To create a new blank database in Microsoft Access 2016, I would follow a clear set of steps. First, I would start the computer and open MS Access 2016 by clicking its icon from the Start menu or the desktop. When the program opens, the start screen appears with various templates and a Blank database option. I would select Blank database because I want to create an empty database without using a ready-made template. Next, a small dialog box appears asking for a file name. I should type a meaningful name, such as SchoolRecords.accdb, because the .accdb extension shows that it is an Access 2007 and later database file. I must also check the location where the file will be saved so that I can find it later. After typing the name and selecting the location, I would click the Create button. MS Access then creates and opens the new database. The screen shows the Access interface with the ribbon at the top, the navigation pane on the left, and the object window in the center. At this point, the database is empty, like a new filing cabinet with no drawers. The next step, which belongs to the next topic, would be to create tables to hold the actual data. In the exam, it is important to mention all three parts of the interface and to remember the .accdb extension, because these details show that you understand both the process and the structure of an Access database.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Your school principal wants a simple database to manage the school library. Create a plan for the database, including a name for the database and at least two tables you would include.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would create a database named SchoolLibrary.accdb to manage the school library. The first table would be called Books. It would contain fields such as BookID, Title, Author, Publisher, Subject, and NumberOfCopies. Each record in this table would represent one book available in the library. For example, one record might have the title "The Discovery of India" by Jawaharlal Nehru, in the subject of History, with three copies. The second table would be called Members, and it would contain fields such as MemberID, StudentName, Class, RollNumber, and ContactNumber. Each record would represent one student who is allowed to borrow books. For example, one record might belong to a student named Priya Sharma of Class 7A. In the future, a third table could be added to record which student has borrowed which book, but that is not required at this stage. The database would be created as a blank .accdb file in MS Access 2016. The Books and Members tables would then be created and shown in the navigation pane. The principal or librarian could open any table from the navigation pane and view it in the object window. This plan shows how a database can keep library information organized, prevent repeated writing of student or book details, and make searching easy through the DBMS features of MS Access.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to define a DBMS in a single clear sentence and correctly identify Microsoft Access 2016 as an example of a DBMS, distinguishing the software from the data it manages. The student must be able to name and describe the three main components of the Access interface (the ribbon, the navigation pane, and the object window) and state the function of each in their own words. The student must also be able to list the correct sequence of steps to create a new blank database in MS Access 2016, including choosing Blank database, giving a meaningful file name with the .accdb extension, selecting a save location, and clicking Create, and must be able to explain at least one clear difference between a spreadsheet and a database.

title: Access tables - data types, primary key, naming fields
subject: cs
definition:
A table in MS Access is a database object that stores information in rows and columns. Each horizontal row is a record, while each vertical column is a field. The table is the heart of the database, and every other object such as a query, form or report depends on it. To create a table, the user works in either the Datasheet View or the Design View. The Datasheet View is the simpler of the two; it looks like an Excel spreadsheet and allows the user to type data directly into cells. The Design View is the more professional approach, because the structure of the table is defined first by naming each field, selecting its data type and setting the primary key before any records are entered.

Field names are the labels given to columns so that anyone who opens the table understands what data is stored in each one. In MS Access there are specific rules for naming fields. A field name can be up to 64 characters long. It may contain letters, numbers and spaces, but it cannot contain a period, an exclamation mark, square brackets or an accent grave. It cannot begin with a blank space, and it cannot be the same as an Access reserved word such as Name, Date or Table. A strong field name like "RollNumber" or "DateOfAdmission" is clear and short, while a weak name like "Field1" or "Stuff" does not tell the reader what the data means.

Data types are the categories that tell MS Access what kind of data a field will hold. The main data types you must know are Text, Number, Date/Time, AutoNumber and others such as Currency, Yes/No, Memo and Hyperlink. Text is for words, names and addresses, such as a student's home address on M.G. Road in Bengaluru or a school in Lajpat Nagar, Delhi. Number is for values on which arithmetic may be performed, such as marks or quantities. Date/Time is for calendar values and clock values, such as a date of birth or the departure time of a train from Howrah station. AutoNumber is a special data type that automatically assigns a unique number to each record, like a serial number. The correct data type must be chosen at the design stage, because the wrong choice will prevent correct calculations and sorting later. For example, if marks are stored as Text, you cannot use SUM or AVERAGE on them, but if they are stored as Number, those functions can be used just as they were in Excel.

The primary key is a field or a group of fields that uniquely identifies each record in a table. It is like a unique ID card number that belongs to one person only. No two records can have the same value in the primary key field. If a table contains a field such as "RollNumber" and every student has a different roll number, that field can be set as the primary key. To set a primary key in MS Access, open the table in Design View, select the field and click the Primary Key button on the Design tab, or use the right-click menu. A small key symbol appears next to the chosen field. Finally, the database must be saved. Saving is like locking a filing cabinet so that the data is safe. In MS Access, the database file is saved with an .accdb or .mdb extension, and the table can also be saved by pressing Ctrl+S or choosing Save from the File menu.
eli5: A table in MS Access is like a notebook with rows and columns. A data type is a label that tells what kind of information goes in a column: Text for words, Number for counting and Date/Time for birthdays. A primary key is like a roll number that belongs to only one student. A field name is the heading at the top of a column. Saving the database is like closing and locking your notebook so the work is safe.

misconceptions.belief: Writing the steps without naming the data type or field name. CISCE examiners have observed that some candidates give direct answers without showing the required steps, such as drawing a logic gate without writing its name or writing an answer without explaining the choice. In Access, a weak answer might simply say, "I made a table," without naming the field and its data type. The correct response must always mention the field name and the data type you chose, and explain why that data type fits the data, just as you would not draw a symbol without naming it.

Confusing the Text and Number data types. Just as some candidates in other topics have mixed up related ideas such as XNOR and XOR, students often store numbers as Text and then wonder why they cannot use SUM or AVERAGE. If you store marks as Text, Access treats them as words, not values. The correct choice is Number for values you may add or average, and Text for words, phone numbers or postal codes that are not used in arithmetic.

Forgetting the primary key or choosing a field that can have duplicate values. Examiner comments show that students sometimes miss important parts of a process, such as the loop construct in an algorithm or the null condition in a linked list. In the same way, some students create a table but forget to set the primary key, or they set Name or Class as the primary key even though two students can have the same name or study in the same class. The correction is to choose a field that is guaranteed to be unique, such as a student roll number or an automatically generated AutoNumber, because the primary key must be a unique ID for each record.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the main steps for creating a table in MS Access, including the two views, rules for naming fields, data types and the primary key.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The first step is to open or create a database in MS Access, because a table is an object inside a database. Once the database is open, you can create a table using either the Datasheet View or the Design View. Datasheet View looks like a spreadsheet and lets you enter data directly, but it does not let you define the structure carefully. Design View is the better choice for a board answer because you first set the structure. In Design View, you enter the field name in the Field Name column, then choose a data type from the drop-down list, and you can add a description if needed. Field names can be up to 64 characters long and may contain letters, digits and spaces, but they cannot include a period, exclamation mark, square brackets or accent grave, and they cannot begin with a space. They also should not be Access reserved words such as Name or Date. The main data types are Text for words and labels, Number for arithmetic values, Date/Time for calendar values and times, and AutoNumber for automatically generated unique values. After defining the fields, you select the field that will be the primary key and click the Primary Key button on the Design tab. The primary key is the unique ID that identifies each record. Finally, you save the table and the database using Ctrl+S or the Save option.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A teacher asks you to design a table to store student information for a school in Mumbai. The fields are StudentName, DateOfBirth, MarksInScience, ContactNumber and Address. Which data type will you choose for each field, and why?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For StudentName I would choose the Text data type because it contains alphabets and spaces such as "Arjun Mehta" and we do not perform arithmetic on names. For DateOfBirth I would choose the Date/Time data type because it stores calendar values like 12 March 2010 and Access can later sort and filter dates correctly. For MarksInScience I would choose the Number data type because marks are numerical values on which we may want to calculate the total, average or rank; if we stored them as Text, we could not use SUM or AVERAGE, just as a formula in Excel would fail on text. For ContactNumber I would choose the Text data type because a phone number such as +91-9876543210 may contain the plus sign, dashes and leading zeros, and we never add or subtract phone numbers. For Address I would choose the Text data type because an address like "23, Marine Lines, Mumbai - 400020" contains letters, numbers, commas and a pin code but is not a value for calculation. This choice of data types makes the table structured and reliable.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate says, "Setting a primary key is not important because MS Access can still store records without one. We should only set a primary key if we have time at the end." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true in a very narrow sense but mostly false, so it needs a balanced evaluation. It is true that MS Access will allow you to create a table and store records even if you do not set a primary key. In that limited sense, the database will still open and accept data. However, the statement is false in its conclusion that a primary key is optional or a finishing touch. A primary key is the unique ID that identifies each record, and without it the database cannot guarantee that each record is different from every other record. Imagine a school in Kolkata where two students named "Priya Das" are admitted in the same year. If the table does not have a primary key such as a roll number or an automatically generated AutoNumber, the database cannot tell which Priya Das is which. This can lead to duplicate records and wrong information in reports, forms and any future queries. In addition, a primary key makes searching, sorting and creating relationships with other tables much faster and more reliable. Access itself may create a hidden AutoNumber field if you do not set one, but an exam answer must show that the student understands the purpose. Therefore, the correct view is that a primary key is not legally required for the table to open, but it is professionally essential and should be set during the design stage, not left as an afterthought.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You need to create a table in MS Access for a public library in Bengaluru to track borrowed books. The fields are BookID, BookTitle, Author, BorrowerName, DateBorrowed and NumberOfCopies. Design the table by naming the fields correctly, choosing data types and setting the primary key. Write your answer as if you are explaining the steps to a classmate.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First I would open the library database in MS Access. Then I would go to the Create tab and choose Table Design to open the Design View. In the first row I would type "BookID" in the Field Name column and set the Data Type to AutoNumber, because the library can give every book a unique number automatically. Then I would set BookID as the primary key by clicking the Primary Key button on the Design tab, so that no two books can share the same ID. In the next row I would add "BookTitle" with the Text data type, for example "Indian Art and Culture" or "A Brief History of Time". The "Author" field would also be Text, such as "Ruskin Bond" or "Stephen Hawking". The "BorrowerName" field would be Text, for example "Rohan Verma" from Bengaluru. The "DateBorrowed" field would be Date/Time, because it stores the calendar day when the book was taken, such as 15 August 2024. The "NumberOfCopies" field would be Number, because the librarian may later need to know the total copies or the copies remaining. I would not use the default names "Field1" or "Field2", and I would not include special characters in the field names. After defining all the fields, I would save the table by pressing Ctrl+S and give it a meaningful name such as "tblBorrowedBooks" or "Books". Finally, I would save the database file so that the work is not lost.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you have to design a database table for a railway reservation office in India. The table must store train numbers, train names, source station, destination station, departure date and the number of available seats. Create the table structure in MS Access, including field names, data types and the primary key, and explain why your design is good.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would name the table "TrainSchedule" and create it in Design View. The first field would be "TrainNumber" with the Text data type, because Indian train numbers such as 12627 or "Mangala Lakshadweep Express" are used for identification rather than arithmetic. However, since every train number must be unique, I would set TrainNumber as the primary key. The "TrainName" field would be Text, for example "Karnataka Express" or "Rajdhani Express". The "SourceStation" field would be Text, such as "Bengaluru City Junction" or "New Delhi". The "DestinationStation" field would also be Text, for example "Chennai Central" or "Mumbai CSMT". The "DepartureDate" field would be Date/Time, because it stores a calendar value like 5 October 2024, and Access can sort and filter journeys by date. The "AvailableSeats" field would be Number, because the reservation office may need to add, subtract or total the seats. I would use clear names without dots, exclamation marks or brackets, and I would save the table and the database before entering any records. This design is good because each field has a data type that matches the data it holds, the primary key ensures that no two trains have the same number, and the table can be used later to create queries, forms and reports for the railway office.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to create a table in MS Access Design View by entering meaningful field names that follow the naming rules (no periods, exclamation marks, square brackets, leading spaces or reserved words, and within 64 characters). The student must be able to assign the correct data type — Text, Number, Date/Time, AutoNumber, Currency or Yes/No — to each field by reasoning about whether the values will be used in arithmetic, and must justify the choice in a sentence. The student must be able to identify a unique field (such as RollNumber or an AutoNumber) and set it as the primary key in Design View using the Primary Key button, then save both the table and the database.

title: External hardware - input, output, and storage devices in detail
subject: cs
definition:
External hardware, also called external devices or peripherals, is the group of physical parts of a computer system that stay outside the main case and are connected to it by a cable or a wireless link. While the CPU, RAM, ROM, motherboard and GPU live inside the case and form the internal hardware, external hardware is every piece of equipment that we attach from the outside so that the user and the computer can talk to each other and so that files can be kept safe when the machine is switched off. In Class 7 we learn to classify these outside parts into three main groups: input devices, output devices and storage devices.

Input devices are the parts that carry data from the outside world into the computer. The keyboard lets us type letters, numbers and commands; the mouse controls the pointer on the screen and sends our clicks to the CPU; the scanner is like a photocopier because it converts a printed paper document into a digital image that the computer can store or edit; and the webcam is like a digital eye because it captures live video and sends it into the system for online classes, recordings or video calls.

Output devices are the parts that carry processed information from the computer out to the user. The monitor, or screen, shows the visual output from the graphics card; the printer takes the digital file and produces a hard copy on paper; and the projector receives a video signal from the computer and displays large images on a whiteboard, screen or wall so that many people can see them at once.

Storage devices are the parts that keep data for long periods and can be carried from one machine to another. The external hard disk drive, the USB flash drive and the CD or DVD are all examples of external storage, like a portable locker that holds your files even when the computer is switched off. This is different from the RAM inside the case, which only stores data temporarily while the computer is running. So external hardware is everything outside the case that helps us put data in, get results out, and keep those results safe.
eli5: External hardware is like the hands, eyes, school bag and voice of the computer. The keyboard, mouse, scanner and webcam are the eyes and hands, because they bring information in. The monitor, printer and projector are the voice and face, because they show or print the answers. The USB, CD and external hard disk are the school bag, because they carry files from place to place. All of these live outside the computer case and plug in to help the brain inside.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Name any four external hardware devices and classify each one as an input, output or storage device. Give one function for each device.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The keyboard is an input device because it lets the user type letters, numbers and commands into the computer, sending them to the CPU for processing. The mouse is also an input device because it controls the pointer on the screen and sends the position of the clicks into the system. The monitor is an output device because it receives the video signal from the graphics card and shows the visual output to the user. The USB flash drive is an external storage device because it saves files outside the computer and can be carried from one machine to another. In each case the key idea is the direction of data: the keyboard and mouse bring data in, the monitor shows data out, and the USB keeps data safe outside.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, “Since a scanner and a webcam both produce pictures, they must be output devices, just like a monitor.” Explain why this statement is wrong and how a scanner and a webcam are different from a monitor.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is wrong because the word “produce” is being used in two different ways. A scanner and a webcam do not produce pictures for us to see; they capture pictures from the outside world and send them into the computer. The scanner converts a paper document into a digital image file and the webcam captures live video and sends it to the CPU, so both are input devices. A monitor, on the other hand, receives the processed image from the graphics card and displays it for the user to see, so it is an output device. Therefore, a scanner and webcam put data into the computer, while a monitor takes data out. The student has mixed up the direction of information.

diagnosticQuestions.question: “A projector is an input device because it takes a video file from the computer and shows it to everyone; therefore we should classify it under input devices like the keyboard and mouse.” Evaluate this statement and give a balanced explanation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement contains a small truth but reaches the wrong conclusion. It is true that a projector is connected to the computer and “takes” a video signal from it, but the word “takes” only means that it receives the signal. In computer science, we classify a device by the direction of information relative to the CPU, not by the fact that it is connected. The keyboard and mouse send data from the user into the CPU, so they are input devices. The projector receives the already processed video from the graphics card and displays it for many people to see, so it is an output device. The student is right that the projector gets its content from the computer, but that does not make it an input device. Showing the result to the world is the job of output. A balanced view is that the projector is a bridge between the computer and the audience, but the data flow is from the case out to the users, which places it firmly in the output group.

diagnosticQuestions.question: In your school computer lab in Mumbai, your teacher asks you to set up a display for a science project. You have a computer, a webcam, a projector and a USB flash drive. Explain how you would use each device, and name one internal hardware that makes this activity possible.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, you would use the webcam as an input device to record a short video of your science experiment and send that video into the computer. Then you would save the video file on the USB flash drive, which is an external storage device, so that the file can be carried safely from your machine to the lab computer. When it is time to present, you would connect the projector to the computer as an output device so that the large video can be displayed on a screen for the whole class to see. The computer also needs a monitor to let you check the video before showing it. The internal hardware that makes this possible is the CPU, because it processes the video from the webcam and tells the graphics card to send the picture to the projector.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a small home study desk for a Class 7 student who attends online classes. Choose at least one input, one output, one storage and one internal hardware. Explain the data flow when the student types an answer and saves it.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The study desk has a keyboard and a webcam as input devices, a monitor as an output device, a USB flash drive as external storage, and the CPU and RAM as internal hardware. When the student types the answer to a question, the keyboard sends the text into the computer, where the CPU processes it with the help of the RAM. The monitor then displays the answer on the screen so that the student can check it. When the class ends, the student saves the answer on the USB flash drive, which keeps the file safe outside the computer. This setup works because the input devices bring information in, the internal components process it, the output device shows it, and the external storage carries it away.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to take any named external device (such as a keyboard, mouse, scanner, webcam, monitor, printer, projector, external hard disk, USB flash drive, CD or DVD) and correctly place it into one of three groups: input, output or storage, justifying the choice by stating the direction of data flow relative to the CPU. The student must also write one precise function sentence for each device that names what the device does and which internal component it works with, rather than giving a vague everyday description such as “a keyboard is for typing.” Finally, the student must distinguish external storage (USB, CD, external hard disk) from internal memory (RAM and ROM studied in c7_cs_001) by explaining that external storage keeps data when the power is off and can be carried between machines, while RAM is inside the case and loses its contents when the computer is switched off.

title: Access queries - creating and running simple queries
subject: cs
definition: A query in Microsoft Access is a question you ask the database so that it shows only those records from a table that satisfy a particular condition. It is one of the most powerful features of a database management system because it saves you from scrolling through hundreds of records to find what you need. To create a query, you open the Query Design View, select the table or tables that hold the data, and drag the fields you want to see into the query design grid. In the Criteria row of the grid, you type the condition that the records must match. For example, if you have a Students table in a Delhi school with fields such as RollNo, Name, Class, Section, Marks and City, a criterion such as >80 under the Marks field will ask Access to find every record where the marks are greater than 80. When you run the query, Access searches the table, applies the filter and displays the result, which is a smaller, more useful set of records. The result is not a new table; it is a dynamic view of the existing data, so if the table is edited later, the query result can change. Queries are different from simply opening a table and viewing all records, because a table view shows every record while a query shows only matching records. This is like the difference between looking at the entire attendance register and asking the class teacher for the names of all students who scored more than 80 in the last test. In addition to finding records, the chapter also covers editing tables: adding new records, modifying existing records and deleting records. Adding a record means typing a new row at the end of the table or in a form; modifying means opening an existing record and changing the value in one or more fields; deleting means selecting the row and removing it, which must be done carefully because the primary key keeps each record unique and the loss of data can affect related tables. Common conditions used in simple queries include comparison operators such as >, <, =, >=, <= and <>, and text criteria such as "Mumbai" or "A". When building a query, it is important to choose the correct field name and data type; a number comparison will not work properly on a text field, and a misspelled field name will give an error or no results. Learning to create, run and read a query is therefore an essential step in using a database to find information quickly and accurately.
eli5: A query is like asking your class register a question. Instead of reading every page, you ask, “Show me the students who scored more than 80 marks.” The computer looks through the table, picks the matching records and shows only those. You can also add or change records when needed. It is a fast, smart way to find exactly what you want.

misconceptions.belief: A query is the same as a filter or a sort. Some students think that because a query also shows fewer records, it is just like clicking the filter arrow in a table. The CISCE PPA data reminds us that examiners often see candidates confusing closely related ideas, for example “dual” and “complement” in earlier topics. In Access, the same kind of confusion appears: a filter is a quick, temporary way to hide records in a table view, while a query is a saved object that you can run again and can also use to show selected fields from one or more tables. A query stays in the database as a separate object, but a filter disappears when you close the table.
misconceptions.correction: remember that a query is a saved question with a name, and it can be opened and run whenever you need it.

misconceptions.belief: Running the query gives a new permanent table. Some students believe that after they click Run, a brand-new table is created and stored in the database. This is like the CISCE observation that candidates sometimes gave the direct answer without showing the steps or without understanding what the result represented. In Access, the result of a query is only a view of the data in the original table. If you delete or change records in the original table, the query result changes too.
misconceptions.correction: a query result is dynamic; it shows live data from the table, not a separate copy.

misconceptions.belief: Any value can be typed in the Criteria row the same way. Some students write a number condition without understanding the data type of the field, just as CISCE examiners noticed that some candidates used an OR gate instead of an AND gate or drew the wrong circuit because they did not match the correct inputs. In a query, if the Marks field is set to Number, you can write >80, but if it is set to Text, you must enclose the value in quotes. Writing >80 in a Text field will not work.
misconceptions.correction: always check the data type of the field before you type the condition.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is a query in Microsoft Access and what are the main steps to create a simple query?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A query is a question you ask a database so that it shows only the records that match a given condition. In Microsoft Access, the main steps are to open Query Design from the Create tab, add the table you want to use from the Show Table dialog, drag the fields you need into the query design grid, type the condition in the Criteria row under the correct field, and then click the Run button to see the result. For example, if a Students table has RollNo, Name, Class, Section and Marks, and you want to see all students who scored more than 80, you drag the RollNo, Name and Marks fields to the grid and type >80 under the Marks field. When you run the query, Access reads every record in the table, checks whether the value in the Marks field is greater than 80, and displays only the matching rows. The query therefore saves time and gives a focused answer instead of the whole table.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student created a query to find all students from Class 7-C but saw no records. What could have gone wrong, and how should the correct criterion be written?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: If a query returns no records even though the table contains students from Class 7-C, the most likely problem is an error in the condition. First, the student should check whether the field used in the query is really the Class field. If the condition was typed under the Section field by mistake, the result would be empty. Second, the spelling or case might be wrong, such as "7-c" or "VIIC" instead of "7-C". Third, the data type matters: if the Class field is a Text field, the value should usually be enclosed in double quotes, so the criterion should be "7-C". If the field is a Number field, the quotes would not be needed, but then "7-C" would not be valid at all. Fourth, the student might have added a condition in the wrong row; in Query Design, the Criteria row is for conditions that must be met, while the or row is for additional possibilities. The correct way is to drag the Class field into the grid, type "7-C" in the Criteria row under that field, and then click Run. If the table really has matching records, the query will now show them.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate says, “A query and a filter in Access do exactly the same thing, so it does not matter which one I use.” Do you agree? Give a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true but mostly incorrect, because a query and a filter can both show a smaller set of records, but they are not the same in purpose, power or durability. It is true that a filter and a query both help you see only the records you are interested in. For example, if you open a Students table and filter the Section column to show only Section A, the screen will look similar to the result of a query that asks for Section A students. However, the differences are important. A filter is temporary and works inside the table or form that is currently open. When you close the table, the filter disappears, and the next time you open the table you will see all the records again. A query, on the other hand, is a saved object in the database. It has its own name and can be opened, run and reused whenever you need it. Because a query can be based on more than one table and can show selected fields, it is more powerful than a simple filter. A query can also be used as the source for a form or a report later. Therefore, for a quick temporary look, a filter is fine, but for serious, repeated work in a database, a query is the better choice. The classmate is wrong because it does matter which one you use: a query is the proper tool for saving and reusing a search condition in a database.

diagnosticQuestions.question: In a Students table of a school in Chennai, the fields are RollNo, Name, Class, Section, Marks and City. Write a query condition to find all students who live in Chennai and scored more than 75 marks. Describe how you would create and run the query.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To find the required records, I would first open Query Design and add the Students table. Then I would drag the RollNo, Name, Class, Section, Marks and City fields into the query design grid, or at least the fields I want to see in the result, such as RollNo, Name, Marks and City. Under the City field in the Criteria row, I would type "Chennai" with the quotes because City is a Text field. Under the Marks field in the Criteria row, I would type >75 because Marks is a Number field. When both conditions are on the same Criteria row, Access treats them as an AND condition, meaning both must be true at the same time. After typing the conditions, I would click the Run button. The result would show only those students whose City is Chennai and whose Marks are greater than 75. If a student lives in Chennai but scored 70, that student would not appear. If a student scored 80 but lives in Mumbai, that student would also not appear. This is a practical example of how a query filters the table for specific data.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are the teacher in charge of a school library in Pune. Design a query that helps you find all Science books that cost less than Rs. 250. What fields would you include, what table would you use, and what conditions would you set?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would create a LibraryBooks table in Access with fields such as BookID, Title, Author, Publisher, Subject, Price and NumberOfCopies. The BookID field would be the primary key so that each book has a unique identity. To design the query, I would open Query Design, add the LibraryBooks table and select the fields BookID, Title, Author, Subject and Price for the result. Under the Subject field in the Criteria row, I would type "Science" in double quotes because Subject is a Text field. Under the Price field in the Criteria row, I would type <250 because Price is a Number field. Since both conditions are in the same row, Access will look for records where the Subject is Science AND the Price is less than 250. I would save the query with a clear name such as ScienceBooksUnder250. When I run it, the result will show only the Science books that are affordable for the library budget. If I later add a new Science book priced at Rs. 200, the next time I run the same query, the new book will appear automatically, because the query reads the live data from the table.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to open Query Design in Microsoft Access, add the correct table from the Show Table dialog, drag the required fields into the design grid, and type a valid condition in the Criteria row using the correct syntax for the field's data type (numbers without quotes, text inside double quotes). The student must also be able to run the query and explain that the result is a dynamic view of the matching records, not a new permanent table. In addition, the student must be able to combine two conditions on the same Criteria row (an AND condition) and describe how to add, modify and delete records in a table without damaging the primary key.

title: Cyber ethics capstone - responsible digital citizenship
subject: cs
definition:
Digital citizenship is the responsible and ethical way a person thinks, communicates, and behaves whenever they use computers, the internet, mobile phones, or any digital technology. A responsible digital citizen understands that being online is not a private world without rules; it is a shared public space where every action can affect others. Good digital citizenship is built on three main habits: communicating respectfully, protecting personal information, and respecting the privacy and rights of other people. This means that a student should not send hurtful messages, should not share passwords or personal details, and should not take or spread someone else’s photographs or messages without permission.

One of the most important ideas inside digital citizenship is intellectual property. Intellectual property is the result of human creativity and skill—stories, drawings, photographs, music, films, software, inventions, and designs. Because these creative works take time, effort, and talent, the law protects them. Copyright is the legal protection given to the creator of an original work. In India, the Copyright Act of 1957 (later amended) gives creators the exclusive right to make copies, distribute their work, adapt it, perform it, and display it in public. Copyright applies to books, poems, songs, paintings, photographs, computer programs, and even maps. The creator does not have to register the work for protection; as soon as the work is created in a fixed form, it is protected. This means that an image you find on a search engine, a song on a music app, or a paragraph from an NCERT textbook is usually protected by copyright even if no copyright symbol is shown.

Fair use is a limited exception to copyright that allows people to use small parts of a copyrighted work for specific purposes such as education, research, criticism, news reporting, or comment. In the classroom, fair use lets you quote a few lines from a poem, use a small picture in a project with proper credit, or show a short video clip to explain an idea. However, fair use has boundaries. It does not mean you can copy an entire movie, download a full song, or paste large sections of a website into your own project and call it your own. When fair use is ignored, the result is copyright infringement, which is the use of a copyrighted work without permission or legal excuse. Infringement can also mean plagiarism, which is passing off someone else’s work or ideas as your own without giving credit.

Giving credit means clearly naming the creator, the title of the work, and where it was found. This is not only honest but also shows respect. Responsible digital citizenship, therefore, is the combination of good internet safety and strong ethical behaviour: you keep yourself safe, you keep others safe, and you treat people’s creative work the same way you would want your own work to be treated.
eli5: Being a digital citizen is like being a good person on the internet. You talk nicely, keep your secrets safe, and do not steal or copy other people’s pictures, songs, or stories. If you use a small part of someone else’s work for school, say thank you by giving them credit. This keeps everyone happy and fair.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define digital citizenship, copyright, and fair use in your own words.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Digital citizenship is the responsible and ethical behaviour of a person who uses digital technology and the internet. It includes communicating respectfully with others, protecting personal information, respecting the privacy of other people, and following the rules that keep online spaces safe and fair. Copyright is the legal right that protects an original creative work from being copied, used, or distributed without the creator’s permission. This protection applies to books, poems, songs, pictures, photographs, films, and computer programs. In India, the Copyright Act of 1957 provides this protection, and the owner has the exclusive right to reproduce, publish, perform, and adapt the work. Fair use is a limited exception that allows someone to use a small part of a copyrighted work for purposes such as education, research, news reporting, criticism, or comment. For example, a student may quote a few lines from a poem or use a small image in a school project with proper credit. However, fair use does not allow copying the whole work or using it for commercial profit.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is it important to respect copyright when using pictures, music, or text you find online?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Respecting copyright is important because creative work takes time, skill, and effort to produce. When a photographer takes a picture, a musician records a song, or an author writes an article, they are creating something of value. Copyright gives them the legal right to control how that work is used and to receive recognition or payment for it. If we copy their work without permission or credit, we take away their right to benefit from their own creation. This is unfair to the creator and can also be illegal. Respecting copyright also encourages people to keep creating new and useful content for everyone. In a school setting, respecting copyright means using only small parts of works, choosing material carefully, and giving clear credit. It also helps students learn honesty and responsibility, which are important qualities of a good digital citizen.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, “I found an image on Google, so I can use it in my school project without asking because it is educational.” Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true but mostly incorrect, and it shows a misunderstanding of how copyright and fair use work. It is true that education is one of the purposes for which fair use may apply. A student may be allowed to use a small part of a copyrighted image in a school project if the use is limited, non-commercial, and properly credited. However, simply finding an image on a search engine does not mean it is free to use. Most images on Google are protected by copyright, and the owner’s rights still exist whether or not the image has a copyright symbol. Using the full image without permission, downloading it, and placing it in a project without giving credit would usually be considered copyright infringement, not fair use. The student also confuses the idea of educational purpose with unlimited permission. Fair use is not a free pass; it is a narrow exception with conditions. A correct approach would be to use a small portion of the image, or an image with a Creative Commons or public-domain licence, and always provide credit. Therefore, the statement is not fully correct because it ignores both the need for credit and the limits of fair use.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Your teacher asks you to prepare a short digital poster about famous Indian monuments. You find a photograph of the Taj Mahal and a paragraph from a travel website. Describe the correct steps you would take to use these materials ethically.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, I would decide what I really need from the photograph and the paragraph. For the photograph, I should not copy the full high-resolution image if a smaller version is enough. I would check the website for a copyright or licence statement. If the image is marked as free for educational use or Creative Commons, I would still give full credit. For the Taj Mahal image, I would write the caption like this: “Photograph of the Taj Mahal, by [name if known], from [website name], used for educational purpose under fair use.” For the paragraph from the travel website, I would not copy it word-for-word. Instead, I would read the information, close the website, and write the facts in my own words. If I want to use a short quotation, I would keep it brief, place it inside quotation marks, and mention the source. This way I avoid plagiarism and copyright infringement. I would also make a list of all sources at the bottom of my poster. These steps show that I am a responsible digital citizen who respects both copyright and the hard work of creators.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a “Digital Citizen Pledge” that a Class 7 student could sign and follow for one week. Include at least four promises that show responsible and ethical online behaviour.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: My Digital Citizen Pledge: “This week, I promise to be a responsible and respectful digital citizen. First, I will think before I post, comment, or share, making sure my words are kind and helpful, not hurtful. Second, I will protect my own privacy and the privacy of others by not sharing personal information, passwords, photographs, or messages without permission. Third, I will respect copyright and intellectual property by giving credit to creators and using only small parts of online content for schoolwork under fair use. Fourth, I will not copy and paste others’ work and claim it as my own; instead, I will write in my own words and list my sources. Fifth, I will ask a teacher or parent if I am unsure whether something is safe or fair to use. By following these promises, I will show that I am a responsible digital citizen who helps make the internet a better place for everyone.”

masteryCriteria: To master this node, the student must be able to clearly define digital citizenship, copyright, and fair use in their own words and distinguish fair use from copyright infringement and from plagiarism using at least one concrete example for each. The student must also be able to evaluate a real online situation (such as copying an image found on a search engine for a school project) and correctly judge whether it is fair use, infringement, or plagiarism, giving reasons that reference the size of the portion used, the purpose, and whether credit was given. Finally, the student must be able to apply these ideas by listing the correct ethical steps for using a photograph and a paragraph from a website in a school poster, and by creating a personal Digital Citizen Pledge that includes respectful communication, privacy protection, and respect for intellectual property.

title: Ports and connectors - USB, HDMI, VGA, Ethernet, audio
subject: cs
definition:
A port is a physical socket or opening on the body of a computer through which an external device can be plugged in. It is the visible end of a connector system, and it allows electrical signals, data, or sound to move between the computer and the outside world. Whenever you slide a USB flash drive into the side of a laptop, push an HDMI plug into the back of a monitor, or insert an Ethernet cable into a desktop, you are using a port.

The first important port is the Universal Serial Bus, or USB port. It is one of the most common ports found on Indian laptops, desktops, and even school projectors. A USB port can accept a small rectangular plug and it supports many devices. With a USB port, a student can connect a keyboard, a mouse, a printer, a web camera, or a USB flash drive. Because one port can serve so many different devices, it is often described as a universal socket. Data moves in both directions through a USB port, meaning files can be copied to a flash drive and also read from it.

The High-Definition Multimedia Interface, or HDMI port, is used to send high-quality video and audio together from the computer to a display. When a teacher connects a laptop to a smart television or an LCD monitor in a classroom in Delhi, Mumbai, or Bengaluru, the thin wide plug of an HDMI cable carries both the picture and the sound in one go. This makes it ideal for watching videos, showing presentations, and connecting projectors.

The Video Graphics Array, or VGA port, is an older type of video connector. It is usually blue and has fifteen small pins. A VGA cable can carry only analog video from the computer to the monitor. It does not carry sound, and it is not designed for the very sharp high-definition images that HDMI supports. Many older monitors in Indian computer labs and cyber cafes still have VGA ports, so it is useful to recognise the trapezoid-shaped plug.

The Ethernet port is the rectangular opening used to connect a computer to a wired network. An Ethernet cable, which looks like a thick telephone cable with a plastic clip, is plugged into this port to give the computer access to the internet through a local area network. In a school computer lab, each machine may have an Ethernet cable running to a switch or a router so that all computers can share the same network connection.

Finally, the audio port, often called the headphone jack, is a small round socket used for speakers, headphones, and microphones. It carries sound into or out of the computer. Some computers have separate green and pink sockets, while others combine them into one. It is the port that lets a student listen to recorded lessons, join online classes, or record voice notes.

In short, a port is a physical interface, a connector is the plug or cable that fits into it, and a device is the external piece of hardware that the connector joins to the computer. Understanding each port means knowing both its shape and the kind of device that belongs to it.
eli5: A port is a hole or socket on a computer where you plug things in. There are five common ports you should know. USB is the one for your keyboard, mouse, and pen drive. HDMI sends both picture and sound to a TV or monitor. VGA is an older port that only sends picture. Ethernet connects the computer to the internet with a cable. The audio port is where you plug your headphones or microphone.

misconceptions.belief:
"A port is the same as the user interface of an operating system."
CISCE examiners have observed that some candidates write a vague definition of an interface and sometimes confuse it with the user interface of the operating system. In the context of hardware, a port is a physical socket, not the menus or icons on the screen. The user interface is software that you see and click, whereas a port is metal, plastic, and wires that you can touch.

"If I can list the names, I do not need to explain the meaning or the device."
Examiners have pointed out that some candidates write only examples such as USB, HDMI, and VGA without giving a proper definition, and others give the definition but forget the examples. A complete answer must do both. For example, "A port is a physical interface for connecting external devices; the USB port connects a flash drive, the HDMI port connects a monitor, and the Ethernet port connects to a network."

"All ports carry both picture and sound."
Many students think that because HDMI carries video and audio, every video port must do the same. VGA only carries analog video and does not carry audio at all. Ethernet carries data packets, not the picture that appears on the screen. Each port has its own direction and type of signal, so you must match the right cable to the right port.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define the term "port" and name the five types of ports mentioned in this node.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A port is a physical socket or opening on the body of a computer that acts as an interface for connecting external devices. The five main types of ports studied at this level are the USB port, the HDMI port, the VGA port, the Ethernet port, and the audio port. A USB port is a rectangular socket that can accept a wide range of peripherals such as a keyboard, mouse, printer, and USB flash drive, and it supports two-way data transfer. An HDMI port is a wide, flat socket that carries both high-definition video and audio to a display such as a monitor or a television. A VGA port is a older trapezoid-shaped, usually blue, fifteen-pin connector used for analog video output to older monitors. An Ethernet port is a larger rectangular socket with a plastic clip that connects the computer to a wired local area network for internet access. An audio port is a small round socket, often called the headphone jack, that connects speakers, headphones, or microphones. In every case, the port is the physical meeting point between the computer and the device.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why will a monitor that uses an HDMI cable not work if you try to plug the cable into an Ethernet port?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The monitor will not work because the HDMI cable and the Ethernet cable carry completely different kinds of signals and have plugs of different shapes. An HDMI cable is designed to carry digital audio and video together from the computer to a display, and its plug is wide and flat. An Ethernet port is designed to carry network data packets between the computer and a router or switch, and its socket is a wider, rectangular opening that accepts an RJ45 plug with a plastic clip. The two plugs do not fit, the two ports do not expect the same signals, and the computer does not route video through the network port in this way. Even if the plug could be forced, the monitor would receive only data packets, not a video signal, so it would show no picture. This is why each port has a specific matching connector and a specific purpose.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A VGA port is the same as an HDMI port because both are used to connect a monitor." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is partly true but mostly misleading, so it should not be accepted as correct. It is true that both the VGA port and the HDMI port are used to send video from a computer to a monitor, so at a very simple level they serve the same general purpose. However, they are very different in the quality of the signal, the number of signals they carry, and the physical shape of the connector. VGA, which stands for Video Graphics Array, is an older analog video port. It has fifteen pins arranged in three rows and can send only video, not sound. Because it is analog, the picture can become less sharp, especially on larger monitors, and the image may look slightly faded or distorted. HDMI, which stands for High-Definition Multimedia Interface, is a newer digital port. It can send both high-definition video and audio through one cable, and it supports much sharper images and clearer sound. The plug is also different: the HDMI plug is wider and flatter, while the VGA plug is trapezoidal and has visible pins. Therefore, saying they are the same is incorrect. A more accurate statement would be, "Both VGA and HDMI ports are used to connect a monitor, but VGA is an older analog video-only port, while HDMI is a newer digital port that carries both high-definition video and audio."

diagnosticQuestions.question: In your school computer lab, a new student wants to connect a USB flash drive, a headphone for an online class, and an LCD monitor to a desktop computer. Identify the three ports the student should use and explain why each is correct.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student should use three different ports for the three different devices. First, the USB flash drive must be inserted into the USB port, which is the small rectangular socket found on the front or back of the computer. The USB port is correct because it is designed to read and write data from portable storage devices and can transfer files in both directions. Second, the headphone should be plugged into the audio port, which is a small round socket usually coloured green and often marked with a headphone symbol. This port is correct because it carries sound from the computer to the headphones, allowing the student to hear the online class clearly. Third, the LCD monitor should be connected to the HDMI port, which is a wide, flat digital socket. This is the correct choice because an LCD monitor needs a high-quality digital video signal, and the HDMI port can also carry the audio if the monitor has built-in speakers. If the monitor is older and only has a VGA port, then the student should use a VGA cable, but for a modern LCD monitor the HDMI port will give a much clearer picture. Using the correct port for each device ensures that the computer can send and receive the right kind of signal.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a small poster to label the back panel of a computer in your school lab. Each of the five ports must be shown with one correct device next to it.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A good poster should begin with a large heading, "Ports and Connectors of a Computer." The poster should show a simple drawing of the back panel of a desktop computer with clear labels. Next to the USB port, the student should draw a USB flash drive and also mention that a keyboard or mouse can be connected. Next to the HDMI port, the student should draw an LCD monitor or a smart television, and write that it carries both video and sound. Next to the VGA port, the student should draw an older CRT or LCD monitor and write that it carries only analog video. Next to the Ethernet port, the student should draw a cable running to a router or a switch and write that it gives internet access through a wired network. Next to the audio port, the student should draw a headphone and a microphone and write that it carries sound. Each label should include the full name of the port and at least one example of a device. The poster should be neat, use the correct shapes for the plugs, and avoid mixing up the ports. If the shapes are drawn carefully, the poster will also act as a memory aid for other students.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to define a port as a physical socket on the computer body and correctly name all five ports studied in this node (USB, HDMI, VGA, Ethernet, audio) without confusing them with one another. The student must be able to match each of the five ports to at least one correct external device and state the kind of signal it carries, for example that HDMI carries both high-definition video and audio while VGA carries only analog video. The student must also be able to explain, in one or two sentences, why a cable from one port cannot be used in a different port, referring to the shape of the plug and the type of signal it is designed to carry.

title: Binary number system and computer arithmetic
subject: cs
definition:
The binary number system is a method of writing numbers that uses only two digits, 0 and 1, because it is a base 2 system. In our normal decimal or base 10 system we have ten digits 0 through 9 and every place value is a power of 10: units, tens, hundreds, thousands and so on. In the binary system every place value is a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and so on. Each position in a binary number is called a bit, which is the smallest piece of information a computer can store. The word binary comes from the idea of two choices, just like a simple on or off switch.
Computers use binary because their electronic circuits are made of tiny switches called transistors. A transistor can be in one of only two clear states: it can be on or it can be off. It is much easier and more reliable for a machine to tell the difference between two strong signals, high voltage meaning 1 and low voltage meaning 0, than to measure many different levels. In a noisy circuit, a tiny extra voltage could change a 6 into a 7, but in a two state circuit a small change in voltage will still be read as either 0 or 1. That is why every number, letter, picture and sound inside a computer is finally stored as a long string of 0s and 1s.
Conversion from decimal to binary is done by the division by 2 method. We divide the decimal number by 2 again and again and collect the remainders. Each remainder is either 0 or 1. We stop when the quotient becomes zero, then write the remainders in reverse order, from the last remainder to the first. For example, 25 divided by 2 gives quotient 12 and remainder 1; 12 divided by 2 gives 6 with remainder 0; 6 divided by 2 gives 3 with remainder 0; 3 divided by 2 gives 1 with remainder 1; and 1 divided by 2 gives 0 with remainder 1. Reading the remainders from bottom to top gives 11001. This is the binary for 25. To convert back, we multiply each bit by its positional weight and add the results: 1 times 16 plus 1 times 8 plus 0 times 4 plus 0 times 2 plus 1 times 1 equals 25.
Binary addition and subtraction work in the same positional way as decimal arithmetic. In addition, 0 plus 0 is 0, 0 plus 1 is 1, 1 plus 0 is 1, and 1 plus 1 is 10, which means 0 in the current column and a carry of 1 to the next higher column. This is exactly like adding 5 and 5 in decimal and writing 0 with a carry of 1 to the tens place. For subtraction, when we need to take 1 from 0, we borrow 1 from the next left column. The borrowed 1 is worth 2 in the current column because each place is twice the one to its right. The key vocabulary is binary, decimal, bit, base 2, base 10, conversion, addition, subtraction, carry, 0 and 1.
eli5: Imagine you have a switch that can only be off or on. If off is 0 and on is 1, you can count by turning switches on and off. That is how computers use binary. It is like talking in a secret code made of only two sounds, and then doing normal adding and taking away, but carrying when you get two.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is the binary number system and why do computers use it?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The binary number system is a base 2 number system that uses only the two digits 0 and 1. Each position in a binary number is called a bit and its place value is a power of 2, such as 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Computers use binary because their electronic circuits are made of tiny switches, called transistors, that have only two clear states: on and off. It is easier, faster and more reliable for a machine to distinguish between a high voltage, which represents 1, and a low voltage, which represents 0, than to measure ten or more different voltage levels. If a circuit is noisy or a little voltage drifts, a multi level signal could easily be misread, but a two level signal will still be read correctly as either 0 or 1. Therefore, all data and instructions inside a computer are finally stored as long strings of 0s and 1s, and learning binary is the first step in understanding how a computer really counts.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Convert the decimal number 25 into binary using the division by 2 method. Show every step and then verify the answer by converting it back to decimal.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To convert 25 into binary, we repeatedly divide by 2 and keep the remainders. Step 1: 25 divided by 2 gives a quotient of 12 and a remainder of 1. Step 2: 12 divided by 2 gives a quotient of 6 and a remainder of 0. Step 3: 6 divided by 2 gives a quotient of 3 and a remainder of 0. Step 4: 3 divided by 2 gives a quotient of 1 and a remainder of 1. Step 5: 1 divided by 2 gives a quotient of 0 and a remainder of 1. We stop when the quotient is zero. We now have the remainders in the order 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, but the binary number must be written by reading them from last to first, which gives 11001. To verify, we convert 11001 back to decimal using the place values 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 from left to right. So 1 times 16 is 16, 1 times 8 is 8, 0 times 4 is 0, 0 times 2 is 0 and 1 times 1 is 1. Adding these gives 16 plus 8 plus 1, which equals 25. Since the reverse conversion gives the original number, our binary form is correct. This reverse check should always be done to catch ordering mistakes.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Binary numbers are a waste of space because the number 25 needs five digits in binary but only two in decimal. Decimal would be a better system for computers." Do you agree with this statement? Give a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is partly true in one narrow sense but not correct overall. It is true that binary numbers often need more digits than decimal numbers to represent the same value, because base 2 has fewer symbols and each place is worth less. For example, 25 in decimal is two digits, but in binary it is 11001, which is five digits. If we only cared about the number of digits on paper, then a larger base would look more compact. However, the argument ignores the physical reality of how a computer is built. A computer is an electronic machine made of billions of tiny switches. A switch can only be reliably on or off; it cannot easily hold ten different levels without expensive, slow and error prone circuitry. Using binary makes the hardware simple, cheap, fast and reliable, because each bit only has to distinguish between two states. It also makes arithmetic rules simple: there are only a few addition and subtraction facts to learn, and the carry and borrow rules are the same as in decimal. So even though binary strings are longer, the system is better for computers because it matches the two state nature of electronic signals. In short, compactness for humans is not as important as reliability and speed for machines. Therefore the statement is not a balanced view and should not be agreed with without these important qualifications.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Perform the following binary calculations. Show the carry or borrow at each step. (a) 101 + 110 (b) 1010 - 0111
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (a) For 101 plus 110, align the numbers by their rightmost bits. The right column is 1 plus 0, which gives 1 with no carry. The middle column is 0 plus 1, which gives 1 with no carry. The left column is 1 plus 1. Since 2 is not a binary digit, we write 0 in this column and carry 1 to the next new column on the left. The final answer is 1011. In decimal this is 5 plus 6 equals 11, so the binary answer 1011 is worth 8 plus 0 plus 2 plus 1, which is 11, confirming the result. (b) For 1010 minus 0111, we start from the right. The rightmost column is 0 minus 1, so we borrow 1 from the twos column. The 1 in the twos column becomes 0, and the rightmost 0 becomes 2. Now 2 minus 1 gives 1. The next column is now 0 minus 1, so we borrow from the fours column. The 1 in the fours column becomes 0, and the twos column, which had become 0, becomes 2. Now 2 minus 1 gives 1. The next column is now 0 minus 1, so we borrow from the eights column. The 1 in the eights column becomes 0, and the fours column becomes 2. Now 2 minus 1 gives 1. The leftmost column is now 0 minus 0, which is 0. The final answer is 0011, or simply 11. In decimal this is 10 minus 7 equals 3, and binary 11 is worth 2 plus 1, which is 3, so the answer is correct.
